1802_heap_implementation.ipynb · cells 5–23
Enqueue adds a new entry at the next open leaf position so the complete shape is preserved. All old parent-child relations are unchanged. Only the new entry's path toward the root can violate min-heap order. Bubble-up compares with the parent and swaps while the child is smaller. Moving upward strictly decreases its index, so repair terminates.

Start with [2, 5, 4] and enqueue 1. Appending produces [2, 5, 4, 1]. Comparing 1 with parent 5 gives [2, 1, 4, 5]. Comparing that 1 with root 2 gives [1, 2, 4, 5]. Do not sort the whole array; that would enforce a stronger and more expensive condition than the operation needs.

Dequeue first saves the root result. Move the last live entry to the root and reduce Count. The only possible ordering defects now lie downward from that replacement. Choose the smaller existing child before swapping; exchanging with an arbitrary child can leave a smaller sibling above a larger parent relation.

| Heap after removing 1 | Inspection | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [5, 2, 4] | Children 2 and 4 | Choose 2 |
| [2, 5, 4] | 5 has no child | Stop |

A singleton removal needs no child access after Count becomes zero. An empty removal must follow the stated failure policy without first reading position zero. Also clear unused reference slots when the implementation owns a backing array and should release references to removed objects. Reducing Count hides a slot from the abstract sequence, but it does not itself erase a stored reference.

The height of a complete heap is logarithmic in its live size, which bounds the number of repair levels. Array growth can add copying to an enqueue, so qualify an operation's cost rather than ignoring representation maintenance. Bulk building by bottom-up repair is a related algorithm with a different aggrega

        items.Add(item);
        int child = items.Count - 1;
        while (child > 0)
        {
            int parent = (child - 1) / 2;
            if (comparer.Compare(items[parent], items[child]) <= 0) break;
            (items[parent], items[child]) = (items[child], items[parent]);
            child = parent;
        }
    }

    {
        if (items.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Heap is empty.");
        return items[0];
    }

    public T Dequeue()
    {
        T minimum = Peek();
        T last = items[^1];
        items.RemoveAt(items.Count - 1);
        if (items.Count == 0) return minimum;
        items[0] = last;
        int parent = 0;

            int right = left + 1;

## Separate Chaining and Complete Operations




```{index} separate chaining; collision; hash-table update
```

A collision occurs when different keys choose the same bucket. **Separate chaining** stores a collection of entries at each bucket. A lookup computes the bucket and compares keys within that chain. An update must search the chain before appending; otherwise it can create duplicate keys. Removal must preserve the other colliding entries.

With four buckets, IDs 101, 105, and 109 all choose bucket one. To find 109, inspect 101, then 105, then 109. To report that 113 is absent, inspect the entire chain. A successful lookup may stop early; an unsuccessful one must establish that no matching key exists.

The complete `TicketMap` stores integer ticket IDs and string owners. `Put` returns true for a new key and false for replacement. `Remove` reports whether membership changed. `TryGetValue` returns false on absence; ignore its output value in that case.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

var owners = new TicketMap();
owners.Put(101, "Amina"); owners.Put(105, "Diego"); owners.Put(109, "Mina");
Console.WriteLine("before=" + owners.DescribeBuckets());
Console.WriteLine($"replacement inserted={owners.Put(105, "Lee")}, count={owners.Count}");
owners.Put(113, "Noor");
Console.WriteLine($"after growth: buckets={owners.BucketCount}, count={owners.Count}");
Console.WriteLine(owners.DescribeBuckets());
owners.Remove(101);
Console.WriteLine($"109 survives={owners.TryGetValue(109, out string owner)}, owner={owner}");
Console.WriteLine($"missing={owners.TryGetValue(101, out _)}, count={owners.Count}");

## Dispatch from Two Consistent Indexes




```{index} priority queue; dictionary; consistency
```

The service desk keeps active records in a dictionary and pending IDs in a priority queue. A simple cancellation policy removes the active record while leaving its old queue entry in place. On dequeue, skip IDs no longer active. This is **lazy deletion**: defer physical cleanup until an obsolete entry reaches the front.

This example allows each ID to be registered once during the batch. If an ID can be reused or reprioritized, an old entry may still refer to an active ID. Use a generation/version field and verify it on dequeue, or implement an indexed heap with explicit updates. Presence alone would then be insufficient.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

var active = new Dictionary<string, string>();
var registered = new HashSet<string>();
var pending = new PriorityQueue<string, (int Urgency, long Arrival)>();
long arrival = 0;
bool Register(string id, string owner, int urgency)
{
    if (!registered.Add(id)) return false;
    active.Add(id, owner);
    pending.Enqueue(id, (urgency, arrival++));
    return true;
}
Register("T-100", "Amina", 2);
Register("T-101", "Diego", 0);
Register("T-102", "Mina", 2);
Console.WriteLine($"duplicate accepted={Register("T-100", "Other", 0)}");
active.Remove("T-101");
while (pending.TryDequeue(out string? id, out _))
{
    if (!active.TryGetValue(id, out string? owner)) { Console.WriteLine($"skip cancelled {id}"); continue; }
    active.Remove(id);
    Console.WriteLine($"serve {id}: {owner}");
}
Console.WriteLine($"active={active.Count}, pending={pending.Count}");

public class TicketMap
{
    private List<Entry>[] buckets = CreateBuckets(4);
    public int Count { get; private set; }
    public int BucketCount => buckets.Length;
    public double LoadFactor => (double)Count / buckets.Length;

    public bool Put(int id, string owner)
    {
        int index = Bucket(id, buckets.Length);
        for (int i = 0; i < buckets[index].Count; i++)
        {
            if (buckets[index][i].Id == id)
            {
                buckets[index][i] = new Entry(id, owner);
                return false;
            }
        }
        if ((Count + 1.0) / buckets.Length > 0.75)
        {
            Grow();
            index = Bucket(id, buckets.Length);
        }
        buckets[index].Add(new Entry(id, owner));
        Count++;
        return true;
    }

    public bool TryGetValue(int id, out string owner)
    {
        foreach (Entry entry in buckets[Bucket(id, buckets.Length)])
        {
            if (entry.Id == id) { owner = entry.Owner; return true; }
        }
        owner = default!;
        return false;
    }

    public bool Remove(int id)
    {
        List<Entry> chain = buckets[Bucket(id, buckets.Length)];
        for (int i = 0; i < chain.Count; i++)
        {
            if (chain[i].Id != id) continue;
            chain.RemoveAt(i);
            Count--;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

2003_graph_traversal.ipynb · cells 5–24
A facilities graph answers which rooms can be reached and how many doorways a shortest route uses. Every edge in this lesson contributes one hop. The queue is not a list of completed rooms; it holds discovered rooms whose neighbors still need examination. This is the queue policy from Chapter 15 applied to the graph model from the preceding sections.

Use directed edges A→B, A→C, B→D and C→D, plus an isolated E. Neighbor order is written explicitly. Begin with A discovered, distance zero and no predecessor. The small program exposes the traversal core; the full graph class and validation examples remain below.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
var next = new Dictionary<string, string[]>
{
    ["A"] = new[] { "B", "C" }, ["B"] = new[] { "D" },
    ["C"] = new[] { "D" }, ["D"] = Array.Empty<string>(), ["E"] = Array.Empty<string>()
};
var distance = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["A"] = 0 };
var previous = new Dictionary<string, string>();
var waiting = new Queue<string>();
waiting.Enqueue("A");
while (waiting.Count > 0)
{
    string current = waiting.Dequeue();
    foreach (string neighbor in next[current])
    {
        if (distance.ContainsKey(neighbor)) continue;
        distance[neighbor] = distance[current] + 1;
        previous[neighbor] = current;
        waiting.Enqueue(neighbor);
        Console.WriteLine($"Discover {neighbor}: distance {distance[neighbor]}, from {current}");
    }
}
Console.WriteLine($"D hops: {distance["D"]}; E reached: {distance.ContainsKey("E")}");

2004_depth_first_components.ipynb · cells 5–39
Depth-first search is ordinary recursive control flow applied to a graph. A call must remember which neighbor it is considering while a child explores its branch. This connects the suspended calls in Chapter 17 to Chapter 20's cycles and shared destinations. A discovered set avoids repeated discovery; it does not erase the caller's unfinished neighbor loop.

Use the undirected diamond A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, and isolated E. In each array below, the listed neighbor order determines the trace. Watch enter and exit events separately. A vertex is entered once; returning from a child resumes an already active parent rather than entering that parent again.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
var neighbors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>
{
    ["A"] = new[] { "B", "C" }, ["B"] = new[] { "A", "D" },
    ["C"] = new[] { "A", "D" }, ["D"] = new[] { "B", "C" }, ["E"] = Array.Empty<string>()
};
var seen = new HashSet<string>();
void Visit(string room, int depth)
{
    seen.Add(room);
    Console.WriteLine($"Enter {room} depth {depth}");
    foreach (string next in neighbors[room])
        if (!seen.Contains(next)) Visit(next, depth + 1);
    Console.WriteLine($"Exit {room}");
}
Visit("A", 0);
Console.WriteLine($"E reached: {seen.Contains("E")}");


C is first entered from D, not from A. A's neighbor loop has not finished, but C is already discovered by the time A resumes and considers it. C's DFS depth is three although A has a direct edge to C. A first DFS route therefore need not minimize hops.

| Event | Active frames from oldest to newest | What waits in the caller? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enter A | A | A will consider C after B returns |
| Enter B | A,B | B will finish after D returns |
| Enter D | A,B,D | D will finish after C returns |
| Enter C | A,B,D,C | C fi

1304_iterators.ipynb · cells 10–25
The pattern `IEnumerable<T> Produce(...) { ... yield return value; ... }` defines an iterator. Yielding supplies one element and suspends that enumeration's progress until the consumer requests another. An ordinary return from a value-returning method finishes that call; yield return participates in a sequence of resumptions. Explain this distinction before treating yield as abbreviated list construction.

Laziness changes when work and failures occur. Obtaining an enumerable need not run every statement that will produce its values. If the consumer stops after two elements, later elements may never be computed. An expensive calculation inside an iterator is not paid simply because an enumerable variable has been declared, but repeated enumerations may repeat that work. Do not promise caching unless the implementation explicitly provides it.

The producer also needs a mutation policy. An enumeration over shared mutable storage can be affected by changes made after the enumerable is obtained. Library collections may detect invalid mutation during enumeration; custom types must state their own behavior. Returning IEnumerable<T> does not automatically create a snapshot or make private storage immutable.

Guided prediction: an iterator announces each produced number and yields 2, 4, 6. A caller breaks after consuming 4. Which production announcements should appear? Then run a second enumeration and ask whether it starts with a fresh progress state. Use the existing runnable iterator examples to check your prediction and distinguish fresh enumeration from continuing one enumerator.

class UndoLog<T>
{
    private readonly List<T> items = new List<T>();
    public int Count { get { return items.Count; } }
    public void Push(T value) { items.Add(value); }
    public bool TryPop(out T value)
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) { value = default!; return false; }
        int last = items.Count - 1;
        value = items[last]; items.RemoveAt(last); return true;
    }
    public T[] Snapshot() { return items.ToArray(); }
}

    public bool TryPop(out T value)
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) { value = default!; return false; }
        int last = items.Count - 1;
        value = items[last]; items.RemoveAt(last); return true;
    }

}

1105_value_record_types.ipynb · cells 5–20
An order line refers to a product, but a point on a warehouse plan may simply consist of two coordinates. Before choosing class, struct or record, ask what one value means, whether it can change, and what callers should expect when it is assigned or compared. The forms below solve related modeling problems, but none is an automatic replacement for every ordinary class.

Assigning a struct variable copies its value. That copy contains the values of its fields; if one of those fields is itself a reference, both copies can still refer to a shared object. Value-type copying is not a promise that every reachable object has been recursively duplicated. A record class is a reference type with compiler-supported value-oriented equality and copying syntax; assigning its variable still copies a reference. A record struct combines record features with value-type copying.

| Choice | Assignment behavior | Design question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary class instance | Another reference to the same object | Is identity and a controlled lifecycle important? |
| Struct value | Copy of its fields | Is this a small coherent value with a meaningful default? |
| Record class instance | Another reference on assignment | Does value-oriented equality fit a reference-based data model? |
| Record struct value | Copy of its fields | Do both value copying and record conveniences fit? |

For positional records, the parameter list declares the data used by generated members. A with expression creates a copied result with selected changes; it is not a deep-cloning operator. If a copied record contains a mutable list, later changes to that list may be visible through both record objects. Keep this distinction beside the syntax so that a concise expression does not suggest stronger isolation than i

static bool TryParseStudent(string line, out string name, out int score, out string major)
{
    name  = "";
    major = "";
    score = 0;

    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line)) return false;

    string[] parts = line.Split(',');
    if (parts.Length != 3) return false;

    name  = parts[0].Trim();
    major = parts[2].Trim();

    return int.TryParse(parts[1].Trim(), out score);
}

1602_basic_sorting.ipynb · cells 5–50
Sorting has at least two obligations: output order must satisfy the chosen comparison policy, and output must contain exactly the input occurrences. Producing 1, 2, 3 from input 3, 1, 2 looks right, but so would returning a fixed 1, 2, 3 regardless of input. Tests need to challenge preservation as well as ordering.

Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix. The next item is saved outside the moving region. Larger prefix items shift one position right until the saved item fits. Assigning the saved item back closes the hole. This explains why writing over the next item before saving it can lose data even though the remaining positions appear ordered.

| Input prefix and next item | Work | Resulting prefix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [4], next 2 | Save 2, shift 4, insert 2 | [2, 4] |
| [2, 4], next 3 | Save 3, shift 4, insert 3 | [2, 3, 4] |

Before each outer iteration, the processed prefix is sorted and is a permutation of the corresponding original prefix. The inner shifts preserve all saved occurrences while opening the correct position. When the prefix includes the full array, both obligations hold. This is a reasoning structure, not simply a description of what a successful example happened to print.

Equal keys reveal another contract. If the inner loop moves only items strictly greater than the saved key, equal-key items retain their previous relative order. This is stability. Moving equal items as well can change that order. Use labeled records, such as two invoices with the same total but different IDs, to see the distinction; identical integer values cannot show which occurrence moved.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

0505_summary.ipynb · cells 5–21
An invoice caller repeats price-times-quantity arithmetic in several places. Extracting LineTotal can give that calculation one name, but a safe refactoring needs more than moving those characters into braces. First record the existing accepted inputs, numerical outputs, formatting and mutation behavior. Then choose the new method's inputs/result so that callers can express the same work without depending on its internal temporary variables.

For price 12 and quantity three, independently calculate 36 before running either version. A fixed packing charge of four makes the order total 40. Keep these two contracts distinct: LineTotal returns 36; OrderTotal returns 40. If the extracted line calculation starts adding packing as well, a caller that already adds packing can charge it twice even though both helper methods contain plausible arithmetic.

| Refactoring stage | Evidence to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Before extraction | Expected amount and current observable output |
| After extracting LineTotal | Same line amount for ordinary and zero inputs |
| After composing OrderTotal | Exactly one application of the fixed charge |
| After formatting a report | Same numerical meaning; display policy stays explicit |

A useful composition passes returned values between helpers. It does not make each helper prompt independently for the same data. If CalculateTotal reads a second quantity while the caller formats the first, the report can display one order and charge another. Keep interaction in the caller and pass the accepted values into calculation helpers.

{

0101_cs_ideas.ipynb · cells 34–34
A **statement** instructs the program to do something. In the example, statements execute in order from top to bottom. This is **sequential execution**. A later instruction does not change output already printed by an earlier one.

Other programming constructs select between actions or repeat them. Chapters 3 and 5 teach decisions and iteration. You do not need those constructs to write your first useful output program.

A **syntax error** violates the language's rules and can prevent compilation. A **logical error** occurs when instructions run but produce an unintended result. Printing an outdated appointment time may compile successfully while still misleading a customer. Compilation is one check, not proof that the program is correct. Chapter 6 develops debugging and testing.

**Practice:** Change the two messages in the cell to describe a fictional bookstore appointment. Predict both lines before running. Reverse the statement order and explain the result. Use fictional information throughout your exercises.

0702_twodim.ipynb · cells 14–16
All rows must be the same length when using this notation.

Often two dimensional arrays, like one dimensional arrays, are processed
in loops. Multiple dimension arrays are often processed in nested loops.
We could print out this table using columns 5 spaces wide with the code:

```csharp
         for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) {
               Console.Write("{0, 5}", table[r, c]);
            }
            Console.WriteLine();
         }
```

If we wanted to make a more general function out of that code,
we have a problem: the number of rows and columns were literal values
that we knew. We need something more general. For one dimensional
arrays we had the Length property, but now there are more than one
lengths!

The following standalone example illustrates the syntax needed:


int[, ] table = { {2, 4,  7, 55},
                  {3, 1,  8, 10},
                  {6, 0, 49, 12} };
Console.WriteLine(table.Length);        // get the total number of elements
Console.WriteLine(table.GetLength(0));  // get number of elements in the 1st dimension (rows)
Console.WriteLine(table.GetLength(1));  // get number of elements in the 2nd dimension (columns)
foreach (int n in table) {
   Console.Write($"{n} ");
}


Note:

- The meaning for the Length property,
  is now the *total* number of elements, (3)(4) = 12.
- The separate method `GetLength` is needed to find the number of rows and columns.
  The entries in the list of array indices in the multi-dimensional array notation
  are themselves indexed to provide the `GetLength` method parameter for each dimension.
  In this case index 0 gives the row length (left index of the array notation),
  and 1 gives the column length (right index of the array notation).
- The `foreach` statement behavior i

using System;

string[] branches = { "Downtown", "Airport", "Campus" };

    { 1500, 1450, 1400, 1350,  900,  600,  700 }
};

int rows = sales.GetLength(0);
int cols = sales.GetLength(1);

Console.WriteLine("Branch totals:");
int bestBranch = 0;
int bestTotal = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
{
    int branchTotal = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
    {
        branchTotal += sales[r, c];
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"  {branches[r]}: {branchTotal}");
    if (branchTotal > bestTotal)
    {
        bestTotal = branchTotal;
        bestBranch = r;
    }
}

Console.WriteLine("Day totals:");
for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
{
    int dayTotal = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    {
        dayTotal += sales[r, c];
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"  {days[c]}: {dayTotal}");
}

Console.WriteLine($"Top branch: {branches[bestBranch]} ({bestTotal})");

C01-O1 · supported

Describe hardware, software, data, and the input-process-output model.

IPO is applied to a report, not merely named.

Explanation

0101_cs_ideas.ipynb · cells 5–11
```{index} hardware; software; bit; byte; data representation
```


**Hardware** is the physical equipment, including a processor, memory, storage, and input/output devices. **Software** supplies instructions. An operating system manages hardware and provides services to applications, such as reading a file or displaying text.

Computers encode data as bits, each with two possible values, conventionally written `0` and `1`. Eight bits form a byte. An encoding determines what a sequence of bits means: a number, text, an image, or another kind of data. The same bit pattern can mean different things under different encodings. You will choose C# data types in Chapter 2; a type constrains the values and operations your program uses.

For an appointment service, a date is data, a reminder application is software, and the computer that runs it is hardware. A correctly functioning computer can still execute instructions that send the wrong date. Hardware operation and application correctness are different questions.

**Check Your Understanding:** Identify one input device, one output device, and one stored data item used by the appointment service.

One possible answer is a **keyboard** for entering appointment details, a **screen** for displaying a reminder, and the **scheduled appointment date and time** as a stored data item. Other suitable devices are possible; distinguish physical devices from the data they receive or display.
```

## Describe Input, Processing, and Output

Worked example/case/trace

0101_cs_ideas.ipynb · cells 10–11
The **input-process-output (IPO) model** describes a task through the information it receives, the work it performs, and the result it produces.

| Stage | Appointment reminder example |
| --- | --- |
| Input | Appointment time, contact destination, and permission to send a reminder. |
| Processing | Select the appointment that needs a reminder and compose an appropriate message. |
| Output | A message telling the recipient when to arrive. |

The model separates a problem from its implementation. A receptionist and a computer can follow the same reminder procedure using different tools. Input can also come from a file or another system rather than a keyboard; output can be stored rather than displayed.

Specify an observable result: “A reminder displays the correct appointment time without including the reason for the visit.” That statement supports both a correctness check and a privacy decision. “Make a good reminder app” does not say what to test.

**Check Your Understanding:** Describe input, processing, and output for a bookstore's daily sales summary. Name a result the manager could check.


```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
**Input:** the day's sales records, including item quantities and selling prices. **Processing:** calculate each sale amount and add the amounts for that day. **Output:** a report showing the daily sales total. The manager could check that a day with two sales of $10 and $15 reports $25. A fuller report would need explicit rules for returns, discounts, and taxes.
```

0101_cs_ideas.ipynb · cells 18–20
An **algorithm** is a precise procedure for completing a task. A person should be able to follow its steps without inventing missing rules. For the reminder service:

1. Obtain an appointment approved for reminders.
2. Read its scheduled time.
3. Compose a message containing the time and a way to contact the office.
4. Review the message for accuracy and unnecessary personal details.
5. Send it through the approved channel.

“Send reminders to everyone” leaves important decisions unspecified. Which appointments? Which recipients? What information should be shown? Clarifying those rules is part of development.

The **software development life cycle (SDLC)** includes understanding requirements, designing a solution, implementing it, testing it, deploying it, and maintaining it. These activities repeat as you learn more. Writing source code is one activity in that cycle. A small exercise follows the same habit: state the intended result, predict an example, write code, run it, and compare the result with the prediction.[^0101_cs_ideas-workflow]

Identify stakeholders and apply questions about harm, necessary data, and responsible action.

Stakeholder reasoning is integrated with the reminder task and conceptual checks.

Explanation

0102_computing_responsibility.ipynb · cells 6–14
A **stakeholder** is a person or group affected by a system or a decision about it. The person who operates the software is one stakeholder, but others may never touch it. In a bookstore, a cashier uses the sales system, a customer relies on its receipt, a manager uses its reports, and warehouse staff act on its stock requests. A change that saves the cashier time might create extra work for another group.

Consider a bookstore that introduces automatic overdue notices for rented textbooks. Its goal is reasonable: reduce the time staff spend checking rentals and help customers return books. The system compares a stored due date with a recorded return date and selects customers to notify. Before examining any code, we can identify several possible consequences.

| Stakeholder | What they rely on | What could go wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer | Accurate return status and a way to correct mistakes | An incorrect notice causes worry or an unfair charge. |
| Desk staff | Records that reflect accepted returns | Staff must investigate repeated complaints. |
| Manager | Reports that distinguish outstanding rentals from record errors | A misleading report leads to a mistaken business decision. |
| Another person using a shared account or device | Appropriate limits on information displayed | A notice exposes someone else's borrowing details. |

**Harm** is a negative consequence, such as financial loss, disclosure of information, exclusion from a service, or damage to trust. A useful analysis identifies the consequence and who experiences it. Saying that a program is “bad” d

0102_computing_responsibility.ipynb · cells 14–14
**Personal data** identifies a person or can be connected to one. Names and contact details are familiar examples. Purchase history, borrowing history, and account activity can also describe someone when linked to an identifier. Replacing a name with a customer number does not necessarily make a record anonymous: another record may connect the number to the person.

**Privacy** concerns appropriate collection, use, sharing, and retention of information about people. **Security** concerns protecting information and systems from unauthorized access or changes and keeping services available. The concerns overlap, but they are not interchangeable. Restricting access to a report does not establish that its recipients need every detail in it. Removing a name from a report does not establish that its storage is protected.

**Data minimization** means limiting the information handled to what the purpose needs. Begin with the task, then justify the fields. Consider a manager asking how many notebooks were sold each day last week. Daily totals and product information may answer that question. Individual customer names and telephone numbers do not become necessary merely because the sales system has them.

0102_computing_responsibility.ipynb · cells 17–19
**Accessibility** means designing a system so people with disabilities can use it. It involves how people perceive information, understand it, navigate the system, and perform actions. A screen that works for its developer may still present a barrier to someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, enlarged text, or another way of interacting.[^0102_computing_responsibility-accessibility]

Consider an order-status display that uses a green square for “ready” and a red square for “delayed.” A customer who cannot distinguish those colors needs another way to learn the status. Adding the words “Ready for collection” and “Delayed” communicates the distinction in text. Choosing two different colors alone would not address that need. Similarly, an unlabeled button may look obvious beside a picture while giving a screen-reader user no useful description of its action.

Understandable messages are another part of usable communication. Compare the following fictional order-status responses:

| Message | What the reader can determine |
| --- | --- |
| “Error 19” | A problem occurred, but its meaning and next action are unclear. |
| “Invalid!” | The program rejected something, but does not identify what to correct. |
| “Enter a collection date on or after October 16.” | The reader has a specific condition to check. |

A message should also describe what the system actually knows. “Your order was saved” is misleading if saving failed. “Your order has not been saved. Try again or contact the desk” separates the outcome from the next action. The date and contact route in a real application

Explain the roles of source code, the compiler, runtime, editor, and terminal.

Explanation and conceptual review cover execution/tool roles.

Explanation

0101_cs_ideas.ipynb · cells 25–31
```{index} source code; compiler; compilation; runtime; .NET; editor; terminal
```


**Source code** is the program text written in a programming language. An editor lets you change and save that text. A **compiler** translates C# source into a compiled form; the **.NET runtime** executes the compiled program, normally translating intermediate instructions into machine instructions as needed. A **terminal** gives you access to a shell, which accepts commands that start tools and programs.

The .NET **software development kit (SDK)** includes the compiler and development commands. An editor and the SDK have different jobs: saving a file changes its text, while building checks and translates it. Running starts execution. Section 1.3 connects these operations in a saved console project.

Here is a complete small browser-runnable example. `Console.WriteLine` displays a line of text. You will study its structure in Section 1.3.


using System;

Console.WriteLine("Appointment reminder");
Console.WriteLine("Please arrive at 9:00.");


The source contains two instructions; the output contains their messages. Changing the displayed time changes what the program says. It does not connect this example to a real scheduling system or send a notification.

Installation instructions belong to {doc}`Appendix B <../appendices/command_line>`. You can run this short example in the browser while preparing a local environment, then complete the saved-project workflow in Section 1.3.


```{index} compiler; interpreter; intermediate language; JIT compilation
```



```{index} Compilation, Interp

HelloWorld/
├── Program.cs

├── bin/
└── obj/
```

Edit `Program.cs`. Keep the `.csproj`, which records build settings. `bin/` contains compiled output; `obj/` holds intermediate build information. They are generated folders, so do not write your source there.

`dotnet run` uses the project file in the current folder to build and start the application. **Compilation** translates source into compiled code that .NET can execute. The `.csproj` uses XML tags, including `TargetFramework` and `ImplicitUsings`; you do not need to change those settings for this lesson. A **solution** can group several projects, but this application needs only one.


```{index} dotnet new list; template; solution; project reference
```

```

### Templates, Projects, and Solutions



The SDK supplies **templates**: starting structures for console applications, class libraries, test projects, and other application kinds. From the operating-system shell, `dotnet new list` lists the installed templates. In its output, identify `console` (a text-based application), `classlib` (a reusable library), and a test template such as `mstest`. The available list depends on the installed SDK and optional templates.

A **project** has a `.csproj` file that describes how its source files are built. A **solution** groups related projects so tools can manage them together. For example, a business system can have an application project, a library of pricing rules, and a test project. A project refer

## Create and Run Your First Console Application



Open your terminal and navigate to the workspace folder you created in Appendix B. If you are still inside `csharprepl`, enter `exit` first so that you can type shell commands. Run these commands one at a time:

```bash
dotnet new console --use-program-main -n HelloWorld
cd HelloWorld
code .
```

The first command creates a console project in a new folder named `HelloWorld`. The `--use-program-main` option makes the template show the `Program` class and `Main` method explicitly.[^0103_program_structure-1] The second command moves the shell into that folder. The third opens the folder in VS Code. If `code .` is unavailable, use **File > Open Folder** in VS Code and select `HelloWorld`.

A **project** groups source files and the settings needed to build an application. The `HelloWorld` folder is your project folder. In VS Code's **Explorer**, expand that folder and identify these two files:

| File | What you do with it |
| --- | --- |
| `Program.cs` | Open and edit the C# source code. The `.cs` extension identifies a C# source file. |
| `HelloWorld.csproj` | Inspect the project settings. The `.csproj` extension identifies a C# project file. |

Opening the project folder lets VS Code work with the source files and their build settings together. The folder is where you keep the files; the `.csproj` tells .NET how to build the application. The project name, `HelloWorld`, is not itself an executable C# instruction.

Distinguish an AI-generated suggestion from verified behavior and describe how to check it.

The conceptual boundary counterexample is taught; independent assessment is one true/false judgment rather than review of a fresh prepared candidate.

Explanation

0102_computing_responsibility.ipynb · cells 25–25
**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a broad area of computing concerned with systems that perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, making predictions, or generating content. **Generative AI** produces content such as text, images, and source code. A **large language model (LLM)** is a model used to generate text, including programming explanations, from a **prompt**, the instructions and context supplied to it. An AI coding assistant may combine a model with tools for reading files, running programs, or proposing edits.

Using such an assistant while learning is different from building an application that calls an AI service. This course's foundations do not require a paid assistant or a live service. When later activities examine a proposed AI answer, prepared examples let everyone inspect the same material.

An assistant can explain unfamiliar wording or suggest an approach. Its response is still something to evaluate. A fluent explanation may contain a wrong rule, omit an important condition, or claim that a check succeeded without showing evidence. Computing educators therefore distinguish opportunities for learning from risks of over-reliance and difficulties assessing independent understanding.[^0102_computing_responsibility-ai-education]

For a conceptual example, suppose a fictional store offers a discount on purchases of at least $100. An assistant explains this as “purchases over $100 qualify.” The wording sounds close, but it leaves out the exact $100 case. You can identify the discrepancy from the requirement without knowing any C#. A polite, detailed respons

0102_computing_responsibility.ipynb · cells 25–25
**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a broad area of computing concerned with systems that perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, making predictions, or generating content. **Generative AI** produces content such as text, images, and source code. A **large language model (LLM)** is a model used to generate text, including programming explanations, from a **prompt**, the instructions and context supplied to it. An AI coding assistant may combine a model with tools for reading files, running programs, or proposing edits.

Using such an assistant while learning is different from building an application that calls an AI service. This course's foundations do not require a paid assistant or a live service. When later activities examine a proposed AI answer, prepared examples let everyone inspect the same material.

An assistant can explain unfamiliar wording or suggest an approach. Its response is still something to evaluate. A fluent explanation may contain a wrong rule, omit an important condition, or claim that a check succeeded without showing evidence. Computing educators therefore distinguish opportunities for learning from risks of over-reliance and difficulties assessing independent understanding.[^0102_computing_responsibility-ai-education]

For a conceptual example, suppose a fictional store offers a discount on purchases of at least $100. An assistant explains this as “purchases over $100 qualify.” The wording sounds close, but it leaves out the exact $100 case. You can identify the discrepancy from the requirement without knowing any C#. A polite, detailed respons

## Statements, Expressions, and Literal Values



An **expression** produces a value. A **literal** writes a value directly: `"Northwind Store"` is text, and `3` is a number. The expression `2 + 1` produces `3`; the statement `Console.WriteLine(2 + 1);` tells the program to display that value.

Text and numbers have different roles. `"2 + 1"` is text containing five characters, including spaces; C# does not calculate the addition inside ordinary quotes. Predict the next two output lines before running.

using System;
Console.WriteLine(2 + 1);
Console.WriteLine("2 + 1");

**String interpolation** inserts expression values into text. Begin the string with `$`, then put each expression inside `{` and `}`. In `$"Items ready: {2 + 1}"`, the braces mark an expression inside text; they do not define a code block. This lets the store label its output clearly without introducing variables yet.

using System;
Console.WriteLine($"Items ready: {2 + 1}");

0201_variables_types.ipynb · cells 7–32
A declaration statement declares a new local variable, local constant, or local
reference variable. To declare a local variable, specify a type and provide
a variable name. You can declare multiple variables of the same type in one
statement:

> `type variableName;`

In this syntax,

- **type**
  is a C# type (such as int or string),
- **variableName**
  is the name of the variable (such as x or name)
- the semicolon `;`
  is the statement terminator.

For example, you may declare the following variables



string greeting;     // declaring one string variable
int a, b, c;         // declaring multiple int variables
List<double> xs;     // a reference type (double list) variable



You can also provide initial values when declaring a variable.
The syntax is:



```text
type variableName = value;
```


For example,



string greeting = "Hello";
int a = 3, b = 2, c = a + b;
List<double> xs = new();



In this syntax,

- the equal sign `=`
  is the assignment operator (note that it is not the equal sign in mathematics)



```{index} The var Keyword
```



```{index} The var Keyword
```

## The `var` Keyword




Local variables can be declared without giving an explicit type. The complier
will then infer the type of a variable from its initialization expression.
The keyword `var` is used in case of this. For example:



var greeting = "Hello";
Console.WriteLine(greeting.GetType());  // output: System.String

var a = 100;
Console.WriteLine(a.GetType());  // output: System.Int32

var xs = new List<double>();
Console.WriteLine(xs.GetType());  // output: System.Collections.Generic

Worked example/case/trace

0201_variables_types.ipynb · cells 20–32
If you need to change
the value to a variable, you need to use the **assignment statement**.
Note that an assignment statement is read from right to left. For example, if we
create a variable "area" and assign the value of "width * height" to it like:



int area = 10;
int height = 10;
int width = 10;
area = width * height;



The assignment statement starts by evaluating the **expression** on the right-hand side: `width * height`. Since width * height is an
expression, the expression will be evaluated to a value like when evaluating an
expression in math, so the values are substituted as

```none
5 * 7
```

which is then evaluates to 35 and finally assigned to the variable, `area`, on the left.
The whole block of code could look something like follows. You may notice that we
are operating with three variables here.

int width = 5, height, area;
height = 7;
area = width * height;
Console.WriteLine(area);

In the example above,
`width * height`, as an expression, evaluates to a value; while
`int width = 5, height, area;` is a declaration statement and `height = 7;`
an assignment statement.

You should also notice that the value of the most *recent* assignment is
remembered until reassigned. Also, it is common to use the same variable name
when we intend to change the value to the variable without keeping the previous
value, and after the initial declaration you don't need to declare type anymore:

int a = 10;
a = 100;       // reassignment



To further illustrate how expression and statement work in C#, or in programming
languages in general, we can take a look at the exam

0201_variables_types.ipynb · cells 30–32
```{index} Trace Reassignment: Playing Computer
```

### Trace Reassignment: Playing Computer



To understand assignment, follow each statement using the most recently stored values. This is sometimes called **playing computer**. Predict the output of this small program before running it:

```csharp
int x = 3;
int y = x + 2;
y = 2 * y;
x = y - x;
Console.WriteLine(x + " " + y);
```

A state table records the values **after** each statement. A dash means that a local variable has not yet been declared; it is not a default zero.

| Statement | `x` afterward | `y` afterward | Reason |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `int x = 3;` | 3 | — | Initialize `x`. |
| `int y = x + 2;` | 3 | 5 | Use the current `x`: `3 + 2`. |
| `y = 2 * y;` | 3 | 10 | Read the old `y`, calculate 10, then replace `y`. |
| `x = y - x;` | 7 | 10 | Read the current values: `10 - 3`. |
| `Console.WriteLine(x + " " + y);` | 7 | 10 | Print `7 10`; output does not change the variables. |

Unlike an equation asserting a permanent relationship, an assignment changes one stored value at that moment. Assigning `y = x + 2` does not make `y` automatically change whenever `x` changes. In this sequential program, the trace follows source order; later decisions and loops will make the order itself part of the reasoning.

Use the restored {doc}`Tracing and Expression Practice <assignments/additional_practice>` for a prediction task and a table to complete yourself.

int y = x + 2;
y = 2 * y;
x = y - x;
Console.WriteLine(x + " " + y);

0204_types_conversion.ipynb · cells 9–29
Every specific type you will meet in this book — `int`, `string`, an array, a class you write yourself — is an instance of a small number of umbrella concepts. Learning those umbrella concepts first means every new type you meet afterward already has a slot to fit into, instead of feeling like a fresh, unrelated fact. This section covers four of them: the value/reference split that governs assignment, `void` (the type that means "no value"), and default values (what a variable holds before you give it one).

```{index} value type
```

#### Value Types

A variable of a **value type** directly contains its data. Value types include the numeric primitives (`int`, `double`, `long`, and the rest), `bool`, `char`, and user-defined `struct` and `enum` types. Despite their keyword status, each built-in value type is simply an alias for a .NET struct in the `System` namespace — `int` is `System.Int32`, `bool` is `System.Boolean`.[^0201_variables_types-types-ref]

Assigning one value-type variable to another **copies the value**. The two variables are then completely independent — changing one never affects the other:

int original = 10;
int copy = original;   // copies the value
copy = 99;              // changing copy does not touch original

Console.WriteLine($"original={original}, copy={copy}");

```{index} reference type
```

#### Reference Types

A variable of a **reference type** does not hold its data directly — it holds a reference (an address) pointing to where the data actually lives. Reference types include `class`, `interface`, `delegate`, and `record`; `string` and `ob

Worked example/case/trace

0204_types_conversion.ipynb · cells 28–59
The following subsections explore each built-in type through examples you can
run with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or VS Code.


```{index} integer type; int; long; byte; sbyte
```

#### Integer Types

**Integer types** store whole numbers with no fractional part. The most common
choice is `int` (32-bit signed), which covers roughly ±2.1 billion. Use `long`
(64-bit) when you need a larger range, or `byte` for small non-negative values
(0–255).

Unsigned variants (`uint`, `ulong`, `ushort`, `byte`) hold only non-negative
values, which doubles the positive range but disallows negatives.

Numeric literals default to `int`. Use suffixes to specify other types:
`L`/`l` for `long`, `U`/`u` for `uint`, `UL`/`ul` for `ulong`.


int population = 2_147_483_647;        // int max (~2.1 billion); _ is a digit separator
long worldPopulation = 8_000_000_000L; // needs L suffix — too large for int
byte age = 25;                         // 0–255, no negative values
sbyte temperature = -10;               // -128–127
uint score = 1_000_000U;               // unsigned: 0–4.29 billion

// Signed vs unsigned: same bits, different interpretation
int  signed   = -1;
uint unsigned = (uint)signed;           // becomes 4294967295 (all bits set)
Console.WriteLine(signed);
Console.WriteLine(unsigned);

```{index} floating-point type; float; double; decimal
```

#### Floating-Point Types

C# has three types for fractional numbers:

| Type | Size | Precision | Suffix | Use for |
|------|------|-----------|--------|---------|
| `float` | 32-bit | ~6–9 digits | `f` or `F` | Graphics, sensors |
| `double` | 6

Section practice

0204_types_conversion.ipynb · cells 78–81
Suppose three employees share ten work hours. The expression `10 / 3` has two integer operands, so it produces the integer 3. Assigning that result to a double afterward produces 3.0; the missing fractional part cannot be recovered. Converting an operand before division changes which arithmetic operation is performed. This is the same evaluation-order reasoning used for ordinary expressions: work out each intermediate value and its type before considering the destination variable.

| Step | Value | Type | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read the literal 10 | 10 | int | Ten whole hours in this example |
| Evaluate 10 / 3 | 3 | int | Integer quotient |
| Convert that quotient | 3.0 | double | Conversion preserves the already truncated result |
| Evaluate 10.0 / 3 | approximately 3.3333 | double | Fractional division happened before assignment |

A cast is written `(DestinationType)expression`. The parentheses identify a requested conversion; they do not mean that conversion is lossless. Converting a floating-point value to an integer discards its fractional part within the supported range. Parsing is different: `int.Parse(text)` interprets a textual representation under a format contract. Neither a cast nor a parse proves the resulting business value is allowed. A successfully parsed negative package count may still violate the application rule.

Predict arithmetic, comparison, logical, and string-expression results using C# precedence and division rules.

Core arithmetic and Boolean use is independently practiced; bitwise/time material is an extension.

Explanation

0202_operators_built_in_methods.ipynb · cells 8–66
Every expression in C# is built from **operands** (values or variables) and
**operators** (symbols that define the operation). Operators are grouped by
what they do to their operands.

:::{note}
**C# vs Other Languages**: Different language may have different operators doing the same thing.

| Feature | C# | C / C++ | Python | JavaScript |
|---------|----|---------|----|------------|
| Logical AND / OR | `&&` `\|\|` | `&&` `\|\|` | `and` `or` | `&&` `\|\|` |
| Logical NOT | `!` | `!` | `not` | `!` |
| Integer division | `/` (auto when both `int`) | `/` (auto) | `//` | no built-in |
| Remainder | `%` | `%` | `%` | `%` |
| Exponentiation | `Math.Pow(x, y)` | `pow(x,y)` | `**` | `**` |
| Increment | `++` `--` | `++` `--` | no `++`/`--` | `++` `--` |
| String equality | `==` (value) | `==` (pointer!) | `==` | `==` (loose) / `===` |
| Null coalescing | `??` | — | `or` idiom | `??` |

In C# and JS, `&&`/`\|\|` use *short-circuit* evaluation: the right-hand side
is only evaluated if needed. Python's `and`/`or` do the same but return one of
the operands rather than a strict `bool`. C/C++ lack a dedicated boolean type
in older standards — `0` is false, anything else is true. [^0202_operators_built_in_methods-1]
:::

```

```

### Assignment Operators




An **assignment operator** stores a value into a variable. The basic form is
`=`, which should not be confused with `==` (equality test). C# also provides
**compound assignment operators** that combine an arithmetic operation with
assignment in on

Worked example/case/trace

0202_operators_built_in_methods.ipynb · cells 28–60
The `=` operator assigns a value. Compound operators (`+=`, `-=`, etc.) combine an operation with assignment. `++` and `--` increment or decrement by 1:


int x = 1;
x++;       // post-increment operator; x++ increments the value of variable x after it's evaluated in an expression
Console.WriteLine(x);
x = 2;
++x;       // pre-increment operator; ++x increments the value of variable x before it's evaluated in an expression
Console.WriteLine(x);

### Arithmetic




Basic arithmetic operations on numeric types:


int a = 10, b = 3;
Console.WriteLine(a + b);  // 13 — addition
Console.WriteLine(a - b);  // 7  — subtraction
Console.WriteLine(a * b);  // 30 — multiplication
Console.WriteLine(a / b);  // 3  — integer division (truncates toward zero)
Console.WriteLine(a % b);  // 1  — remainder

(division-and-remainders)=

### Division




Division can be a little tricky in C#. For example:

Console.WriteLine(5.0/2.0);
Console.WriteLine(14.0/4.0);

But C# will implicitly turn the following expression to an `int` type:

Console.WriteLine(14/4);

Adding a decimal point would inform C# that you are using `double` instead of `int`:

Console.WriteLine(14.0/4.0);
Console.WriteLine(14.0 / 4);  // one of the operands is double type
Console.WriteLine(6.0/3.0);  // when the remainder is 0, the quotient is an int.

Note that C# stores values with only a limited precision, so the results of
mathematical operations are only approximate in

0202_operators_built_in_methods.ipynb · cells 69–94
Operators cover arithmetic and comparison, but many everyday tasks have no symbol: rounding a price, picking the larger of two numbers, or turning typed text into a number. The .NET library ships thousands of ready-made **methods** for jobs like these. You do not need to know how a built-in method works inside; you only need to know its name, what it expects, and what it gives back. Chapter 5 shows how to write your own methods.

`Math` and `string` belong to the `System` namespace, which the generated console project makes available automatically (see {doc}`../01_context/0103_program_structure`), so the examples here need no extra setup.


```{index} method call; argument; return value
```



```{index} Calling a Method
```

### Calling a Method




**Keyword or library name?** `int`, `string`, and `if` are keywords, which belong to the language itself (see Section 2.1). `Math`, `Console`, and `Parse` are not keywords. They are names from the .NET library, and you use them by calling them.


You have already called one method: `Console.WriteLine`. A **method call** has a name, parentheses, and zero or more **arguments** inside the parentheses. Many methods also hand back a **return value** that you can store in a variable or use in an expression.

| Part | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Method name | `Math.Round` | The task to perform; `Math.` says which class provides it |
| Arguments | `subtotal * 1.0825, 2` | The inputs, separated by commas |
| Return value | `155.34` | The result, which you can assign to a variable |

A method that returns nothing is declared with

Worked example/case/trace

0202_operators_built_in_methods.ipynb · cells 77–82
`Math` provides common calculations. Each method takes numbers and returns a number.

| Method | Returns | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Math.Abs(x)` | absolute value | `Math.Abs(-42)` | `42` |
| `Math.Max(a, b)` / `Math.Min(a, b)` | larger / smaller value | `Math.Max(120, 95)` | `120` |
| `Math.Round(x)` / `Math.Round(x, digits)` | nearest value | `Math.Round(4.567, 1)` | `4.6` |
| `Math.Ceiling(x)` / `Math.Floor(x)` | round up / down | `Math.Ceiling(4.2)` | `5` |
| `Math.Sqrt(x)` | square root | `Math.Sqrt(81)` | `9` |
| `Math.Pow(x, y)` | x raised to y | `Math.Pow(2, 10)` | `1024` |

The `Ceiling` method answers "how many whole boxes do I need?", because a partial box still takes a whole box. Note that `Math.Round` rounds a value exactly halfway between two integers to the nearest *even* integer (banker's rounding); pass `MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero` for the schoolbook rule.


using System;

double cartTotal = 143.50;
int boxes = (int)Math.Ceiling(cartTotal / 50);   // a partial box still needs a whole box
Console.WriteLine($"Boxes needed: {boxes}");

Console.WriteLine(Math.Abs(-42));
Console.WriteLine(Math.Floor(4.8));
Console.WriteLine(Math.Sqrt(81));
Console.WriteLine(Math.Pow(2, 10));

Console.WriteLine(Math.Round(4.5));   // 4: halfway rounds to the even neighbor
Console.WriteLine(Math.Round(5.5));   // 6
Console.WriteLine(Math.Round(2.5, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero));   // 3

0204_types_conversion.ipynb · cells 61–81
C# variables have specific types, but values sometimes need to move between
types. Type conversions are either **implicit** (automatic) or **explicit**
(manual cast required).

**Implicit casting** happens automatically when converting a smaller type to a
larger one — no data is lost:

```text
char → int → long → float → double
```

**Explicit casting** is required when converting a larger type to a smaller one,
because precision or range may be lost:

```text
double → float → long → int → char
```

For example:

```csharp
int a = 123;
long b = a;        // implicit: int fits in long, no cast needed
int c = (int) b;   // explicit: long → int, cast required
```

Use `GetType()` to inspect a variable's type at runtime. When types are *not*
cast properly, C# raises a compile-time error. For example, assigning a `double`
directly to an `int` fails:


double d = 2.0;
int i = d;

Note that if you choose to agree with the message and perform a type casting, you lose the
precision of `double` over an `int`.

double d = 2.5;       // create a double type variable d
Console.WriteLine(d);  // display the value of d

int i = default;       // explicitly ask for the default int value
Console.WriteLine(i);  // display the default value of an int

i = (int)d;            // explicitly tell the compiler you intend the conversion
Console.WriteLine(i);  // display i; the .5 is lost

0203_input_output.ipynb · cells 6–58
At console or terminal, input is done in two parts: Prompt and read.
Because the lack of better visual cues, we use a *prompt* to instruct the user
how to respond. For example:



Console.Write("Enter your name: ");



The user input from keyboard is automatically shown
in the terminal or console window. For a program to take in the characters typed,
another method in the `Console` class is used:
`Console.ReadLine`.

The read method reads the data from a line typed at the keyboard by the user.
When the user presses the Enter (Return) key, the sequence of characters,
form the string *value* of the read method.

With any method producing a value, the value is *lost* unless it
is *immediately* used. We therefore assign the value from the read method
to a variable like in



string name;                                // declare variable

Console.WriteLine("Enter your name: ");     // prompt for input
name = Console.ReadLine();                  // save value to variable


Or, declare your variable and read in the input one line (e.g., "string name = Console.ReadLine();")
You can then print out the variable.


Console.WriteLine("Enter your name: ");
string name = Console.ReadLine();

Console.WriteLine("Your name: " + name);                    // print to test


Now we have a variable containing the value for us to operate on.

## Composite Formatting




Instead of using the `+` operator, **composite format** (the
"fill-in-the-braces") gives us better control over output using `Console.WriteLine`
by using positional **string format index** to separate the string and the data variables.

In composite formatting, you use two arguments: 1) a composite format **string** with
**parameter specifier** (`format item` index) and 2) an **object list**. When printing,
the objects (variables or literal values) substitute the parameter specifiers one by one.

Observe the last two statements:



string firstName;

Console.Write("Enter you first name: ");    // input will start here
firstName = Console.ReadLine();

Console.WriteLine("Hiya, " + firstName + "!");
Console.WriteLine("Hiya, {0}!", firstName);



You can imagine that there would be \{1}, \{2}... like this:



string firstName = "Alex";
string lastName = "Kim";
Console.WriteLine("Hiya, {0} {1}!", firstName, lastName);



With composite formatting, we have the flexibility of writing the output string
and place the variables anywhere we prefer in the string.

A more elaborate silly examples that you could test in csharp would be:



string first = "Peter";
string last = "Piper";
string what = "pick";
Console.WriteLine("{0} {1}, {0} {1}, {2}.", first, last, what);



It would print:

```
Peter Piper, Peter Piper, pick.
```

where parameter 0 is `first` (value `"Peter"`),
parameter 1 is `last` ( value `"Piper"`), and
parameter 2 is `what` (value `"pick"`).

0204_types_conversion.ipynb · cells 78–81
Suppose three employees share ten work hours. The expression `10 / 3` has two integer operands, so it produces the integer 3. Assigning that result to a double afterward produces 3.0; the missing fractional part cannot be recovered. Converting an operand before division changes which arithmetic operation is performed. This is the same evaluation-order reasoning used for ordinary expressions: work out each intermediate value and its type before considering the destination variable.

| Step | Value | Type | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read the literal 10 | 10 | int | Ten whole hours in this example |
| Evaluate 10 / 3 | 3 | int | Integer quotient |
| Convert that quotient | 3.0 | double | Conversion preserves the already truncated result |
| Evaluate 10.0 / 3 | approximately 3.3333 | double | Fractional division happened before assignment |

A cast is written `(DestinationType)expression`. The parentheses identify a requested conversion; they do not mean that conversion is lossless. Converting a floating-point value to an integer discards its fractional part within the supported range. Parsing is different: `int.Parse(text)` interprets a textual representation under a format contract. Neither a cast nor a parse proves the resulting business value is allowed. A successfully parsed negative package count may still violate the application rule.

Explanation

0302_ifstatement.ipynb · cells 13–44
The `if` statement specifies a block of C# code to be executed if a condition is True.

```none
if (condition)
{
    // block of code to be executed if the condition is True
}
```



:::{note}
Note that C# is case sensitive, so `If` is not the same as `if`. "If" or "IF" will
generate an error.
:::

In `if` statements, the comparison operators (`>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `==`, and `!=`) are used to evaluate the comparison expressions to derive a value of either `true` or `false` from the Boolean expression.

The first step to learn about the `if` statements is to perform some tests on the operators
with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a small test project, such as:

```csharp
if (20 > 10)
{
Console.WriteLine("20 is greater than 10");
}
```

with the output:

```none
20 is greater than 10
```

When coding, we often play with variables rather than simple values. Observe the
following code and test it with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a small VS Code project to practice `if` statements with variables:

```csharp
int num1 = 20;
int num2 = 18;
if (num1 > num2)
{
Console.WriteLine("num1 is greater than num2");
}
```

Consider simple arithmetic comparisons that directly translate from math into C#.
Run this C# code:

```csharp
int num = 11;
```

Now think of which of these expressions below are true and which false,
    and then enter each one into your csharp session to test:

```csharp
2 < 5
3 > 7
num > 10
2*x < num
```

You see that the expressions evaluate to either `true` or `false`. These are the only possible *Boolean* values.

Run the example program below. Try it at least twice, with

0302_ifstatement.ipynb · cells 5–10
An order desk charges 8 for express service, 3 for standard service, and 0 for pickup. This is one rule with mutually exclusive alternatives. An if/else-if chain asks conditions in order and chooses the first true branch. A switch statement selects a matching case. The two forms can implement the same mapping, but choosing a form is not a reason to change the rule.

Start with a decision table before writing either version. Include a value outside the allowed set; otherwise an incomplete program may appear correct merely because all supplied examples happen to name a case.

| Service code | Intended charge | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E | 8 | Express |
| S | 3 | Standard |
| P | 0 | Pickup |
| Anything else | Reject or report an invalid code | No service was selected |

The general statement form is `switch (expression) { case value: statements; break; default: statements; break; }`. This is a syntax pattern, not a complete program. The switch expression is evaluated and matching follows the case rules; `break` leaves the switch. It is not a request to end the application. Modern C# also supports patterns and switch expressions, but those forms are not prerequisites for the basic constant-case statement here.

An if chain is particularly direct when conditions are ranges, such as a quantity below ten or an age above a boundary. A simple constant-case switch reads naturally when one value selects among named alternatives. Do not use three independent if statements when the intended result is exactly one category unless you have established that their tests cannot overlap. A

Explanation

0301_intro_decision.ipynb · cells 12–29
To drive decision-making in selection statements, Boolean expressions are typically
built using **comparison operators** (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`):

| Operator | Name | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | Relational | Compare numeric (and `char`) values; supported by all integral and floating-point types |
| `==` | Equality | `true` when the compared numbers, characters, Boolean values, or string contents are equal |
| `!=` | Inequality | Opposite of `==` |

Examples:

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(7.0 < 5.1);   // False
Console.WriteLine(7.0 > 5.1);   // True
Console.WriteLine(7.0 <= 5.1);  // False
Console.WriteLine(7.0 >= 5.1);  // True

int a = 1 + 2 + 3;
int b = 6;
Console.WriteLine(a == b);      // True

char c1 = 'a';
char c2 = 'A';
Console.WriteLine(c1 == c2);    // False (different character codes)
```

For the string comparisons used here, `==` compares text contents and is case-sensitive. `"paid"` and `"Paid"` differ. Comparing the identity of custom objects belongs to Chapter 11.


string status = "paid";
Console.WriteLine(status == "paid");  // True
Console.WriteLine(status == "Paid");  // False


Understanding boolean expressions above should give you a good sense of how
conditional/select statement syntax works:

```csharp
if (condition)
{
    // block of code to be executed if the condition is True
}
```

You should know that the `condition` is a `Boolean expression`, which will evaluate to either `true` or
`false`. The parentheses is a testing construct. If the testing construct results to
`true`, then the code bloc

## Switch Syntax and Case Behavior




The switch statement is used to select one of many code blocks ("cases")
to be executed. Logically, it resembles the use of a series of `else-if` clauses.

The syntax for `switch` statement is as follows:



```csharp
switch(expression)
{
case x:
    // code block
    break;
case y:
    // code block
    break;
default:
    // code block
    break;
}
```


Note that:
\- The switch expression is evaluated once.
\- The value of the expression is **compared** with the values of each case.
\- If there is a **match** between the `expression` value and the `case` value, the associated block of code is executed.
\- The `break` and `default` keywords will be described later in this chapter.

As an example, we can use the weekday number to figure out weekday name:



int day = 4;
switch (day)
{
case 1:
    Console.WriteLine("Monday");
    break;
case 2:
    Console.WriteLine("Tuesday");
    break;
case 3:
    Console.WriteLine("Wednesday");
    break;
case 4:
    Console.WriteLine("Thursday");
    break;
case 5:
    Console.WriteLine("Friday");
    break;
case 6:
    Console.WriteLine("Saturday");
    break;
case 7:
    Console.WriteLine("Sunday");
    break;
}



The outcome of this code will be Thursday. The code will stop
executing because of the `break` keyword after the print line.
Also, there is not `default case` in this code block.



```{index} The default Keyword
```



```{index} The default Keyword
```

}

## Multiple Choice

**1.** Which operator represents logical OR in C#?

a) |
b) ||
c) OR
d) or

```{dropdown} Answer
**b) ||** — `||` is the short-circuit logical OR; `|` is the bitwise OR.
```

**2.** In a `switch` statement, which keyword exits the current case?

a) exit
b) end
c) break
d) stop

```{dropdown} Answer
**c) break** — `break` prevents fall-through to the next case.
```

**3.** Which expression is `true` when `x = 5`?

a) x > 10 && x < 3
b) x > 3 && x < 10
c) x > 10 || x < 3
d) !(x == 5)

```{dropdown} Answer
**b) x > 3 && x < 10** — 5 > 3 is true AND 5 < 10 is true, so the whole expression is true.
```

**4.** What does `condition ? a : b` return when `condition` is `false`?

a) condition
b) a
c) b
d) null

```{dropdown} Answer
**c) b** — The ternary operator returns `b` on false.
```

**5.** Which statement best describes an `if-else if-else` chain?

a) All branches always execute
b) Only the first matching branch executes
c) The last branch always executes
d) Branches execute in parallel

```{dropdown} Answer
**b) Only the first matching branch executes** — Execution stops at the first condition that evaluates to true.
```

The problem-solving scenario that you want to model may require
complex branching behavior by combining conditionals and,
in particular, by nesting conditionals. Namely, we can create more
complex branching behavior by nesting conditional blocks.
When more than one condition needs to be true and one of the
condition is the sub-condition of parent condition, nested if can be used.
In other words, when we want to further test certain condition
when a condition tested true.

## Nested `if` Statements




The syntax for a nested if statement is as follows:

    if( boolean_expression 1)
    {
       /* Executes when the boolean expression 1 is true */
       if(boolean_expression 2)
       {
          /* Executes when the boolean expression 2 is true */
       }
    }

As an example, consider the following code where two separate but
related ideas are tested using two independent if statements:

    int num = 7;

    if (num > 0)
    {
       Console.WriteLine("POSITIVE");
    }

    if (num % 2 == 0)
    {
       Console.WriteLine("EVEN");
    }

We find that the output is POSITIVE, even though 7 is odd and so
nothing should be printed in the 2nd if statement. This code
doesn’t work as desired if we only want to test for evenness only
when we already know the number is positive. We can enable this
behavior by putting the second conditional inside the first as:

    int num = 7;

    if (num > 0)
    {
       Console.WriteLine("POSITIVE");

       if (num % 2 == 0)
       {
          Console.WriteLin

0302_ifstatement.ipynb · cells 5–10
An order desk charges 8 for express service, 3 for standard service, and 0 for pickup. This is one rule with mutually exclusive alternatives. An if/else-if chain asks conditions in order and chooses the first true branch. A switch statement selects a matching case. The two forms can implement the same mapping, but choosing a form is not a reason to change the rule.

Start with a decision table before writing either version. Include a value outside the allowed set; otherwise an incomplete program may appear correct merely because all supplied examples happen to name a case.

| Service code | Intended charge | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E | 8 | Express |
| S | 3 | Standard |
| P | 0 | Pickup |
| Anything else | Reject or report an invalid code | No service was selected |

The general statement form is `switch (expression) { case value: statements; break; default: statements; break; }`. This is a syntax pattern, not a complete program. The switch expression is evaluated and matching follows the case rules; `break` leaves the switch. It is not a request to end the application. Modern C# also supports patterns and switch expressions, but those forms are not prerequisites for the basic constant-case statement here.

An if chain is particularly direct when conditions are ranges, such as a quantity below ten or an age above a boundary. A simple constant-case switch reads naturally when one value selects among named alternatives. Do not use three independent if statements when the intended result is exactly one category unless you have established that their tests cannot overlap. A

0402_for_statements.ipynb · cells 5–9

## For Statement Syntax




`for` loops are usually favored for iteration because the
all the information about the local loop variable are available in one place at the top,
which helps quickly visualize the overall sequence in the loop.

The C# for loop statement syntax is:

```csharp
for ( *initializer* ; *condition* ; *iterator* )
{
// code block (statements)
}
```

Let us practice with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a small VS Code project:


for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++)
{
      Console.WriteLine(i);
}

You can see that the `for` loop has four parts, a three-section semicolon-separated **header**
and a **body**:

- **Initializer**: This section is a **variable declaration statement** that
  declares a `local loop variable` (or `iterator variable` or the counter) and initialize it with an initial value.
- **Condition**: The condition section is a **boolean expression** that determines
  if the next iteration in the loop should be executed or should the loop be terminated. If it evaluates to true,
  the next iteration is executed; otherwise, the loop is exited.
- **Iterator**: The iterator (**iteration expression**) section that defines what happens to the counter after each
  execution of the body of the loop. A common behavior is reassigning
  (increment or decrement) the value of the counter.
- The **body** of the loop, which must be a statement or a block of statements.

In the example above, the *initializer* is `i = 1`, *condition* is `i <= n`,
and *iterator* is `i++` (see {ref}`arithmetic operators <arithmetic-operators>`).

Note t
0403_while_statement.ipynb · cells 4–8
```csharp
// initialization
while (condition)
{
    // statement(s)
    // iterator expression
}
```


Note that, because the condition (boolean expression) is evaluated before each execution
of the loop body, a `while` loop can execute **zero** times (if the condition
evaluates to `false` immediately) or more times.

Run the following code to get familiar with the C# `while` loop:

```csharp
int n = 0; // initialization

while (n < 5) // conditional expression in the while loop header
{
    Console.Write(n); // body of while loop
    n++;             // iterator/update
}

// output: 01234
```

This `while` loop does the same counting work as this `for` loop:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    Console.Write(i);
}

// output: 01234
```

Both pieces of code have an `initializer`, `conditional expression`, and `iterator expression`
(see {ref}`for-loop-header`); except that in a `for` loop, the three sections are


placed together in the header, while they are placed in different locations in
    the `while` loop.

    **Stepping**

    Test yourself: Follow the code below to figure out what is printed:


int i = 4;
while (i < 9)
{
    Console.WriteLine(i);
    i = i + 2;
}


int i = 4;
while (i < 9)
{
    i = i + 2;
    Console.WriteLine(i);
}

- **Initializer**: This section is a **variable declaration statement** that

- **Condition**: The condition section is a **boolean expression** that determines
  if the next iteration in the loop should be executed or should the loop be terminated. If it evaluates to true,
  the next iteration is executed; otherwise, the loop is exited.
- **Iterator**: The iterator (**iteration expression**) section that defines what happens to the counter after each
  execution of the body of the loop. A common behavior is reassigning
  (increment or decrement) the value of the counter.
- The **body** of the loop, which must be a statement or a block of statements.

In the example above, the *initializer* is `i = 1`, *condition* is `i <= n`,
and *iterator* is `i++` (see {ref}`arithmetic operators <arithmetic-operators>`).

Note that the initializer section is executed **only once**, before entering the loop.
Also, the declared variable is local to the `for` loop heading and
the loop body and can not be accessed from outside the for statement.

The two semicolons are always needed in the `for` heading, but any of the
parts they normally separate may be omitted.

interpreted as always true, leading to an infinite loop, that can only
terminate due to a `retur

```{index} Iterator/Step

## Iterator/Step




The iterator, also known as **step**, section can contain zero or more expressions, separated by commas.
Commonly used iterators include:

- prefix or postfix increment expression, such as ++i or i++
- prefix or postfix decrement expression, such as --i or i--
- assignment

The arithmetic unary operators (decrement operator `--` and
increment operator `++`) are probably the most common ones used in for and while loops, especially
the postfix increment operator. The result of a postfix increment operation is that it
increments the value of the local loop variable (`i`) and still evaluates to the original value
as before the operation and will update the value in next iteration. Namely, `i++` will retain
the old value in the body of the for statement until next next iteration.

For example, test this with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a small VS Code project:


int num = 3;
Console.WriteLine(num);
num++;       // postfix expression, the value remains
Console.WriteLine(num);  // i is evaluated again. Now it shows 4.

Observe the code below to compare the behavior of postfix and prefix operations and you will see
the difference between the postfix expression and prefix expression:

int i = 0;
Console.WriteLine($"Before: {i}");

A foreach loop expresses traversal in terms of sequence values.

(foreach-syntax)=

## `foreach` Statement




A string can supply characters to a loop. For these introductory examples, use ordinary English letters, digits, and punctuation. `text.Length` is the number of UTF-16 code units, and `text[i]` reads one `char` at zero-based index `i`. The valid indexes run from zero through `text.Length - 1`; an empty string has length zero and no valid index. Some Unicode characters require more than one `char`.

A counted loop visits the positions:

```csharp
string text = "ABC";
for (int i = 0; i < text.Length; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text[i]);
}
```

A `foreach` visits the values without managing an index:

```csharp
string text = "ABC";
foreach (char letter in text)
{
    Console.WriteLine(letter);
}
```

Both print A, B, and C on separate lines. `foreach` is useful when each value receives the same treatment; an indexed loop is useful when positions or reverse order matter. Strings are immutable sequences, not arrays. Arrays and other collections follow in Chapters 7-8. Cleaning, searching, and extracting text are developed in Chapter 5; none is required here.
