We are using `(i < text.Length)` because we want to loop through all the characters.

number, we use:

`break` exits the nearest loop or switch. `continue` skips the rest of the current loop body. In a `for` loop, the update runs before the next condition check; in a `while` loop, the next condition is checked directly. Ensure an update is not skipped accidentally.

## `break` and `continue` Statements




`break` exits the nearest enclosing loop. Execution resumes after that loop. `continue` skips the remaining body and proceeds to the next update/condition check. Decisions inside loops can select when either action occurs. Method returns are taught in Chapter 5 and are not needed here.

Before searching text, introduce its two access operations: `text.Length` counts UTF-16 code units, and `text[i]` reads one `char` at zero-based index `i`. Index zero is first; the last valid index is `text.Length - 1`. An empty string has length zero and no valid index. Use ordinary English letters/digits in these examples; some Unicode characters occupy multiple `char` values.

The next examples search a string directly, without requiring arrays or the later Strings and Their Methods lesson.


string text = "INV-204";
char target = '-';
bool found = false;
int foundIndex = -1;

for (int i = 0; i < text.Length; i++)   // loop for text.Length times
{
   if (text[i] == target)               // if one character == target
   {
      found = true;                    // set found to true
      foundIndex = i;
      break;                           // break out of the enclosing loop
   }
}

if (found)                             // if found == true (from the previous block)
{
   Console.WriteLine("Target found at index " + foundIndex);
}
else
{
   Console.WriteLine("Target not found");
}

string text = "INV-204";

int foundIndex = -1;

for (int i = 0; i < text.Length && !found; i++) {
   if (text[i] == target) {
      found = true;
      foundIndex = i;
   }
}

   Console.WriteLine("Target found at index " + foundIndex);
} else {
   Console.WriteLine("Target not found");
}

has an expression `!found` ({ref}`logical-operators`), meaning found is not true.

if the condition can be embedded in the header of the loop, you don't have to use break.

## Loop Planning Rubric




Looking ahead to more complicated and interesting problems,
here is a list of questions to ask yourself when
designing a program with a loop:

1. Data & loop variables: What data is involved? Make sure you give good variable names.
2. Initialization: What needs to be initialized and how? This certainly includes any
   variable tested in the condition.
3. Condition: What is the condition that will allow the loop to *continue*? It
   may be easier to think of the condition that will *stop* the loop.
   That is fine - but remember to *negate* it (with `!`) to turn it
   into a proper *continuation* condition.
4. Distinguish: What is the code that should only be executed once?
   What action do I want to repeat?
5. Repetition: How do I write the repeating action so I can modify it for the next time
   through the loop to work with new data?
6. Update: What code is needed to do modifications to make the same action code work
   the next time through the loop?
7. Locale variables: Have I thought of variables needed in the middle and declared them;
   do other things need initialization?
8. Condition again: Will the continuation condition eventually fail?
   *Be sure to think about this!*
9. Structure: Separate the actions to be done once before the repetition (code before the
   loop) from repetitive actions (in the loop) and from actions not repeated, but
   done after the loop (code after the loop). Missing this distinction
   is a *common error*!

C05-O1 · supported

Define and call methods with names, parameter lists, and return types that communicate their responsibilities.

Calls and definitions are developed before the exercises.

Explanation

0501_intro_methods.ipynb · cells 5–22
A method boundary should express a responsibility that a caller can understand. Imagine an invoice program that reads a quantity, computes a line amount, adds a packing fee, and prints a report. These actions are related, but they do not all need the same information or have the same effects. Separating them lets a calculation be checked without simulating keyboard input or capturing console output.

Write a short sentence for each proposed task. Then identify the information that varies, what the caller needs back, and which effects are intentional. A method named Process does not tell a reader whether it calculates, prints, changes stock, or does all three. A name such as LineTotal makes a more specific promise when accompanied by its price/quantity contract.

| Proposed task | Inputs | Useful result | Intentional external effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Calculate line total | Unit price and quantity | Decimal amount | None |
| Format receipt line | Description and amount | String | None |
| Display receipt | Formatted text | No returned value | Console output |

The table is a design tool, not a rule that every program must contain precisely these three methods. A very small program may keep printing in the caller. A reusable formatting policy may deserve a method even when it is initially called once. Repetition is one reason for extraction; giving a complicated idea a clear name is another.

A common mistake is to extract a group of adjacent lines simply because they are adjacent. Instead ask whether they share one coherent purpose and whether the proposed interfa

Worked example/case/trace

0501_intro_methods.ipynb · cells 10–22
```{index} A Repeated Task Needs a Name
```


A shop prints a store name and separator on every receipt. Copying those two statements for every receipt works at first, but a store-name change must then be made in several places. A method names the task once so callers can reuse it. This is **decomposition**: divide a larger program into understandable responsibilities.

Before refactoring, the statements appear twice:

```text
print store name
print separator
print store name
print separator
```

After refactoring, two calls use one definition. Predict the output: defining the helper does not print anything by itself.


using System;

PrintHeader();
PrintHeader();

static void PrintHeader()
{
    Console.WriteLine("Campus Books");
    Console.WriteLine("------------");
}


The two-line header appears twice, in call order. Change the store name in the definition and run again: both calls use that change. Add a third call without copying the body. This demonstrates reuse rather than merely asserting that reuse is useful.

```{figure} ../../figures/method_decomposition.svg
:alt: Two repeated sets of receipt-header statements become two calls to one PrintHeader definition.

A task name connects each caller to one definition.
```

Read the left column as duplicated instructions and the right as named calls. A method does not automatically make a program better; it should express a coherent responsibility. Separate calculation, input, and presentation when those have different jobs.

Explanation

0503_parameter.ipynb · cells 11–29
```{index} Map Arguments to Parameters
```


Arguments are expressions at the call; parameters are named variables in the definition. Match them by position and compatible type, not by spelling.

| Call | animal in this call | noise in this call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Verse("cow", "moo")` | cow | moo |
| `Verse("duck", "quack")` | duck | quack |
| `Verse(chosenAnimal, chosenNoise)` with chosenAnimal = cow and chosenNoise = moo | cow | moo |

General syntax for a two-input helper is `static resultType Name(type1 parameter1, type2 parameter2) { ... }`; the call is `Name(expression1, expression2)`. The call does not repeat type declarations. In the simple required-parameter examples here, argument number, order, and allowed conversions must match. Swapping two strings can compile and still produce the wrong meaning, so type checking does not replace contract checking.

Each ordinary parameter receives a copy of its argument value. With integers this gives independent numerical values. Later chapters explain how a copied reference can still identify a shared object; do not generalize this into deep-copying every argument.


using System;
int quantity = 4;
int result = Increase(quantity);
Console.WriteLine($"Caller: {quantity}; returned: {result}");
static int Increase(int count)
{
    count = count + 1;
    return count;
}


```{figure} ../../figures/method_parameter_copy.svg
:alt: quantity in the caller stays 4 while a separate copied parameter count changes from 4 to 5 and returns 5.

Different names and separate values in the caller and helper.
```

## Method Tracing




A method can call other methods to help it do its job. Consider the following code:

using System;
InchesToCentimeters(10);
static void InchesToCentimeters(double inches)
{
    double centimeters = inches * 2.54;
    PrintInCentimeters(inches, centimeters);
}
static void PrintInCentimeters(double inches, double centimeters)
{
    Console.WriteLine(inches + "-->" + centimeters);
}
0502_signature_call.ipynb · cells 9–23
```{index} Returned Values Replace Calls
```


using System;
Console.WriteLine(F(3));
Console.WriteLine(F(3) + F(4));
static int F(int x) { return x * x; }


You probably have used mathematical functions in algebra class, but
they all had calculated values associated with them. For instance
if you defined

> F(x)=x{sup}`2`

then it follows that F(3) is 3{sup}`2` = 9, and F(3)+F(4) is
3{sup}`2` + 4{sup}`2` = 9 + 16 = 25.

Method calls in expressions get replaced during evaluation by the value of the method.
That's why when we can directly print out (line# 12-13) the result of the method call in the
following code.

The corresponding definition and examples in C# would be the
following:




The C# syntax to notice is the **return statement**, with the word
`return` followed by an expression, value, or variable(s). Methods that return values
can be used in expressions (e.g., line# 13: F(3) + F(4)), just like in math class. When an
expression with a method call is evaluated, the method call is
effectively replaced temporarily by its returned value. Inside the
C# method, the value to be returned is given by the
expression in the `return` statement.

Since the method returns data, and all data in C# is typed,
there must be a type given for the value returned. Note that the
method header does not start with `static void`.
In place of `void` is `int`. The `void` in earlier method header
meant nothing was returned. The `int` here means that a value *is*
returned and its type is `int`.

After the method `F` finishes executing from inside



```csharp
Console.WriteLine(F(3));
```

Distinguish a `void` method from a value-returning method and use a returned result in a larger expression.

Printing and returning are distinguished explicitly.

Explanation

0502_signature_call.ipynb · cells 5–45
A returned result need not be a number to print. A method can answer a question, and a bool result can become the condition of an if statement. Suppose an order receives free delivery when its subtotal is at least 50. The question is whether an order qualifies, not how much its delivery costs. Keeping those contracts distinct helps explain why two related methods may have different return types.

Trace the boundary: 49.99 does not qualify, 50 qualifies, and 50.01 qualifies. The equality is part of the rule. Writing `>` instead of `>=` would still compile and would pass examples far from the threshold. The boundary cases distinguish the intended rule from that plausible defect.

The general form is `static bool QuestionName(parameterList) { return condition; }`. Here the condition already has type bool. There is no need to convert it into the strings `"true"` and `"false"`; those are text values and cannot serve as an if condition. Printing the answer inside a void method also does not give the caller a Boolean result to use.

Guided variation: qualification additionally requires a nonnegative subtotal. Explain whether that is an input precondition or a condition the method must check. Either design can be explicit, but silently switching between them makes testing and reuse confusing. State the accepted domain before writing your new tests.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


using System;
Console.WriteLine(Qualifies(49.99m));
Console.WriteLine(Qualifies(50m));
Console.WriteLine(Qualifies(50.01m));

    return price + charge;

Both helpers calculate 12.00. PrintTotal writes it immediately and returns no value. CalculateTotal prints nothing; the caller stores 12 and uses it in another expression to print 15.00. A void call cannot be assigned to a decimal. Conversely, calling CalculateTotal and discarding its result is legal, but useless here because that method has no other effect.

**Variation:** change the inputs, store the returned total, and use it twice without repeating user input. **Mistake to diagnose:** `decimal total = PrintTotal(10m, 2m);` asks a void method for a value. The compiler rejects it. Keep calculation reusable and let the caller decide how to display it.

An invoice caller repeats price-times-quantity arithmetic in several places. Extracting LineTotal can give that calculation one name, but a safe refactoring needs more than moving those characters into braces. First record the existing accepted inputs, numerical outputs, formatting and mutation behavior. Then choose the new method's inputs/result so that callers can express the same work without depending on its internal temporary variables.

For price 12 and quantity three, independently calculate 36 before running either version. A fixed packing charge of four makes the order total 40. Keep these two contracts distinct: LineTotal returns 36; OrderTotal returns 40. If the extracted line calculation starts adding packing as well, a caller that already adds packing can charge it twice even though both helper methods contain plausible arithmetic.

| Refactoring stage | Evidence to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Before extraction | Expected amount and current observable output |
| After extracting LineTotal | Same line amount for ordinary and zero inputs |
| After composing OrderTotal | Exactly one application of the fixed charge |
| After formatting a report | Same numerical meaning; display policy stays explicit |

A useful composition passes returned values between helpers. It does not make each helper prompt independently for the same data. If CalculateTotal reads a second quantity while the caller formats the first, the report can display one order and charge another. Keep interaction in the caller and pass the accepted values into calculation helpers.

0504_strings.ipynb · cells 7–46
`Length` is a property, not a method, so it has no parentheses. It gives the number of UTF-16 code units; for the simple Latin-letter examples here these correspond to the visible characters. Some Unicode symbols occupy more than one code unit. Square brackets with an index give one character (a `char`). Indexes start at 0, so the last character is at `Length - 1`.

using System;

string customer = "Ana Diaz";

Console.WriteLine(customer.Length);              // 8 characters, including the space
Console.WriteLine(customer[0]);                  // A (the first character)
Console.WriteLine(customer[customer.Length - 1]); // z (the last character)

An index outside `0` to `Length - 1` stops the program with an `IndexOutOfRangeException`. Chapter 6 shows how to handle errors like this one.

## Cleaning Text



Text typed by people or copied from other systems often has stray spaces and inconsistent capitalization. Clean it before comparing or storing it:

using System;

string rawEmail = "   Ana.Diaz@Example.COM  ";

string trimmed = rawEmail.Trim();     // removes spaces at both ends
string email   = trimmed.ToLower();   // one consistent case for comparisons

Console.WriteLine($"[{rawEmail}]");
Console.WriteLine($"[{email}]");
Console.WriteLine(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace("   "));  // True: nothing but spaces

| Method | Parameters | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `Trim()` | none | a copy without leading and trailing whitespace |
| `ToUpper()`, `ToLower()` | none | a copy in upper or lower

## Cleaning Text



Text typed by people or copied from other systems often has stray spaces and inconsistent capitalization. Clean it before comparing or storing it:

using System;

string rawEmail = "   Ana.Diaz@Example.COM  ";

string trimmed = rawEmail.Trim();     // removes spaces at both ends
string email   = trimmed.ToLower();   // one consistent case for comparisons

Console.WriteLine($"[{rawEmail}]");
Console.WriteLine($"[{email}]");
Console.WriteLine(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace("   "));  // True: nothing but spaces

| Method | Parameters | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `Trim()` | none | a copy without leading and trailing whitespace |
| `ToUpper()`, `ToLower()` | none | a copy in upper or lower case |
| `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s)` | the string to check | `true` if `s` is null, empty, or only whitespace |

`IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is called on the `string` type itself rather than on one string, because it must also work when there is no string at all (`null`).

```{index} string; immutability
```



```{index} Strings Are Immutable
```

## Strings Are Immutable



A string never changes after it is created. Methods such as `ToUpper` do not modify the string they are called on; they return the resulting string value rather than editing the original. If you want to keep the result, assign it to a variable.

using System;

string region = "midwest";
string label  = region.ToUpper();

Console.WriteLine($"region = {region}");  // unchanged
Console.WriteLine($"label  = {label}");   // a new string

The original region remains midwest; label is MIDW

Choose validation or exception handling for a stated failure and use `TryParse` for expected invalid input.

Homework question 5 applies TryParse; the expected-failure distinction is taught.

Explanation

0601_error_handling.ipynb · cells 5–11
A business calculation should either return a meaningful value or make failure explicit. A returned zero could mean that no payment is due; it must not secretly mean that the calculation never succeeded. Use the method-contract ideas from Chapter 5 to decide which inputs the calculation accepts, and the control-flow ideas from Chapters 3 and 4 to follow what happens next.

The general pattern below is schematic. Replace the operation, exception type, and response with the policy for the actual task. The braces delimit blocks. `catch (ExceptionType name)` selects a compatible exception and gives that exception a local name. It does not execute after every successful operation.

```text
try
{
    operationThatMayThrow();
    workThatRequiresSuccess();
}
catch (SpecificExceptionType problem)
{
    permittedFailureResponse();
}
finally
{
    workRequiredWhenLeavingThisTry();
}
```

There can be several catch blocks, ordered from more specific types to more general ones. Only the first matching catch runs for that thrown exception. A `finally` block is optional, as are catch blocks when a try has a finally. Cleanup is not a substitute for handling the failure, and catching a failure does not restart the interrupted statement.

Consider distributing an invoice amount across a positive number of periods. The method rejects zero periods before division. Its caller knows how to explain that particular argument failure. No file API or collection is needed to understand this example.


using System;
static decimal PerPeriod(decimal total, int periods)
{
    if (periods <= 0)
        t
0601_error_handling.ipynb · cells 18–28
```{index} Validation vs. Exceptions
```

## Validation vs. Exceptions




- **Validation** checks expected bad input *before* doing risky work.
- **Exceptions** handle unexpected failures *at runtime*.

Validation should be your first line of defense. Exceptions are a fallback for when something still goes wrong.

```{index} Basic try / catch / finally
```



```{index} Basic try / catch / finally
```

## Basic `try` / `catch` / `finally`




Use `finally` for cleanup (closing resources, resetting state):

try
{
    Console.Write("Enter a number: ");
    int value = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine()!);
    Console.WriteLine($"You entered {value}");
}
catch (FormatException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Input must be a whole number.");
}
catch (OverflowException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Number is outside the valid int range.");
}
finally
{
    Console.WriteLine("Input attempt complete.");
}

```{index} Prefer TryParse for User Input
```



```{index} Prefer TryParse for User Input
```

## Prefer `TryParse` for User Input




If invalid input is *expected*, avoid throwing exceptions entirely:

Console.Write("Enter age: ");
string raw = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";

if (int.TryParse(raw, out int age) && age >= 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Age recorded: {age}");
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine("Please enter a non-negative whole number.");
}

**Guideline:**
- Use `TryParse` for normal input flow where bad input is common.
- Use `try/catch` around operations that can fail unpredictably (file I/O, network, external dependencies).

Worked example/case/trace

0601_error_handling.ipynb · cells 6–9
using System;
static decimal PerPeriod(decimal total, int periods)
{
    if (periods <= 0)
        throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(periods), "Use a positive period count.");
    return total / periods;
}
static void ShowPlan(int periods)
{
    try
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Begin {periods}");
        decimal amount = PerPeriod(120m, periods);
        Console.WriteLine($"Amount {amount:0.00}");
    }
    catch (ArgumentOutOfRangeException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Choose at least one period.");
    }
    finally
    {
        Console.WriteLine("End attempt");
    }
}
ShowPlan(3);
ShowPlan(0);


Read the two attempts separately. For three periods, the call returns 40 and the success message runs. For zero periods, `throw` ends the method before division. Control leaves the unfinished try block, enters the matching catch, and then executes finally. There is no `Amount` line for the failed attempt.

| Attempt | Does the method return an amount? | Runs the catch? | Runs finally? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Three periods | Yes, 40 | No | Yes |
| Zero periods | No | Yes | Yes |
| Negative periods | No | Yes | Yes |

The exception is created by `new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(...)`; `throw` transfers control. `nameof(periods)` records the parameter name without duplicating its spelling in a string. Do not catch an unrelated type merely because its name sounds like an error. An unmatched exception continues to an enclosing handler after this finally runs. The statement after the failed call is not resumed.


## Follow Control Through an Exception



A try block marks the work whose failure policy you are handling. When an operation throws, normal execution of that block stops at that point; statements after the throwing operation are not completed. A matching catch handles the exception. A finally block provides cleanup when control leaves the try/catch in ordinary managed execution, including when a handled exception occurs. It does not promise that a killed process or failed machine will run your cleanup code.

Catch only a failure for which you have a meaningful policy. An empty catch that continues to print Success converts a visible failure into misleading behavior. Catching every exception and replacing it with zero may also destroy the distinction between an unavailable answer and a real zero result. File-related examples below preview Chapter 9; their resource APIs will be developed there, rather than assumed as prerequisites for validation.

Guided prediction: quantity zero is permitted, a negative quantity is rejected, and nonnumeric text asks for correction. What should the program report for `0`, `-1`, and `x`? Explain why all three should not share one generic Invalid message.

```{dropdown} Compare the outcomes
Zero is a valid value under this contract. Minus one is interpretable but outside the business domain. The letter x has no integer interpretation. Different messages identify what the user can change, while avoiding a false success result.
```

if (!int.TryParse(text, out
0601_error_handling.ipynb · cells 34–43

## Throwing Exceptions Intentionally




Throw when an API is used incorrectly and execution should stop:

static double Divide(double numerator, double denominator)
{
    if (denominator == 0)
        throw new ArgumentException("Denominator cannot be zero.", nameof(denominator));

    return numerator / denominator;
}

Console.WriteLine(Divide(10, 2));   // 5
Console.WriteLine(Divide(10, 0));   // throws

This is better than returning meaningless sentinel values that hide bugs.

```{index} Error Message Quality
```



```{index} Error Message Quality
```

## Error Message Quality




| Bad | Better |
|-----|--------|
| `"Error happened"` | `"Could not open 'scores.txt'. Check that the file exists and that you have read permission."` |

Good error messages are: **specific**, **user-actionable**, and free of raw internal noise.

```{index} Common Mistakes
```



```{index} Common Mistakes
```

## Common Mistakes




- Catching `Exception` everywhere and ignoring details
- Swallowing exceptions without logging or reporting
- Using exceptions for normal control flow (use `TryParse` instead)
- Showing stack traces directly to end users

0602_debugging_workflow.ipynb · cells 5–43
Before the retained array and CSV applications, use a calculation that needs only methods, decisions, and loops. A shop awards one credit for each of the first `days` days. With three days, the expected credits are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. This expectation comes from the problem, not from running the implementation.

The following complete cell deliberately contains a logic defect. It compiles, but the loop stops too soon. A compiler cannot infer that the business rule requires the last day.


using System;
static int Credits(int days)
{
    int total = 0;
    for (int day = 1; day < days; day++) // Intentional defect: excludes the last day.
        total += day;
    return total;
}
Console.WriteLine($"Expected 6; actual {Credits(3)}");


Save this code as the Program.cs of a console project using the Appendix B workflow. Run `dotnet run` to reproduce the failure before starting a debugger. In VS Code, open the folder containing the project, set a breakpoint on `total += day`, and start the C# debugger for that project. The browser cell can demonstrate the result; the editor debugger supplies paused state.

Write the hypothesis: “the loop omits day three.” A breakpoint pauses **before** the marked statement executes. At its first stop, watch `day`, `days`, and `total`. Step Over the update, then continue to the next stop. Use the method's own frame in the Call Stack panel to inspect its local values. The call stack explains who called the method; it is not a list of all previous loop iterations.

| Observation | day | total before addition | total after addition |
| --- | ---: | ---:

using System;
static int Credits(int days)
{
    int total = 0;
    for (int day = 1; day < days; day++) // Intentional defect: excludes the last day.
        total += day;
    return total;
}
Console.WriteLine($"Expected 6; actual {Credits(3)}");


Save this code as the Program.cs of a console project using the Appendix B workflow. Run `dotnet run` to reproduce the failure before starting a debugger. In VS Code, open the folder containing the project, set a breakpoint on `total += day`, and start the C# debugger for that project. The browser cell can demonstrate the result; the editor debugger supplies paused state.

Write the hypothesis: “the loop omits day three.” A breakpoint pauses **before** the marked statement executes. At its first stop, watch `day`, `days`, and `total`. Step Over the update, then continue to the next stop. Use the method's own frame in the Call Stack panel to inspect its local values. The call stack explains who called the method; it is not a list of all previous loop iterations.

| Observation | day | total before addition | total after addition |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| First stopped iteration | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| Second stopped iteration | 2 | 1 | 3 |
| Third iteration required by the contract | 3 | 3 | 6 |

The third row does not occur in the defective run. After the second addition, `day` becomes three and `day < days` is false. This distinguishes a missing iteration from an incorrect addition. If all three additions had occurred, investigate a later overwrite or the printed expression instead of changing the boundary blindly.

Repair only

## Use a Different Symptom to Challenge the Hypothesis


The output compares independently derived expectations with actual results. Zero checks that the loop can run no times; one exposes the original omission immediately; three preserves the original failure; four checks another ordinary case. The negative-input guard is a contract improvement, not the cause of the original wrong total. Record those as separate changes when reviewing a repair.

Guided task: suppose a variant returns 7 for three days. Fill a trace with starting total one instead of zero. Does changing `<` to `<=` alone explain or repair that symptom? Then add an intentional `total = day` in place of `total += day`. Predict the output for four days before debugging.

```{dropdown} Compare the defects
Starting at one adds an unwanted extra credit. With the corrected boundary it yields seven for three days. Assignment instead of accumulation discards earlier credits and returns four for four days. The boundary, initialization and update are separate hypotheses. A trace showing state before and after the update distinguishes them.
```

## Preparing Project

The idea of TDD is to write tests first, so that you will be focused with the requirements and not
to be distracted by your own coding. That's why we start with simple test cases in the test project to test the
units in the application project. After you make sure the application tests can pass, you then improve the
units (methods, classes) in the application project.

Explanation

0603_testing.ipynb · cells 8–14
Assuming that you have a killer app like:

    namespace IntroCSCS
    {
       public class Calculator
       {
          public int Add(int x, int y)
          {
             return x + y;
          }
       }
    }

Let’s say you want to know that this app is doing what you intend for it to do. The best
way to achieve that validation is probably by providing a set of validation code
that does nothing but running the app to **test** if the results come out right, such as the
following:

namespace IntroCSCS
{
    public class Calculator
    {
        public int Add(int x, int y)
        {
            return x + y;
        }
    }

    internal class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            var calculator = new Calculator();

            if (calculator.Add(15, 20) != 35)
            {
                throw new InvalidOperationException();
            }
            Console.WriteLine("OK");
        }
    }
}

Currently, there is only one method (Add) in the Calculator class. As you add more methods,
    you will need more cases and your Program.cs will become disorganized. This is where the
    established tooling comes in.

## The Unit Testing Process




    One of the fundamental principles of adopting unit testing is to follow a
    TDD (Test Driven Development) approach where you will:

    1. Write a failing test (to prove the point that the test works)
    2. Implement the functionality to pass the test
    3. Refactor the code while keeping the test

## Framework Setup and Test Attributes



After the test cases are prepared, a test framework (e.g., xUnit, NUnit, or MSTest) is
added to the project. From there, for NUnit, you can run the following command to add NUnit
to your test project (xUnit and MSTest follow similar syntax) [3]:

dotnet add [location of your test csproj file] reference [location of the csproj file for project to be tested]

The method test code would look like the follows:

    using System;
    using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
    using BasicMath;
    namespace BasicMathTest {

    [TestClass]

Explain why an array is a collection, then declare, initialize, and access one-dimensional arrays within their valid index ranges.

Explanation

0701_onedim.ipynb · cells 5–21
A store records quantities for four delivery slots. Four unrelated variables would require four separate names and repeated processing code. An array gives the values one name and a position-based organization. Its length is fixed when the array object is created; its elements can still change. This connects the collection idea to variables: assignment changes a value in a particular slot, while a loop chooses which slot to visit.

Use these schematic forms to distinguish three actions:

```text
elementType[] name;                         // Declare a variable for an array reference.
name = new elementType[lengthExpression];    // Create an array and store its reference.
name[indexExpression] = valueExpression;    // Replace one element of that array.
```

`[]` after the type describes the array type. Brackets after a variable name select an element. Length counts elements; an index identifies a position. For four slots, the valid indexes are zero through three. Index four is already outside the array.


using System;
int[] quantities = new int[4];
Console.WriteLine($"Before: {string.Join(", ", quantities)}");
quantities[0] = 7;
quantities[1] = 5;
quantities[2] = 9;
quantities[3] = 6;
quantities[2] = 4 * quantities[1] - quantities[3];
for (int index = 0; index < quantities.Length; index++)
    Console.WriteLine($"Slot {index}: {quantities[index]}");


The first line shows default values after allocation. The later assignment reads indexes one and three, computes `4 * 5 - 6`, and stores 14 at index two. It does not insert a fifth quantity or change the array's length.

| Ind

0701_onedim.ipynb · cells 6–11
using System;
int[] quantities = new int[4];
Console.WriteLine($"Before: {string.Join(", ", quantities)}");
quantities[0] = 7;
quantities[1] = 5;
quantities[2] = 9;
quantities[3] = 6;
quantities[2] = 4 * quantities[1] - quantities[3];
for (int index = 0; index < quantities.Length; index++)
    Console.WriteLine($"Slot {index}: {quantities[index]}");


The first line shows default values after allocation. The later assignment reads indexes one and three, computes `4 * 5 - 6`, and stores 14 at index two. It does not insert a fifth quantity or change the array's length.

| Index | After allocation | After four assignments | After the calculation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 0 | 7 | 7 |
| 1 | 0 | 5 | 5 |
| 2 | 0 | 9 | 14 |
| 3 | 0 | 6 | 6 |

Read the table by column to see a whole array state, or by row to follow one element. The loop's condition checks `index < quantities.Length` before each read. The semicolons in a for header separate initialization, condition and update. A comma between condition and update is not the syntax for this loop.

An initializer such as `int[] quantities = { 7, 5, 9, 6 };` creates the same four initial values more compactly. Use `foreach` when only the values matter; use an index when the task selects or changes positions. A foreach loop can stop early with `break`, but it does not directly provide the current position for an indexed update.

```text
else
```

using System;
static void ShowLast(int[] values)
{
    if (values.Length > 0)
        Console.WriteLine($"Last: {values[values.Length - 1]}");
    else
        Console.WriteLine("No deliveries");
}
ShowLast(new int[] { 7, 5, 9, 6 });
ShowLast(Array.Empty<int>());


The comparison is `>`. For an empty array, evaluating index -1 would be invalid, so the read occurs only inside the guarded branch. For one element, Length is one and its last index is zero. Use PrintInts to label the inputs and outputs for all ten original array tasks: PrintInts, ReadInts, Minimum, CountEven, PairwiseAdd, NewPairwiseAdd, IsAscending, PrintAscendingValues, PrintRuns, and DotProduct.

- `void PrintInts(string label, int[] a)` prints the label, then each value preceded by a space, and finishes the line. For `{3,-1,5}` and label `Nums:`, print `Nums: 3 -1 5`.
- `int Minimum(int[] a)` returns the smallest value; require at least one element. With `{5,7,4,9}`, return four. Check every element, including the final one.
- `int CountEven(int[] a)` returns the count of values divisible by two. With `{-4,7,6,12,9}`, return three. Zero and negative even values also count. Empty input has count zero.
- `bool IsAscending(int[] a)` checks **nondecreasing** order: every next value is at least the preceding value. Equal neighbors are allowed. Fewer than two entries is ascending. `{2,5,5,8}` is true, while `{2,5,3,8}` is false. Stop as soon as one descending pair disproves the claim.

C07-O2 · supported

Traverse arrays with `for` and `foreach` to calculate results and update elements where appropriate.

Totals, minimum indexes, counts, and ordering scans have applications.

Explanation

0703_array_processing.ipynb · cells 5–9
An array gives many values one shared organization. To calculate a total, the program still needs a rule for visiting those values and combining them. The accumulator pattern connects arrays to Chapter 4: initialize a running result, visit each relevant element, and update the result exactly once for that element. The array changes where input values come from; it does not change the meaning of a loop or an assignment.

Suppose daily quantities are 4, 0 and 7. Before the first iteration the total is zero because no entries have been processed. After each iteration, total should equal the sum of the processed prefix. This claim explains both the initialization and the update. It also provides a way to find a defect before the final result is printed.

| Processed positions | Next position | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 4 |
| 0 and 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 0 through 2 | End | 11 |

A for loop exposes positions and is useful when you must report an index or replace elements. A foreach loop exposes each element value directly and is useful when only those values matter. Do not assume that changing a foreach iteration variable updates an array element. Use explicit indexing when the operation is defined in terms of changing positions.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

A method parameter of type int[] receives a copy of the reference value. Caller and helper can therefore refer to the same array. Replacing an element through the helper is visible through the caller's reference. Reassigning the helper's parameter to a different array changes that local parameter, not the caller's variable. This connects ordinary parameter passing from Chapter 5 with reference aliasing, without requiring pass-by-reference parameter syntax.

State whether a processing helper may mutate its input. A Total helper normally only reads values. An ApplyAdjustment helper might intentionally replace them. If a reporting task must preserve original values, computing into another array or returning a separate result is a different contract from modifying the original and restoring it afterward.

An empty array is a real collection with Length zero. A total over no quantities naturally returns zero under the sum contract. A request for the first element has no valid result on that same input. Handle the operation's domain rather than giving every array helper the same empty-case behavior. A null reference is different again: there is no array object whose Length can be read.

(alias)=

## References and Aliases




Object variables, like arrays, are references,
and this has important implications for
assignment.

With a primitive type like an `int`, an assignment copies the data:

`{image} ../../figures/intCopy.png :align: center :alt: copying an int :width: 90 pt`

In the diagram, the contents of the memory box labeled `b` is copied to the
memory box labeled `d`. The value of `d` starts off equal to the value of `b`,
but can later be changed independently.

Contrast an assignment with arrays. The value that is copied is the *reference*,
not the array data itself, so both end up pointing at the *same* actual array:

`{image} ../../figures/arrayAlias.png :align: center :alt: copying an array reference :width: 300 pt`

Hereafter, array assignments like:

    b[2] = -10;
    d[1] = 55;

would both change the *same* array. Now `b` and `d` are essentially
names for the same thing (the actual array). The technical term matches English:
The names are *aliases*.

This may seem like a pretty silly discussion. Why bother to give two different
names to the same object? Isn’t one enough? In fact it is very important
in function/method calls. An array reference can be passed as an actual value,
and it is the array *reference* that is copied to the formal parameter, so
the formal parameter name is an **alias** for the actual parameter name.

If an array passed as a parameter to a method has elements changed in the
method, then the change affects the actual parameter array.
The change *remains* in the actual parameter arr

## Ascending Values and Runs

```{index} Ascending Values and Runs
```

`PrintAscendingValues(int[] a)` selects a nondecreasing subsequence, keeping the first value and then only values at least as large as the last printed value. For `{5, 2, 8, 4, 8, 11, 6, 7, 10}`, print `5 8 8 11`. This greedy selection does not sort the input or promise the longest possible subsequence.

`PrintRuns(int[] a)` prints **every** value in input order, starting a new line whenever the next value is smaller than the previous value. For `{2, 5, 8, 3, 9, 9, 8}`, print:

```text
2 5 8
3 9 9
8
```

In the first task compare with the last **selected** value; in the second compare with the previous **input** value. Test empty arrays, one value, equal values, strictly increasing values, and strictly decreasing values. Do not access `a[0]` until you know that an element exists.

## Rectangular Arrays (Two Dimensional)




While a one-dimensional array works for a sequence of data,
you need something more for a two dimensional table,
where data values vary over both row and column.

If we have a table of integers, for instance with three
rows and four columns:

```
2 4  7 55
3 1  8 10
6 0 49 12
```

We could declare an array variable of the right size as



int[,] table = new int[3, 4];



Multiple indices are separated by commas inside the square brackets.
In declaring an array type, no indices are included so the `[,]`
indicates a two dimensional array. Where the `new` object is being created,
the values inside the square brackets give each dimension.

In general the notation for a two dimensional array declaration is:

> **type** `[, ]` **variableName**

and to create a new array with default values:

> new **type** `[` *intExpression1*`,` *intExpression2* `]`

where the expressions evaluate to integers for the dimensions.

To assign the 8 in the table above, consider that it is in the second
row in normal counting, but we start array indices at 0, so there are
rows 0, 1, and 2, and the 8 has row index 1.
Again starting with index 0 for columns, the 8 is at index
1\. We can assign a value to that position with



int[,] table = { {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9} };
table[1, 2] = 8;



In fact a two dimensional array just needs two indices that could mean
anything. For instance, it was just the standard convention,
calling the left index the row. They could have been switched everyw

In general the notation for a two dimensional array declaration is:

and to create a new array with default values:

> new **type** `[` *intExpression1*`,` *intExpression2* `]`

where the expressions evaluate to integers for the dimensions.

To assign the 8 in the table above, consider that it is in the second
row in normal counting, but we start array indices at 0, so there are
rows 0, 1, and 2, and the 8 has row index 1.
Again starting with index 0 for columns, the 8 is at index
1\. We can assign a value to that position with



int[,] table = { {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9} };
table[1, 2] = 8;



In fact a two dimensional array just needs two indices that could mean
anything. For instance, it was just the standard convention,
calling the left index the row. They could have been switched everywhere, and
assume the notation `table[column, row]`:



int[,] table = new int[4, 3];
table[2, 1] = 8;



but we will *stick with* the original `[row, column]` model.

Data indexed by more than two integer indices can be stored in a higher
dimension array, with more indices between the square braces. We
will only consider two dimensional arrays in the examples here.

common storage tasks; write basic `List<T>` code for growing ordered data; and
write basic `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` code for key/value lookup. Students should
also recognize eight collection families, explain their access contracts, and
distinguish sharing a collection reference from copying its elements.

0801_collections.ipynb · cells 5–16
A bookstore handles many groups of values: the quantities sold during a week, the items in a customer's basket, stock quantities indexed by product code, and orders waiting for collection. Each group contains several values, but the program does different work with each one. Finding Tuesday's sales, looking up a product code, and selecting the next order are different questions. The way you organize the values should support the question you need to answer.

A **collection** groups values and provides operations for working with them. Arrays are the first collection type we studied: {doc}`Chapter 7 <../07_arrays/0700_arrays>` introduced fixed-length, indexed sequences. Keeping that chapter separate gave us time to practice indexing, traversal, and multidimensional data. It did not put arrays outside the collection category. This chapter broadens our choices to other ready-made collection types in the .NET standard library. These classes are often called **built-in collections** because they come with .NET, although they are library types used by C#, rather than separate C# language features. Arrays have direct C# language syntax, such as `int[]`; collection classes such as `List<int>` are library types. Both belong in our collection-family comparison.

This section introduces the big ideas before the detailed syntax: what a collection promises, how values can be accessed, and how to choose among collection families. You will see eight useful families and small demonstrations of their behavior. The next two sections develop `List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` in depth. F

## Collection Families




```{index} collection; families; access pattern
```


An **access pattern** describes how a program usually retrieves and processes its data. Do you know an item's position? Do you know a key that identifies it? Do you only need to know whether it is present? Must items be processed in arrival order?

In the type names below, `T` stands for an element type you choose, such as `string` or `int`. `TKey`, `TValue`, and `TPriority` name the corresponding key, value, and priority types. The examples later in this section use `new` to construct a collection and dot notation to call its operations. First, read the table for the organizing idea behind each family; the next discussion explains generic type arguments before you examine the individual examples.

**Table: An introductory map of .NET collection families.** Adapted from Microsoft's collection-selection guidance, with original business examples and an added priority-queue entry.[^0801_collections-collection-guide][^0801_collections-priority-queue] These eight families are a teaching selection, not Microsoft's exhaustive classification. Sorted variants and collections for specialized settings extend this map.

| Family | Representative type | Main access rule | Business use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array | `T[]`, such as `int[]` | Retrieve by index; length is fixed. | Store one quantity for each of five business days. |
| List | `List<T>` | Retrieve by index; the sequence can grow or shrink. | Build a customer's basket as

The family map tells you which question a collection can answer. Now describe an operation with three parts: what must already be true, what changes, and what result the caller receives. This makes the cross-family tables below more useful than a list of names to memorize.

Consider the sequence of product codes PEN, PAD, PEN. Removing by value selects an occurrence matching a value; removing by index selects a position. Popping a stack or dequeuing a queue selects according to processing order instead. Even when each operation reduces a count by one, it need not select the same element. Compare the selection rule before comparing the method spelling.

| Intended action | Information supplied | Question to ask before calling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove a known product code from a list | Value | Which matching occurrence is removed? |
| Remove the third list position | Index 2 | Does that position exist now? |
| Take the next queued request | No identifying key | Is the queue nonempty? |
| Find stock for a product code | Key | What happens when that key is absent? |

Returning a value and mutating a collection are independent possibilities. A lookup can return a result without removing anything. A removal can both change storage and report success. A Try-style operation supplies a Boolean success signal so that an absent result can be distinguished from a legitimate default value. Read both the success flag and the output value under the documented contract.

### Arrays and Lists




```{index} array; list; index; sequence
```


A **sequence** gives its elements positions. In the arrays and lists used here, positions are indexed from zero. Both can contain repeated values. Their order is the order of the sequence, which is not necessarily sorted order.

An array's length remains fixed after creation, but its elements can change. Fixed length does not mean read-only data. A list manages storage as elements are added or removed. Its `Count` reports the number of elements currently in the list; an array uses `Length`.

## Traversal and Shared References




```{index} traversal; enumeration; IEnumerable; reference; alias; mutation
```


**Traversal**, also called **enumeration**, means visiting a collection's elements. `foreach` provides familiar syntax for this work, but the order and the kind of element you receive depend on the collection. Arrays and lists follow their sequence order. A dictionary enumerates key/value entries. A set supports enumeration, but its purpose is membership rather than sorted traversal. `PriorityQueue` is a special case: it exposes an `UnorderedItems` view for enumeration instead of supporting `foreach` directly on the queue. That view does not promise priority order; use successive removals when you need that order.

The enumerable collection types demonstrated here implement `IEnumerable<T>`, an interface describing how to enumerate values.[^0801_collections-collection-interface] You do not need to write an interface to use these library collections. Later chapters explain how a type can provide this capability itself. Also distinguish traversal from removal: looping through a queue with `foreach` does not serve and remove its waiting items.

Here a traversal computes a total without changing the stored quantities. The accumulator starts at zero, so an empty list would produce a total of zero.

using System.Collections.Generic;

List<int> quantities = new List<int> { 2, 1, 3 };
int total = 0;
foreach (int quantity in quantities)
{
    total += quantity;

The declaration and construction patterns are:

```text
List<elementType> name = new List<elementType>();
List<elementType> name = new List<elementType> { item1, item2 };
List<elementType> copy = new List<elementType>(existingSequence);
```

These are templates. Replace `elementType` with a type such as `string` and supply actual values. Angle brackets choose the stored type. Parentheses supply constructor arguments; an empty argument list creates an empty list. The initializer's braces supply starting items. Copying into a new list differs from assigning another variable to the same list; the last example copies the elements into a new outer collection.

## Lists Basics



A `List<T>` starts with an element type and then supports the everyday sequence operations you expect: add an item, count the items, read an item by index, and loop through the items. The index rules are the same as arrays: the first item is at index `0`.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<int> numbers = new List<int>();
numbers.Add(10);
numbers.Add(20);
numbers.Add(30);

Console.WriteLine(numbers[0]);
Console.WriteLine(numbers.Count);

foreach (int number in numbers)
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);
}


A list can also be initialized with values. A `for` loop is useful when the index is part of the output or logic; a `foreach` loop is simpler when you only need each value.

`Count` is the number of stored elements. `Capacity` is the number of positions reserved internally before another growth allocation is needed; it can

## Lists Basics



A `List<T>` starts with an element type and then supports the everyday sequence operations you expect: add an item, count the items, read an item by index, and loop through the items. The index rules are the same as arrays: the first item is at index `0`.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<int> numbers = new List<int>();
numbers.Add(10);
numbers.Add(20);
numbers.Add(30);

Console.WriteLine(numbers[0]);
Console.WriteLine(numbers.Count);

foreach (int number in numbers)
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);
}


A list can also be initialized with values. A `for` loop is useful when the index is part of the output or logic; a `foreach` loop is simpler when you only need each value.

`Count` is the number of stored elements. `Capacity` is the number of positions reserved internally before another growth allocation is needed; it can exceed `Count`. `Clear()` removes the elements but normally keeps that reserved capacity. Use `Count` for valid element indexes, not `Capacity`. You do not need to tune capacity for the examples in this chapter.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<string> names = new List<string> { "Alice", "Bob", "Charlie" };

for (int i = 0; i < names.Count; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{i}: {names[i]}");
}

0803_dictionary.ipynb · cells 7–55
We can initialize an English-Spanish dictionary `e2sp` with



using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
Dictionary<string, string> e2sp = new Dictionary<string, string>();

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {e2sp.Count}; [{string.Join(", ", e2sp)}]");



That is quite a mouthful! The C# `var` keyword (implicitly-typed local variable) syntax
is handy to shorten it as you do not have to repeat the type name:



using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
var e2sp = new Dictionary<string, string>();

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {e2sp.Count}; [{string.Join(", ", e2sp)}]");



The general generic type syntax therefore is:

> `Dictionary<` **keyType**`,` **valueType** `>`

For example, if you are counting the number of repetitions of words in a document, you are
likely to want a `Dictionary` mapping each word to its number of repetitions so far:



using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
var wordCount = new Dictionary<string, int>();

Console.WriteLine($"New count dictionary entries: {wordCount.Count}");



If your friends all have a personal list of phone numbers, you might look them up
with a dictionary with a string name for the key and a `List` of personal phone number
strings for the value. The type could be `Dictionary<string, List<string>>`.
This example illustrates how one generic type can be built on another.

There is no restriction on the value type. Keys need stable equality and hash behavior while stored; immutable keys such as strings make that easier to ensure. See {ref}`dictionary-efficiency`.

Similar to an array or `List`, you can assign and reference elements of
a `Dictionary`, using square bracket notation. The difference is that the
reference is through a key, not a sequential index, as in:



using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
Dictionary<string, string> e2sp = new Dictionary<string, string>();
e2sp["one"] = "uno";
e2sp["two"] = "dos";

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {e2sp.Count}; [{string.Join(", ", e2sp)}]");



or, you can use the Dictionary.Add() method:



using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
Dictionary<string, string> e2sp = new Dictionary<string, string>();
e2sp["one"] = "uno";
e2sp["two"] = "dos";
e2sp.Add("three", "tres");

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {e2sp.Count}; [{string.Join(", ", e2sp)}]");


```{index} dictionary; duplicate key
```

Unlike the indexer, `Add` does not overwrite an existing key — it throws an `ArgumentException` if the key is already present, since `Add` is meant for inserting a brand-new entry:

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
Dictionary<string, string> e2sp = new Dictionary<string, string>();
e2sp.Add("one", "uno");
try
{
    e2sp.Add("one", "ONE");  // "one" is already a key
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Error: {ex.Message}");
}

e2sp["one"] = "ONE";  // the indexer updates an existing key instead
Console.WriteLine(e2sp["one"]);

A dictionary does not automatically print its entries when you pass the dictionary object itself to `Console.WriteLine`. In application code, display the size with `Count`, access individual values by key, or loop through the entries.

Use `The pen, pen and book!` first. The ignore set excludes articles, `and`, and empty strings produced by adjacent separators. Normalization turns words into lowercase before using them as keys.

| Token | Decision | Counted entries afterward |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the | Ignore | None |
| pen | New key | pen → 1 |
| empty token | Ignore | pen → 1 |
| pen | Existing key: increment | pen → 2 |
| and | Ignore | pen → 2 |
| book | New key | pen → 2; book → 1 |
| trailing empty token | Ignore | Unchanged |

Follow one iteration per row. The important connection is the same insert/update distinction used for stock: a new word starts at 1; a repeated word updates its existing count. The ignore set answers membership; the dictionary associates each word with a number; a list of keys supplies a sortable reporting sequence.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

HashSet<string> ignored = new HashSet<string> { "a", "an", "and", "the" };
Dictionary<string, int> counts = GetCounts("The pen, pen and book!", ignored);
PrintCounts(counts, 1);
Console.WriteLine($"Distinct counted words: {counts.Count}");

static Dictionary<string, int> GetCounts(string s, HashSet<string> ignore)
{
    char[] sep = "\n\t !@#$%^&*()_+{}|[]\\:\";<>?,./".ToCharArray();
    string[] words = s.ToLowerInvariant().Split(sep);
    ignore.Add("");
    var wc = new Dictionary<string, int>();
    foreach (string w in words)
    {
        if (!ignore.Contains(w))
        {
            if (wc.ContainsKey(w)) wc[w]++;
            else wc[w] = 1;
        }
    }
    return wc;
}

## Traversal and Shared References




```{index} traversal; enumeration; IEnumerable; reference; alias; mutation
```


**Traversal**, also called **enumeration**, means visiting a collection's elements. `foreach` provides familiar syntax for this work, but the order and the kind of element you receive depend on the collection. Arrays and lists follow their sequence order. A dictionary enumerates key/value entries. A set supports enumeration, but its purpose is membership rather than sorted traversal. `PriorityQueue` is a special case: it exposes an `UnorderedItems` view for enumeration instead of supporting `foreach` directly on the queue. That view does not promise priority order; use successive removals when you need that order.

The enumerable collection types demonstrated here implement `IEnumerable<T>`, an interface describing how to enumerate values.[^0801_collections-collection-interface] You do not need to write an interface to use these library collections. Later chapters explain how a type can provide this capability itself. Also distinguish traversal from removal: looping through a queue with `foreach` does not serve and remove its waiting items.

Here a traversal computes a total without changing the stored quantities. The accumulator starts at zero, so an empty list would produce a total of zero.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<int> quantities = new List<int> { 2, 1, 3 };
int total = 0;
foreach (int quantity in quantities)
{
    total += quantity;
}

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {quantitie

0804_collection_operations.ipynb · cells 63–69
The mutable library collection classes shown here are **reference types**. A variable refers to a collection object. Assigning that variable to another variable copies the reference, rather than making a second collection. Two names for the same object are **aliases**. Arrays have reference behavior too; this continues the idea introduced in Chapter 7.

Consider a basket shown in two parts of a program. If both variables refer to the same basket, adding an item through one variable is visible through the other. If you need a separate snapshot of a list's elements, you must explicitly create a new collection.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

List<string> basket = new List<string> { "NOTEBOOK" };
List<string> sameBasket = basket;
List<string> snapshot = new List<string>(basket);

sameBasket.Add("PEN");

Console.WriteLine($"Original basket: {basket.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Alias: {sameBasket.Count}");
Console.WriteLine($"Snapshot: {snapshot.Count}");


`basket` and `sameBasket` refer to one list containing two strings. `snapshot` is a different list containing the one string that was present when it was created. This is a copy of the elements, not a general promise to duplicate every object an element might refer to. Chapter 11 revisits that distinction with objects and composition.

Mutation means changing an existing object's state, such as adding to a list. Reassigning a variable to a different list is a different action. This distinction matters when collections are passed to methods or shared between parts of a program. An operation can affect more

0703_array_processing.ipynb · cells 8–8
A method parameter of type int[] receives a copy of the reference value. Caller and helper can therefore refer to the same array. Replacing an element through the helper is visible through the caller's reference. Reassigning the helper's parameter to a different array changes that local parameter, not the caller's variable. This connects ordinary parameter passing from Chapter 5 with reference aliasing, without requiring pass-by-reference parameter syntax.

State whether a processing helper may mutate its input. A Total helper normally only reads values. An ApplyAdjustment helper might intentionally replace them. If a reporting task must preserve original values, computing into another array or returning a separate result is a different contract from modifying the original and restoring it afterward.

An empty array is a real collection with Length zero. A total over no quantities naturally returns zero under the sum contract. A request for the first element has no valid result on that same input. Handle the operation's domain rather than giving every array helper the same empty-case behavior. A null reference is different again: there is no array object whose Length can be read.

Guided exercise: replace the quantities with 0, 0 and 7. Predict the accumulator trace. Then predict the result for an empty array. Finally, explain whether the read-only total should change if another variable is assigned the array reference. An alias alone changes no element, but a later mutation through either alias can change what a subsequent total reads.

## Common Pitfall: Modifying a List While Iterating



`foreach` keeps an internal position in the list as it loops. Adding or removing elements through that same list while a `foreach` is still running invalidates that position, and C# detects it: the loop throws an `InvalidOperationException` rather than silently skipping or duplicating elements.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
List<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
try
{
    foreach (int n in numbers)
    {
        if (n % 2 == 0)
        {
            numbers.Remove(n);  // modifying the list mid-foreach
        }
    }
}
catch (InvalidOperationException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Error: {ex.Message}");
}

Loop over the indices backwards instead, so removing an element does not disturb the indices you still need to visit. (`List<T>` also has a `RemoveAll` method that removes every matching element in one call — it is explained once you have seen the lambda syntax it takes, in a later chapter.)

## Accessing Data in Dictionary



General syntax, using an existing dictionary:

```text
dictionary.Add(key, value);          // Insert a new key; reject a duplicate.
dictionary[key] = value;             // Insert or replace.
valueType found = dictionary[key];   // Key must exist.
bool exists = dictionary.ContainsKey(key);
bool removed = dictionary.Remove(key);
dictionary.Clear();
```

Brackets select a key, not an integer position. `key` and `value` must match the declared type arguments. Removal takes a key and reports success. `Clear` empties the same dictionary object; assignment to a new dictionary is a different action. The runnable examples below show both ordinary usage and the missing/duplicate-key mistakes.



Similar to an array or `List`, you can assign and reference elements of

reference is through a key, not a sequential index, as in:

e2sp["one"] = "uno";
e2sp["two"] = "dos";

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {e2sp.Count}; [{string.Join(", ", e2sp)}]");



or, you can use the Dictionary.Add() method:



using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
Dictionary<string, string> e2sp = new Dictionary<string, string>();
e2sp["one"] = "uno";
e2sp["two"] = "dos";
e2sp.Add("three", "tres");

Console.WriteLine($"Entries: {e2sp.Count}; [{string.Join(", ", e2sp)}]");

## Check the Help Desk’s Contract

```{index} Check the Help Desk’s Contract
```


Before submitting, test the connections between text processing, list access, and dictionary lookup. The matching policy is the first recognized word in message order, not the first key in dictionary traversal. The supplied examples assume at least one fallback reply.

| Test | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `Where is my INVOICE?` | Match invoice after case normalization. |
| `Hello there!` or an empty message | Use a fallback; do not index a missing dictionary key. |
| `slow slow` | Count one matched message for slow, not two word occurrences. |
| `refund invoice` | Choose refund under the first-recognized-word rule. |
| More unmatched messages than fallbacks | Rotate through fallback replies without an out-of-range index. |
| Empty fallback list | Explain why `% fallbacks.Count` is invalid and specify a validation or default-response policy before extending the program. |

0901_stream_file.ipynb · cells 17–40
Among the file handling methods is the convenience class `File`, which provides `static methods` for the creation,
copying, deletion, moving, and opening of a single file, and aids in the creation of `FileStream` objects. For example,
the Create(), WriteAllText, ReadAllText() and File.Exists() can be used to perform basic file operations
among other methods:

**Methods in File Class**

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `AppendText()` | Appends text at the end of an existing file |
| `Copy()` | Copies a file |
| `Create()` | Creates or overwrites a file |
| `Delete()` | Deletes a file |
| `Exists()` | Tests whether the file exists |
| `ReadAllText()` | Reads the contents of a file |
| `Replace()` | Replaces the contents of a file with the contents of another file |
| `WriteAllText()` | Creates a new file and writes the contents to it. If the file already exists, it will be overwritten. |

Sine class `File` provides `static methods`, we can `call` the methods directly by using the `dot notation`
without having to create a new instance of the class. For example, with `File` class, when you want to write
some content to a file, you can simply say `File.ReadAllText(string path, string content)` to write the
string content to the path file.

You can perform tests such as the following in a small VS Code project to get familiar with the methods:

1.  Create a file using `File.Create (path)`: // path means filename + the file's directory path

        > File.Create("MyTest.txt");

2.  Check if a file exists using `File.Exists (path)`:

        > if (File.Exists("

0902_file_operations.ipynb · cells 5–25
A report has two different identities: its contents and its location. Reading valid quantities from the wrong file is still a failed workflow. Start by constructing one known path, use it consistently, and make ownership of temporary files explicit. This connects Chapter 6's cleanup policy with the stream operations introduced in the preceding section.

`Path.Combine(directory, fileName)` returns a string using the platform's path rules. It does not create a directory or a file. `Directory.CreateDirectory(path)` creates the directory if needed. The general using-statement form is a syntax pattern:

```text
using (ResourceType name = acquireResource())
{
    statementsThatUse(name);
}
```

The closing brace marks disposal of the acquired resource. The related declaration form, `using ResourceType name = acquireResource();`, keeps the resource until the end of its enclosing scope. Choose the scope deliberately: a writer must be disposed before another operation relies on its completed output.

This example creates a uniquely named temporary directory owned by this run, writes two lines, closes the writer, reads those lines, closes the reader, and deletes only that owned directory. It does not overwrite a student's report or depend on a preexisting file.

Directory.CreateDirectory(workspace);
try
{
    string reportPath = Path.Combine(workspace, "report.txt");
    using (StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter(reportPath, append: false))
    {

Worked example/case/trace

0902_file_operations.ipynb · cells 6–10
using System;
using System.IO;
string workspace = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "cscs_report_" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N"));
Directory.CreateDirectory(workspace);
try
{
    string reportPath = Path.Combine(workspace, "report.txt");
    using (StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter(reportPath, append: false))
    {
        writer.WriteLine("Order 101");
        writer.WriteLine("Units 3");
    }
    using (StreamReader reader = new StreamReader(reportPath))
    {
        Console.WriteLine(reader.ReadLine());
        Console.WriteLine(reader.ReadLine());
        Console.WriteLine($"At end: {reader.EndOfStream}");
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"Exists before cleanup: {File.Exists(reportPath)}");
}
finally
{
    Directory.Delete(workspace, recursive: true);
}
Console.WriteLine($"Directory remains: {Directory.Exists(workspace)}");


Each using block releases its stream when the block ends, even if processing leaves it because of an exception. The outer finally attempts workspace cleanup after the streams have been disposed. Cleanup can itself fail in a real application; finally does not grant permissions or guarantee that a disk operation will succeed.

| Point in this program | Resource state | What is established |
| --- | --- | --- |
| After constructing reportPath | No report opened yet | A location string exists |
| Inside writer block | Writer open | Lines are being written |
| After writer block | Writer disposed | Buffered output has been finalized normally |
| Inside reader block | Reader open | The same path is being consumed |
| After reader block | Reader dispos

Explanation

0903_text_operations.ipynb · cells 5–28
An inventory file contains code, quantity and unit price separated by commas. Splitting a line gives pieces of text; it does not prove that there are exactly three fields, that a quantity is an integer, or that a price is nonnegative. Work from the schema toward conversion, not from a convenient Parse call toward assumptions about everything that came before it.

For a deliberately simple format without quoted separators, process a line through distinct stages. Preserve the original text and line number so that a rejected record can be explained. First count fields, then normalize only fields whose rules permit it, then parse numeric representations, and finally check the business domain. A zero quantity may be allowed even when an empty quantity field is not.

| Line | First relevant result |
| --- | --- |
| PEN,3,1.25 | Three fields; numeric and domain checks can proceed |
| PEN,three,1.25 | Quantity representation is invalid |
| PEN,-3,1.25 | Quantity is numeric but violates a nonnegative rule |
| PEN,3 | Schema is incomplete |

The order matters. Indexing the third field before checking field count can throw instead of producing a useful rejection. Normalizing every character in the entire line can alter meaningful free text. Catching every exception can hide a programming defect such as an incorrect index as though it were bad source data.

A regular expression can describe the shape of one field, such as a fixed prefix followed by digits. It does not replace business validation. A code may match a shape and still refer to an unknown product. For a small fixed delimite

Input often has extra whitespace — trim each field after splitting:

string line = " Ada , 98 , CS ";
string[] parts = line.Split(',');

for (int i = 0; i < parts.Length; i++)
    parts[i] = parts[i].Trim();

foreach (var p in parts)
    Console.WriteLine($"'{p}'");

When input may contain repeated delimiters, remove empty entries:

string line = "Ada,,CS";
string[] parts = line.Split(',', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);

Console.WriteLine(parts.Length);  // 2

0903_text_operations.ipynb · cells 28–28
static bool TryParseStudent(string line, out string name, out int score, out string major)
{
    name  = "";
    major = "";
    score = 0;

    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line)) return false;

    string[] parts = line.Split(',');
    if (parts.Length != 3) return false;

    name  = parts[0].Trim();
    major = parts[2].Trim();

    return int.TryParse(parts[1].Trim(), out score);
}

using System;
using System.IO;

File.WriteAllText("orders.txt",
    "Latte,3,5\n" +
    "Muffin, 2 ,3\n" +
    "Espresso,two,4\n" +
    "\n" +
    "Bagel,4\n" +
    "Mocha,1,6\n");

int revenue = 0;
var reader = new StreamReader("orders.txt");
while (!reader.EndOfStream)
{
    string line = reader.ReadLine()!;

    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line))
    {
        continue;
    }

    string[] fields = line.Split(',');
    if (fields.Length != 3
        || !int.TryParse(fields[1].Trim(), out int quantity)
        || !int.TryParse(fields[2].Trim(), out int price))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Skipped: {line}");
        continue;
    }

    string product = fields[0].Trim();
    int amount = quantity * price;
    revenue += amount;
    Console.WriteLine($"{product}: {quantity} x ${price} = ${amount}");
}
reader.Close();

Console.WriteLine($"Revenue: ${revenue}");

static bool TryParseStudent(string line, out string name, out int score, out string major)
{
    name  = "";
    major = "";
    score = 0;

    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line)) return false;

    string[] parts = line.Split(',');
    if (parts.Length != 3) return false;

    name  = parts[0].Trim();
    major = parts[2].Trim();

    return int.TryParse(parts[1].Trim(), out score);
}

using System;

static bool TryReadStockLine(string line, out string sku, out int quantity)
{
    sku = "";
    quantity = 0;
    // Your code starts here.
    string[] fields = line.Split(',');
    if (fields.Length != 2) return false;
    string candidateSku = fields[0].Trim();
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(candidateSku)) return false;
    if (!int.TryParse(fields[1].Trim(), out int candidateQuantity)) return false;
    if (candidateQuantity < 0 || candidateQuantity > 500) return false;
    sku = candidateSku;
    quantity = candidateQuantity;
    return true;
    // Your code ends here.
}

using System;
using System.IO;

File.WriteAllText("sales.txt", "120\n85\nN/A\n\n42\n4O\n230\n");

static int SumSales(string fileName, out int skipped)
{
    skipped = 0;
    int total = 0;

    if (!File.Exists(fileName))
    {
        return -1;
    }

    var reader = new StreamReader(fileName);
    while (!reader.EndOfStream)
    {
        string line = reader.ReadLine()!.Trim();
        if (line.Length == 0)
        {
            continue;
        }
        if (int.TryParse(line, out int amount))
        {
            total += amount;
        }
        else
        {
            skipped++;
        }
    }
    reader.Close();

    return total;
}

## Declaring Classes




To declare a class, you need to use the `class` keyword and give a unique `identifier` (name) to the class. For example,
you want to create a customer class to include some data and methods in one unit:

```csharp
// [access modifier] - [class] - [identifier]

public class Customer
{
   // Fields, properties, methods and events go here...
}
```

Attributes to be considered when creating a class include:

- Access Modifiers: The default access for a class type is internal. Basic levels of access for a class include [2] :
  - **public**: Access is not restricted. Anyone code can create instances of this class.
  - **protected**: Access is limited to the containing class or types derived from the containing class.
  - **internal**: Access is limited to the current assembly. [3]
  - **private**: Access is limited to the containing type.

- Class Identifier: A unique name for the class. An identifier is the name you assign to a type (class, interface, struct, delegate, or enum),
  member, variable, or namespace. An identifier begins with a letter or underscore. As a convention, use PascalCase for class names and method names.

- Class Body: The class body is surrounded by { }. The behavior and data are defined in the class body, including **fields**, properties, **methods**, and events on a class and
  are collectively referred to as **class members**.

- Base Class or Super Class: Optional. Name of the class’s superclass; preceded by a colon (:).

- Interfaces: Interface names implemented by the class; preceded by a c
