## Properties




Although the content are still valid, this section will be updated later to reflect
the more current syntax and discussion of properties such as in [Using Properties](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/using-properties#the-get-accessor).

A property is a member that provides a flexible mechanism to read, write, or compute
the value of a data field. Properties appear as public data members, but they’re
implemented as special methods called accessors.

(getters)=

### Getters




In instance methods you have an extra way of getting data in and out of the method:
Reading or setting instance variables (fields). The simplest methods do nothing but reading
or setting instance variables. We start with those:

The `private` in front
of the field declarations was important to keep code outside the
class from messing with the values. On the other hand we do want
others to be able to *inspect* the name, phone and email,
so how do we do that? Use **public methods**.

Since the fields are accessible anywhere *inside* the class’s instance methods,
and public methods can be used from *outside* the class, we can simply code

```csharp
      public string GetName()
      {
         return name;
      }

      public string GetPhone()
      {
         return phone;
      }

      public string GetEmail()
      {
         return email;
      }
```

These methods allow one-way communication of the name, phone and email

## Properties Describe the Public Surface




```{index} Properties Describe the Public Surface
```


Station has a getter and is assigned during construction. Total and ItemCount have public getters and private setters, so callers can read them but must use Add or Clear to change them. This is the idiomatic C# property form of controlled access; separate GetTotal and SetTotal methods would add no useful business behavior here. Validation rejects a negative price before either value changes. A public setter could otherwise let a caller change Total without its corresponding count.


using System;

CashRegister register = new CashRegister("Front"); register.Add(5m);
try { register.Add(-2m); } catch (ArgumentOutOfRangeException) { Console.WriteLine("Rejected negative price."); }
Console.WriteLine($"{register.ItemCount} item, {register.Total:F2}");

class CashRegister
{
    public decimal Total { get; private set; }
    public int ItemCount { get; private set; }
    public string Station { get; }
    public CashRegister(string station)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(station)) throw new ArgumentException("Station required.");
        Station = station.Trim();
    }
    public void Add(decimal price)
    {
        if (price < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(price));
        Total += price; ItemCount++;
    }
    public decimal Average { get { return ItemCount == 0 ? 0m : Total / ItemCount; } }
    public void Clear() { Total = 0m; ItemCount = 0; }
}

## Static Classes & Methods




In some conditions you may want to create **static classes** that provide static methods without
instantiation. That means you do not need to use the `new` operator keyword to create a variable
of the class type. Also, without the class instance variable, you access the members of a static
class by using the class name itself. For example, if you have a static class called SomeMath:

    static class SomeMath
    {
       public static int Sum(int a, int b)    // a public static method
       {
          return a + b;
       }
    }

To use the Sum method in the SomeMath class, you call it directly without creating a new object:

    internal class Program
    {
       static void Main(string[] args)
       {
          int aSum = SomeMath.Sum(2, 2);
          Console.WriteLine(aSum);      // output 4
       }
    }

As another example, in the .NET Class Library, the `static` [System.Math](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.math)
class contains methods that perform mathematical operations, without any requirement to store or
retrieve data that is unique to a particular instance of the [Math](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.math)
class. You can use the math methods directly in your code by referring to the static class name `Math`:

    double dub = -3.14;
    Console.WriteLine(Math.Abs(dub));               // 3.14
    Console.WriteLine(Math.Floor(dub));             // -4
    Console.WriteLine(Math.Round(Math.Abs(dub)));   // 3

## 4. Share Store-Wide Data with Static Members

The shop now rings up a whole receipt at once with `Checkout(decimal[] prices)`, which replaces `RingUp`. Decide where each piece of data belongs:

- **Static field** `nextReceiptNumber`: receipt numbers must be unique across the *whole store*, so all registers share one counter. One copy for the class, not one per register.
- **Static property** `TaxRate`: there is one sales-tax rate for the store. Changing it once (`CashRegister.TaxRate = 0.07m;`) changes it for every register.
- **Static method** `Money`: it formats a number and remembers nothing, so it stays a stateless static helper. Turning it into an instance method would gain nothing.
- **Instance fields** `total` and `receiptCount`: each register's own running results.
- **Local variables** `subtotal`, `tax`, `amountDue`, and `receipt`: they start over for every checkout and mean nothing afterward, so they stay local, just like `lineAmount` did.

Complete `Checkout`: add up the prices into `subtotal`, compute `tax` as `Math.Round(subtotal * TaxRate, 2)`, take the next receipt number (then advance the shared counter), add the amount due to `total`, add 1 to `receiptCount`, and print the receipt in this format:

```text
Receipt 1001 (Front, Avery): $21.00 + tax $1.68 = $22.68
```

1004_averager.ipynb · cells 14–18
```{index} Beyond Getters and Setters
```

```{index} Averager; incremental average; running sum
```

Thus far we have had very simple classes with instance variables and
getter and setter methods, and maybe a ToString method.
These classes were designed to introduce the basic syntax for
classes with instances. The classes have just been containers for data
that we can read back, and change if there are setter methods - pretty
boring and limited. Many objects have more extensive behaviors, so we will
take a small step and imagine a somewhat more complicated `Averager` class:

- A new `Averager` starts with no data acknowledged.
- Be able to enter data values one at a time (method `AddDatum`).
  We will use `double` values.
- At any point be able to return the average of the numbers entered so far
  (method `GetAverage`).
  The average is the sum of all the values divided by number of values.
  With `double` values we assume a `double` average.
  This does not make sense if there
  are no values so far, but with double type we can use the value
  `NaN` (Not a Number) in this case.
- Be able to return the number of data elements entered so far
  (method `GetDataCount`)
- Be able to clear the `Averager`, going back to no data elements
  considered yet, like in a new `Averager` (method `Clear`)
- It is good to have a `ToString` method. We choose to have
  it label the number of data items and the average of the items.

The object starts from a fixed
state (no data) so we do not need any constructor parameters.

We can imagine a demonstration class `AveragerDemo` with a `Main`

Worked example/case/trace

using System;

namespace IntroCS
{
   class AveragerDemo
   {
      public static void Main()
      {  // body chunk
         Averager a = new Averager();
         Console.WriteLine("New Averager: " + a);
         foreach (double x in new[] {5.1, -7.3, 11.0, 3.7}) {
            Console.WriteLine ("Next datum " + x);
            a.AddDatum (x);
            Console.WriteLine("average {0:G15} with {1} data values",
                              a.GetAverage(), a.GetDataCount());
         }
         a.Clear();
         Console.WriteLine("After clearing:");
         Console.WriteLine("average {0:G15} with {1} data values",
                           a.GetAverage(), a.GetDataCount());
      }                            // end chunk
   }
}



namespace IntroCS
{
/// a class that is more than a container
   class Averager
   {
      private int dataCount;
      private double sum;

      /// new Averager with no data
      public Averager()
      {
         Clear();
      }

      public void AddDatum(double value)
      {
         sum += value;
         dataCount++;
      }

      public int GetDataCount()
      {
         return dataCount;
      }

      /// Gets the average of the data
      ///   or NaN if no data.
      public double GetAverage()
      {
         return sum/dataCount;  // is NaN if dataCount is 0
      }

      public void Clear()
      {
         sum = 0.0;
         dataCount = 0;
      }

      public override string ToString ()
      {
         return string.Format("items: {0}; average: {1:G15}",
                              GetDataCount(), GetAverage());

1101_objects_references.ipynb · cells 5–17
A reference can identify an object or contain null. An empty order object still exists and can answer Count; a missing order reference cannot receive an instance call. A nullable annotation describes intended use for the compiler's analysis. It is not a runtime constructor check, and adding a null-forgiving exclamation mark does not create an object.

When a relationship is required, reject an absent value at the boundary that establishes the relationship. When it is optional, give absence a deliberate meaning and test that path. Returning a default zero for an absent invoice may confuse missing data with an invoice whose real total is zero. The supporting nullability reading retains the operators and all original variants; use them to implement a policy that has already been stated.

Guided check: distinguish an order with no lines, no order object, and an order whose total is zero after discounts. Which operations are valid on each? A useful object contract keeps these cases distinguishable rather than treating every unusual state as null.

## Mutable and Immutable Objects




```{index} Mutable and Immutable Objects
```


An object is **mutable** when its observable state can change after construction. An **immutable** object keeps its observable state fixed. The `Product` below has read-only properties and no method that changes its fields. Its property values are strings and a decimal, so sharing it cannot later change the catalog values through a setter.

Read-only access to a reference is not enough to make a whole object immutable. A read-only property could still return a mutable list or another mutable object. You must inspect what callers can reach through the public members.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

Product catalogVersion = new Product("P100", "Notebook", 6m);
Product quote = catalogVersion;
Product revisedCatalog = new Product("P100", "Notebook", 7m);
Console.WriteLine($"Existing quote: {quote.UnitPrice:F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"New catalog: {revisedCatalog.UnitPrice:F2}");

class Product
{
    public string Sku { get; }
    public string Name { get; }
    public decimal UnitPrice { get; }

    public Product(string sku, string name, decimal unitPrice)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(sku)) throw new ArgumentException("SKU required.");
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)) throw new ArgumentException("Name required.");
        if (unitPrice < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(unitPrice));
        Sku = sku.Trim();
        Name = name.Trim();
        UnitPrice = unitPrice;
    }
}

1105_value_record_types.ipynb · cells 5–20
An order line refers to a product, but a point on a warehouse plan may simply consist of two coordinates. Before choosing class, struct or record, ask what one value means, whether it can change, and what callers should expect when it is assigned or compared. The forms below solve related modeling problems, but none is an automatic replacement for every ordinary class.

Assigning a struct variable copies its value. That copy contains the values of its fields; if one of those fields is itself a reference, both copies can still refer to a shared object. Value-type copying is not a promise that every reachable object has been recursively duplicated. A record class is a reference type with compiler-supported value-oriented equality and copying syntax; assigning its variable still copies a reference. A record struct combines record features with value-type copying.

| Choice | Assignment behavior | Design question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary class instance | Another reference to the same object | Is identity and a controlled lifecycle important? |
| Struct value | Copy of its fields | Is this a small coherent value with a meaningful default? |
| Record class instance | Another reference on assignment | Does value-oriented equality fit a reference-based data model? |
| Record struct value | Copy of its fields | Do both value copying and record conveniences fit? |

For positional records, the parameter list declares the data used by generated members. A with expression creates a copied result with selected changes; it is not a deep-cloning operator. If a copied record contain

Worked example/case/trace

1105_value_record_types.ipynb · cells 9–20
using System;

DeliveryCharge original = new DeliveryCharge(5m, 2);
DeliveryCharge revised = original;
revised = new DeliveryCharge(7m, revised.Zone);
Console.WriteLine($"Original: {original.Amount:F2}, zone {original.Zone}");
Console.WriteLine($"Revised: {revised.Amount:F2}, zone {revised.Zone}");
Console.WriteLine($"Default amount: {default(DeliveryCharge).Amount:F2}");

readonly struct DeliveryCharge
{
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    public int Zone { get; }
    public DeliveryCharge(decimal amount, int zone)
    {
        if (amount < 0m || zone < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException();
        Amount = amount;
        Zone = zone;
    }
}


The two variables contain independent values. A mutable struct would also copy its fields on assignment, but mutable value types can make updates confusing, especially inside collections. Prefer a small, fixed value when introducing structs.

`default(DeliveryCharge)` supplies zero for both numeric properties without running this two-argument constructor. A struct design must account for its default value; constructor validation alone cannot exclude it. A non-nullable struct cannot contain `null`; `DeliveryCharge?` can, as the nullability reading explains.

Value copying is not a promise about stack versus heap storage. A struct can be a field inside a class or an element of an array. Also, if a struct contains a reference such as a `List<string>`, copying the struct copies that reference and can still share the list. Choose a type by its meaning and copying policy, not by assuming structs are always faster.

1105_value_record_types.ipynb · cells 20–20
These declarations define one item's type. A collection such as `List<Address>` or `List<PackageSize>` holds multiple items; neither declaration replaces the collection.

| Declaration | Assignment | Equality to keep in mind | Typical role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary `class` | Copies a reference | Default `==` compares identity unless customized | An order with a lifecycle and shared state |
| `struct` | Copies its value | `Equals` compares fields by default; `==` is not automatically supplied | A small value with explicit members |
| `record` / `record class` | Copies a reference | Generated value-based equality | An address or snapshot compared by data |
| `record struct` | Copies its value | Generated value-based equality and `==` | A small data value with convenient record syntax |

For the class examples in this chapter, continue using ordinary classes. Choose a struct when independent value copying fits the domain; choose record syntax when its generated data comparison fits the intended rule. These choices do not remove validation responsibilities. In particular, positional records do not automatically check business constraints such as positive dimensions.

Before continuing, predict whether `Address b = a;` creates a new object and whether `PackageSize b = a;` can share mutable numeric properties. Then change one value in each runnable example and explain the output using copying and equality separately.

Explanation

1102_composition.ipynb · cells 5–14
An order line requires a product to calculate its amount. An order may optionally have a delivery note. Both are relationships, but absence has different meanings. Reject a missing required product when the line is created; allow an absent optional note only when callers know how that state is represented and displayed.

A nullable reference annotation such as `string?` communicates that absence is permitted for that reference. A nullable value type such as `int?` can distinguish an unknown quantity from a known zero. They are related ways of representing missing information, but nullable reference annotations do not wrap a runtime object or validate the constructor. Runtime guards remain necessary when a public contract rejects null.

| State | Meaning | Suitable check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product reference absent | Required relationship cannot be established | Reject at construction |
| Optional note absent | No note was supplied | Follow the documented no-note path |
| Note is empty text | An existing string contains no characters | Apply a separate text rule if needed |
| Quantity is zero | A known numeric value | Apply the business rule for zero |

Conditional access can skip a member access when a reference is absent; null coalescing can select a fallback value. Neither operator determines whether that fallback is a sensible business result. Returning zero for an unknown quantity may make arithmetic convenient while hiding incomplete data. State the policy first, then choose syntax to express it. The supporting nullability lesson retains the full operator and patte

Worked example/case/trace

1102_composition.ipynb · cells 14–14
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

Product notebook = new Product("P100", "Notebook", 6m);
OrderLine requested = new OrderLine(notebook, 2);
Console.WriteLine($"{requested.Quantity} x {requested.Product.Name}: {requested.LineTotal:F2}");

class Product
{
    public string Sku { get; }
    public string Name { get; }
    public decimal UnitPrice { get; }

    public Product(string sku, string name, decimal unitPrice)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(sku)) throw new ArgumentException("SKU required.");
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)) throw new ArgumentException("Name required.");
        if (unitPrice < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(unitPrice));
        Sku = sku.Trim();
        Name = name.Trim();
        UnitPrice = unitPrice;
    }
}

class OrderLine
{
    public Product Product { get; }
    public int Quantity { get; }
    public decimal LineTotal { get { return Product.UnitPrice * Quantity; } }

    public OrderLine(Product product, int quantity)
    {
        if (product is null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(product));
        if (quantity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(quantity));
        Product = product;
        Quantity = quantity;
    }
}

## Keep Collection Ownership Inside the Order




```{index} Keep Collection Ownership Inside the Order
```


A private field is not protected if a public method hands the same mutable list to callers. A caller could clear the list, add a null, or bypass validation. The order should provide operations that preserve its rules instead.

`Add` creates and validates the line before inserting it. If construction fails, the existing list is unchanged. `Total` loops over current lines, starting at zero, so an empty order has a well-defined total. The private `readonly` field cannot be reassigned after initialization; its list can still change through `Add`. Readonly field binding is different from an immutable collection.

C11-O5 · partial

Test boundaries and refactor while preserving observable behavior.

Rejected-state checks are present; the main homework does not require an actual refactoring with before/after regression evidence.

Explanation

1103_testing_collaboration.ipynb · cells 5–23
A collaboration test should establish observable behavior, not reach into another class's private list to force the result. Create two independent orders, add a line to one, and check both totals. If adding to the first changes the second, shared storage has crossed an ownership boundary even if the added line itself has the right amount.

Arrange a state in which a rejected update would be visible. Record the original count and total, attempt the invalid change, and assert that both remain unchanged. Checking only that an exception was thrown can miss a method that mutates state and then throws. A failure policy includes what happened to state, not merely which message appeared.

| Case | Observation to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Two orders share one immutable product | Independent line lists and totals |
| Invalid quantity is rejected | Prior count and total remain intact |
| A snapshot is obtained | The documented outer-copy/sharing policy holds |
| Optional information is absent | The explicit no-information behavior occurs |

Guided challenge: a developer returns the internal line list to make a report easy. Show how a client could change the order without calling its validation methods. Then compare returning a copied outer sequence whose immutable product/line objects remain shared. Explain which mutation path is blocked and why this is not necessarily a deep copy of every reachable object.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

C12-O1 · supported

Construct a small hierarchy with validated base and derived state.

Base validation and subtype results are applied.

Explanation

1201_inheritance.ipynb · cells 5–23
A derived discount policy may add fields and implementation details, but a caller using the base policy contract should still receive a result satisfying that contract. Inheritance is therefore more than reusing a convenient constructor. Ask whether the derived object can be used wherever the base behavior is promised without forcing the caller to know which subtype it received.

For a contract that accepts nonnegative subtotals and returns a discount between zero and the subtotal, a derived implementation that rejects every subtotal below 100 has strengthened the accepted-input requirement. A caller that was valid for the base contract can now fail. A derived implementation returning more than the subtotal has weakened the promised result. Both problems remain even when the code compiles.

Construction also follows a responsibility order. Base initialization establishes base state; derived initialization establishes additional state. Do not duplicate base validation in every client or assume that a base reference removes the derived object's fields. Reference type controls what the caller can name directly; the object still has its complete runtime identity.

Guided comparison: an Order has a collection of lines. Is it a subtype of a line? No: composition represents that has-a relationship. A special discount policy can plausibly be a policy if it preserves the policy contract. Draw the client call and state the promise being relied on before choosing inheritance merely to avoid a few repeated assignments.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^developme

Worked example/case/trace

1201_inheritance.ipynb · cells 14–19
using System;

DiscountPolicy ordinary = new DiscountPolicy();
PercentageDiscount member = new PercentageDiscount(0.10m);
Console.WriteLine($"Ordinary: {ordinary.Apply(100m):F2}");
Console.WriteLine($"Member: {member.Apply(100m):F2}");

class DiscountPolicy
{
    public virtual decimal Apply(decimal subtotal)
    {
        if (subtotal < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(subtotal));
        return subtotal;
    }
}

class PercentageDiscount : DiscountPolicy
{
    private readonly decimal rate;
    public PercentageDiscount(decimal rate)
    {
        if (rate < 0m || rate > 1m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(rate));
        this.rate = rate;
    }
    public override decimal Apply(decimal subtotal)
    {
        decimal validSubtotal = base.Apply(subtotal);
        return validSubtotal * (1m - rate);
    }
}


The results are 100.00 and 90.00. The percentage constructor validates its rate before storing it. The inherited input contract still matters: a negative subtotal is rejected by both implementations. Private state and validated operations keep the hierarchy's rules understandable.

Constructors are not inherited as ordinary methods. Each constructor must establish the valid state of its own type. When a base constructor requires arguments, use an initializer such as `: base(name)` to supply them before the derived constructor body runs.

C12-O2 · supported

Explain virtual dispatch and distinguish overriding from overloading.

Dispatch has a shared client and retained Shape implementation tasks.

Explanation

1202_polymorphism.ipynb · cells 5–14
A variable's compile-time type determines which members a call can name and participates in overload resolution. A virtual call can then dispatch to an override selected from the runtime object. These are different decisions. Overloading adds a signature choice; overriding changes implementation of an inherited virtual contract. Hiding a nonvirtual member with new is another behavior and should not be described as runtime overriding.

| Situation | What determines the important choice? |
| --- | --- |
| Overloaded method candidates | Compile-time argument/type rules |
| Override of a virtual member | Runtime object for the chosen virtual call |
| Hidden nonvirtual member | The member selected through the reference's static type |

Trace a base-typed reference holding a derived policy object. For a virtual Calculate call, follow the override implemented by that object. Now change only the variable declaration to the derived type: the stored object has not changed, although more members may become available to the caller. A cast is not a request to construct a new object or change the object into another subtype.

An abstract class can leave some behavior unimplemented while supplying common state or concrete operations. It cannot be directly instantiated as a completed object. A concrete derived type must provide the required behavior before clients can use an instance. The requirement belongs to the type contract, not to a convention that an unimplemented method should return zero.

    new DiscountPolicy(), new PercentageDiscount(0.10m), new FixedDiscount(5m)

class DiscountPolicy
{
    public virtual decimal Apply(decimal subtotal)
    {
        if (subtotal < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(subtotal));
        return subtotal;
    }
}

class PercentageDiscount : DiscountPolicy
{
    private readonly decimal rate;
    public PercentageDiscount(decimal rate)
    {
        if (rate < 0m || rate > 1m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(rate));
        this.rate = rate;
    }
    public override decimal Apply(decimal subtotal)
    {
        decimal validSubtotal = base.Apply(subtotal);
        return validSubtotal * (1m - rate);
    }
}

class FixedDiscount : DiscountPolicy
{
    private readonly decimal reduction;
    public FixedDiscount(decimal reduction)
    {
        if (reduction < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(reduction));
        this.reduction = reduction;
    }
    public override decimal Apply(decimal subtotal)
    {
        decimal validSubtotal = base.Apply(subtotal);
        return Math.Max(0m, validSubtotal - reduction);
    }
}

## Abstract Classes Require an Implementation




```{index} Abstract Classes Require an Implementation
```


An **abstract class** cannot be directly instantiated. It can contain shared implementation and abstract members that concrete derived classes must implement. Use it when a general type has useful common behavior but has no sensible complete instance by itself.

The following payment example gives every payment a validated amount. The abstract operation produces a description that each concrete kind supplies. The array demonstrates the same runtime-dispatch idea as the policy loop.


using System;

Payment[] payments = { new CardPayment(30m, "1234"), new CashPayment(12m) };
foreach (Payment payment in payments) Console.WriteLine(payment.Describe());

abstract class Payment
{
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    protected Payment(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(amount));
        Amount = amount;
    }
    public abstract string Describe();
}
class CardPayment : Payment
{
    private readonly string lastFour;
    public CardPayment(decimal amount, string lastFour) : base(amount)
    {
        if (lastFour.Length != 4) throw new ArgumentException("Four-character teaching ID required.");
        this.lastFour = lastFour;
    }
    public override string Describe() { return $"Card ending {lastFour}: {Amount:F2}"; }
}
class CashPayment : Payment
{
    public CashPayment(decimal amount) : base(amount) { }
    public override string Describe() { return $"

C12-O4 · supported

Supply interchangeable components through interfaces and constructors.

Interfaces and injected collaborators have coding tasks.

Explanation

1203_interfaces.ipynb · cells 5–20
A checkout coordinator needs a way to request payment. It need not know every field or helper method of a particular payment provider. An interface names the small capability the client relies on. An implementing class can have a different internal representation and still satisfy that capability, provided its behavior and failure policy meet the contract.

Supplying the collaborator through a constructor makes the dependency visible. The coordinator can reject a missing required collaborator at construction rather than failing unexpectedly during a later transaction. This is an application of composition and null contracts, not a requirement to use an elaborate dependency-injection framework.

A test double can record a requested amount and return a prepared response. That permits a test of the coordinator's interaction without contacting a real payment service. Check more than whether any call occurred: the amount, number of calls, result interpretation and state on rejection can all matter. A recording double observes collaboration; it does not by itself prove that the real external service works.

Guided design: a report formatter needs only a way to produce a line of text. Compare making every formatter inherit a large invoice-processing base class with supplying a small formatting capability. State which parts are actually shared and which are accidental similarities. An interface does not imply that all implementations share state, a base implementation or the same operational cost.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

    }

        if (subtotal < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(subtotal));

An interface is not simply an abstract class with a different name. It describes a capability without requiring a shared instance-field representation or constructor. A class may implement several interfaces but inherits directly from at most one class. This chapter uses only method signatures; modern C# supports additional interface features that are unnecessary here.

Keep contracts small enough that implementations can satisfy them coherently. A single interface requiring discounts, database persistence, console menus, and stock reservations would combine unrelated responsibilities.

## Substitution Preserves the Contract




```{index} Substitution Preserves the Contract
```


A **substitution** is using a derived object where a base type is expected. A client that accepts `DiscountPolicy` should continue to receive a valid result for a valid input. A derived class that returns a negative amount or rejects inputs the base accepts breaks that expectation even if its code compiles.

Write down the behavior you need before designing the hierarchy:

- Accept every nonnegative decimal subtotal in the exercise's domain.
- Reject a negative subtotal.
- Return an amount from zero through the original subtotal.
- Avoid changing the caller's order or printing from the calculation.

These are behavioral obligations. The compiler checks type compatibility and method signatures; it does not prove business invariants. Boundary checks help expose violations. Chapter 21 later develops more formal contract reasoning.

1203_interfaces.ipynb · cells 22–29
```{index} Choose Composition, an Interface, or a Base Class
```

## Choose Composition, an Interface, or a Base Class




```{index} Choose Composition, an Interface, or a Base Class
```


Start with the smallest design that supports the requirements. A concrete collaborator is enough when there is one implementation. Introduce an interface when clients need interchangeable capabilities or a clear testing boundary. Use a base class when the types share a meaningful substitution relationship and common behavior or state.

| Need | Design to consider |
| --- | --- |
| Order owns several lines. | Composition with a concrete line type. |
| Checkout supports several discount calculations. | Composition through a small interface. |
| Several payment kinds share validated amount state. | An abstract base class with overrides. |
| One calculation repeated in one class. | A private helper method. |

Do not create an interface for every class automatically. An interface adds another contract to maintain. Likewise, do not build a deep hierarchy to anticipate features that do not exist yet. Use an explicit use case and a short test to justify an extension point.

In Chapter 13, interfaces become contracts for abstract data types, and generics let one implementation support multiple element types. The connection is behavioral: clients rely on an operation's promise while representation details remain hidden. For persistence after this chapter, use the optional database appendix.

class RecordingDiscount : IDiscountPolicy
{

    public decimal LastSubtotal { get; private set; }
    public decimal Apply(decimal subtotal)
    {
        if (subtotal < 0m) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(subtotal));
        Calls++;
        LastSubtotal = subtotal;
        return subtotal;
    }
}

Observable undo histories support contract-first reasoning.

Explanation

1301_adt_contracts.ipynb · cells 3–20
```{index} Describe the Observable History First
```

## Describe the Observable History First



An undo history is not defined by an array or a linked node. It is defined by what a client can observe after a sequence of operations. If the client records A, records B, and then undoes once, it expects B to be removed before A. An implementation can store those entries in different ways while preserving that behavior. This separates the abstract data type, the behavioral contract, from the data structure used to realize it.

Write the history on paper before writing a class. For each operation, record the result, the resulting abstract contents, and the empty/failure policy. If the contract says an unsuccessful TryPop leaves state unchanged, returning false after already decrementing Count violates the contract even if later tests happen to restore the count.

| Operation | Result | Abstract history, oldest to newest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Empty | [] |
| Push A | Recorded | [A] |
| Push B | Recorded | [A, B] |
| TryPop | Success, B | [A] |
| TryPop | Success, A | [] |
| TryPop | Failure | [] |

The empty failure is part of the behavior, not an implementation detail to settle later. A different ADT might throw on an empty Pop. Both can be coherent contracts, but a client written for one cannot assume the other. Also specify whether null entries, duplicates, or a fixed capacity are allowed. These policies determine which tests should succeed and what failure must preserve.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Sepa

Worked example/case/trace

1301_adt_contracts.ipynb · cells 14–14
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
IStack<string> history = new ListStack<string>();
history.Push("open file");
history.Push("rename variable");
Console.WriteLine(history.Pop());
Console.WriteLine(history.Peek());

interface IStack<T>
{
    int Count { get; }
    void Push(T item);
    T Pop();
    T Peek();
}

class ListStack<T> : IStack<T>
{
    private readonly List<T> items = new();
    public int Count => items.Count;

    public void Push(T item) => items.Add(item);

    public T Pop()
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
        int last = items.Count - 1;
        T value = items[last];
        items.RemoveAt(last);
        return value;
    }

    public T Peek()
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
        return items[^1];
    }
}

1301_adt_contracts.ipynb · cells 6–20
```{index} Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
```

## Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge



A C# interface can express operation names and types, for example a success-returning method with an out result. It cannot by itself express every ordering rule or state invariant. Two classes can compile against the same interface and still behave differently. Tests and explanations connect the syntax to the promised history.

The client should not need to know the backing array's capacity or the head node's field name. If a capacity change affects returned values or exposes unused slots, representation details have leaked through the abstraction. Conversely, the implementer must know enough about storage to maintain its invariants. Abstraction assigns different responsibilities to the two roles; it does not mean that implementation details are unimportant.

Guided exercise: keep the interface unchanged but change removal to return A before B. Identify the first row at which this behavior differs from the specified history. Then explain why a test that checks only Count would miss the defect. Extend the history with a failed removal followed by a new push; this checks whether failure left the structure reusable.

```{dropdown} Contract checkpoint
The first successful removal must return B. A queue-like implementation could keep the right counts while returning the wrong element. Checking returned values, order, state after failure, and later reuse tests more of the contract than checking size alone.
```

``
1302_representations_costs.ipynb · cells 3–18
```{index} One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work
```

## One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work



Use the undo contract from the preceding lesson. An array representation might keep active entries in positions zero through Count minus one. A linked representation might keep the newest entry at the head. The same Push/Pop history can be correct in both, yet their storage and work differ. To compare them fairly, hold the abstract behavior fixed and change only the representation.

For the array, Count and capacity answer different questions. Count describes active entries; capacity describes available slots in the allocated backing storage. A push with unused capacity writes one entry and increases Count. A push into full storage may allocate a larger array, copy active entries, and then append. Calling both pushes constant work ignores the copying performed by the growth case.

For a linked representation, a push can create one node whose next reference identifies the old head. Updating the head then makes the new node first. A pop can advance head to its next node. This avoids an array-wide growth copy, but node allocation and extra references are still real costs. Neither representation is universally better merely because one operation has a simple asymptotic label.

| Representation question | Array-backed history | Linked history |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How are active values located? | Used prefix of slots | Nodes reachable from head |
| What marks empty? | Count equals zero | No head node, with matching Count |
| What may make a push expensive? | Growth

Worked example/case/trace

1302_representations_costs.ipynb · cells 14–18
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
var stack = new ArrayStack<int>();
stack.Push(10);
stack.Push(20);
Console.WriteLine(stack.Pop());
Console.WriteLine(stack.Count);

class ArrayStack<T>
{
    private T[] items = new T[4];
    public int Count { get; private set; }

    public void Push(T item)
    {
        if (Count == items.Length) Array.Resize(ref items, items.Length * 2);
        items[Count] = item;
        Count++;
    }

    public T Pop()
    {
        if (Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Stack is empty.");
        Count--;
        T value = items[Count];
        items[Count] = default!;
        return value;
    }
}

## Linked Nodes and References



A linked representation stores each item in a small object called a node. Each node holds a value and a reference to the next node.

```text
top -> [C | next] -> [B | next] -> [A | null]
```

The variable `top` does not contain the whole stack. It contains a reference to the first node. Following references reveals the rest of the structure.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
Node<string>? top = null;
top = new Node<string>("A", top);
top = new Node<string>("B", top);
top = new Node<string>("C", top);

for (Node<string>? current = top; current is not null; current = current.Next)
{
    Console.WriteLine(current.Value);
}

{
    public T Value { get; }
    public Node<T>? Next { get; }

    public Node(T valu

```{index} Why Generics Exist
```

## Why Generics Exist




Without generics, a stack that holds `int` would need to be a different class from a stack that holds `string`, or it would have to store everything as `object` and lose type safety. Generics let one implementation work for many types:

```csharp
// Non-generic — stores object, loses type safety
var list = new ArrayList();
list.Add(1);
list.Add("oops");  // compiles — bug at runtime

// Generic — type-safe at compile time
var nums = new List<int>();
nums.Add(1);
// nums.Add("oops");  // compile error
```

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types
```



```{index} Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types
```

## Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types



An undo history of product codes and a history of numeric adjustments can follow the same push/pop rules. Writing two unrelated implementations repeats the same invariant and creates two places to repair a defect. A generic type makes the element type a parameter while leaving the behavioral algorithm shared.

Read `History<T>` as a type definition with an element-type placeholder. Read `History<string>` as one constructed type whose element operations must accept strings. The placeholder is not a variable containing an element and is not a request to decide the type afresh on every assignment. A History<int> and a History<string> are different constructed types even though their operation names are the same.

The general class pattern is `class Container<T> { /*

Worked example/case/trace

1303_generics.ipynb · cells 13–29
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
// A generic method works for any type T
static T[] Repeat<T>(T value, int count)
{
    var arr = new T[count];
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) arr[i] = value;
    return arr;
}

int[]    ints    = Repeat(0, 5);       // [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
string[] strings = Repeat("hi", 3);   // ["hi", "hi", "hi"]

Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", ints));     // 0, 0, 0, 0, 0
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", strings));  // hi, hi, hi

## Generic Classes



using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
var score = new Cell<int>(95);
var name = new Cell<string>("Ada");

score.Set(98);
Console.WriteLine(score.Get());
Console.WriteLine(name.Get());

// A minimal generic cell ADT
class Cell<T>
{
    private T value;

    public Cell(T initialValue) => value = initialValue;
    public T Get() => value;
    public void Set(T newValue) => value = newValue;
}

```{index} type constraint
```



```{index} Type Constraints
```

## Type Constraints




Use `where T : ...` to restrict what types `T` can be. Constraints are useful when an ADT operation needs a capability that not every type has.

| Constraint | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `where T : class` | T must be a reference type |
| `where T : struct` | T must be a value type |
| `where T : new()` | T must have a parameterless constructor |
| `where T : ISomeInterface` | T must implement the interface |
| `where T : BaseClass` | T must inherit from `BaseClass` |

    private readonly List<T> items = new List<T>();
    public int Count { get { return items.Count; } }
    public void Push(T value) { items.Add(value); }
    public bool TryPop(out T value)
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) { value = default!; return false; }
        int last = items.Count - 1;
        value = items[last]; items.RemoveAt(last); return true;
    }
    public T[] Snapshot() { return items.ToArray(); }
}


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

UndoLog<int> log = new UndoLog<int>(); log.Push(42); log.TryPop(out int id); Console.WriteLine(id);

class UndoLog<T>
{
    private readonly List<T> items = new List<T>();
    public int Count { get { return items.Count; } }
    public void Push(T value) { items.Add(value); }
    public bool TryPop(out T value)
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) { value = default!; return false; }
        int last = items.Count - 1;
        value = items[last]; items.RemoveAt(last); return true;
    }
    public T[] Snapshot() { return items.ToArray(); }
}

## Counting Work and Big-O




```{index} Big O; input size; auxiliary space
```


Let `n` be the number of records. Count a representative operation before comparing implementations. **Big-O** describes an upper bound on how work grows with input size, ignoring fixed factors for sufficiently large inputs. It is not an elapsed time or automatically a worst-case claim.

| Bound | Example | Effect of doubling input |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | Reading one array slot | Bounded work independent of size. |
| O(log n) | Repeatedly halving a search interval | About one extra halving. |
| O(n) | Scanning all records | About twice the work. |
| O(n log n) | A typical comparison sort | Slightly more than twice the work. |
| O(n²) | Comparing every pair | About four times the work. |

These are useful upper bounds; a linear scan is also O(n²), but O(n) is more informative. A **tight bound**, written Θ, describes the actual growth order under the stated model. Later chapters use Θ when both upper and lower growth bounds are known.


using System.Collections.Generic;
using System;
using System.Linq;

foreach (int n in new[] { 0, 1, 4, 8 })
{
    int[] expenses = Enumerable.Repeat(125, n).ToArray();
    long total = 0, additions = 0;
    foreach (int cents in expenses) { total += cents; additions++; }
    Console.WriteLine($"n={n}, total={total}, additions={additions}");
}

This example counts exactly `n` additions. Array access and fixed-width arithmetic are treated as constant-cost operations. A comparison of long strings can depend on string length.

## Operation Costs



A data structure is not just correct or incorrect. It also has costs.

| Operation | Array/List-backed stack | Linked-node stack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Push` | Usually O(1); occasional resize costs O(n) | O(1) |
| `Pop` | O(1) | O(1) |
| `Peek` | O(1) | O(1) |
| Random access by index | O(1), if exposed | O(n) |
| Extra memory per item | low | one extra reference per node |

The best representation depends on the workload. If a program mostly pushes and pops at one end, either representation can work. If it needs fast index access, linked nodes are the wrong fit.

Implement `IEnumerable<T>` using `yield return` so a custom type supports `foreach`.

No preview/lab/homework item matches the explicit outcome to implement IEnumerable<T> with yield return.

Explanation

1304_iterators.ipynb · cells 4–23
`foreach` is not built-in magic tied to `List<T>` or `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` specifically. It works on *any* type that implements `IEnumerable<T>` — the interface that promises "I can hand out an object that walks through my elements one at a time." That helper object implements `IEnumerator<T>`, with a `MoveNext()` method and a `Current` property.

```csharp
interface IEnumerable<T>
{
    IEnumerator<T> GetEnumerator();
}

interface IEnumerator<T>
{
    T Current { get; }
    bool MoveNext();
}
```

Written out, `foreach (var item in collection)` is shorthand for a loop built from exactly these two members:

```csharp
var e = collection.GetEnumerator();
while (e.MoveNext())
{
    var item = e.Current;
    // loop body
}
```

This is the ADT pattern from earlier sections applied to iteration itself: `IEnumerable<T>` is a contract, and any representation — an array, a linked structure, a database cursor — can satisfy it.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One
```



```{index} Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One
```

## Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One



A collection knows where its elements are stored. A client often needs only to visit those elements in the promised order. Enumeration provides a boundary between those responsibilities. Foreach asks for an enumeration protocol rather than directly reading private array slots or node links.

For a simple countable sequence 2, 4, 6, imagine an enumerator positioned before the first value. A success

Worked example/case/trace

1304_iterators.ipynb · cells 14–20
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
static IEnumerable<int> EvenNumbers(int first, int last)
{
    for (int n = first; n <= last; n++)
    {
        if (n % 2 == 0)
        {
            yield return n;
        }
    }
}

foreach (int n in EvenNumbers(1, 10))
{
    Console.Write(n + " ");
}

Nothing about `EvenNumbers` mentions `IEnumerator`, `MoveNext`, or `Current` — the compiler builds a hidden class that implements all of it. The method's return type is `IEnumerable<int>`, and the body describes *what to produce*, not *how to track position*.

## Making Your Own Type foreach-able




A standalone iterator *method* is useful, but sometimes the thing you want to iterate is a type you have already defined — an ADT you built, not a built-in collection. To make `foreach` work directly on an instance of your type, implement `IEnumerable<T>` and put a `yield return` inside `GetEnumerator()`:

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using System.Collections;

var range = new NumberRange(5, 4);
foreach (int n in range)
{
    Console.Write(n + " ");
}

class NumberRange : IEnumerable<int>
{
    private readonly int start;
    private readonly int count;

    public NumberRange(int start, int count)
    {
        this.start = start;
        this.count = count;
    }

    public IEnumerator<int> GetEnumerator()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)
        {
            yield return start + i;
        }
    }

Section practice

1304_iterators.ipynb · cells 10–10
The pattern `IEnumerable<T> Produce(...) { ... yield return value; ... }` defines an iterator. Yielding supplies one element and suspends that enumeration's progress until the consumer requests another. An ordinary return from a value-returning method finishes that call; yield return participates in a sequence of resumptions. Explain this distinction before treating yield as abbreviated list construction.

Laziness changes when work and failures occur. Obtaining an enumerable need not run every statement that will produce its values. If the consumer stops after two elements, later elements may never be computed. An expensive calculation inside an iterator is not paid simply because an enumerable variable has been declared, but repeated enumerations may repeat that work. Do not promise caching unless the implementation explicitly provides it.

The producer also needs a mutation policy. An enumeration over shared mutable storage can be affected by changes made after the enumerable is obtained. Library collections may detect invalid mutation during enumeration; custom types must state their own behavior. Returning IEnumerable<T> does not automatically create a snapshot or make private storage immutable.

Then run a second enumeration and ask whether it starts with a fresh progress state. ## Contiguous Storage



An array stores elements in numbered positions. If the array has five slots, valid indexes are `0` through `4`.

```text
index:  0   1   2   3   4
value: [10][20][30][  ][  ]
```

The array has a fixed **capacity**: the number of slots available. A dynamic array also tracks **count**: the number of slots currently being used.


int[] storage = new int[5];
int count = 0;

storage[count] = 10;
count++;
storage[count] = 20;
count++;
storage[count] = 30;
count++;

Console.WriteLine($"count={count}, capacity={storage.Length}");
Console.WriteLine(storage[1]);

```



```{index} Resizing by Copying
```

## Resizing by Copying



When the array fills up, the dynamic array cannot stretch the existing array. It allocates a larger array, copies the existing values, then continues adding into the new storage.

A common strategy is to double the capacity each time resizing is needed. This makes individual resize steps expensive, but keeps most `Add` operations cheap.


static int[] Grow(int[] oldStorage)
{
    int[] larger = new int[oldStorage.Length * 2];
    for (int i = 0; i < oldStorage.Length; i++)
    {
        larger[i] = oldStorage[i];
    }
    return larger;
}

int[] storage = new int[5];
storage[0] = 10;
storage[1] = 20;
storage[2] = 30;
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", storage));
Console.WriteLine($"Length of storage: {storage.Length}");

Console.WriteLine();

int[] newStorage = Grow(storage);
newStorage[2] = 30;

## Nodes and References



Each node stores a value and a reference to the next node.

```text
head -> [10 | next] -> [20 | next] -> [30 | null]
```

The list variable stores a reference to the first node, often called the **head**. The last node points to `null`.


IntroNode<int> first = new IntroNode<int>(10);
first.Next = new IntroNode<int>(20);
first.Next.Next = new IntroNode<int>(30);

Console.WriteLine(first.Value);
Console.WriteLine(first.Next.Value);

public class IntroNode<T>
{
    public T Value { get; }
    public IntroNode<T>? Next { get; set; }

    public IntroNode(T value)
    {
        Value = value;
    }
}

```{index} traversal; linked list
```



```{index} Traversal
```

## Traversal



A linked list cannot jump directly to index `7`. To find an item, code follows references one node at a time. This is called **traversal**.


TraversalNode<string> head = new TraversalNode<string>("alpha");
head.Next = new TraversalNode<string>("beta");
head.Next.Next = new TraversalNode<string>("gamma");

int visits = 0;
for (TraversalNode<string>? current = head; current is not null; current = current.Next)
{
    visits++;
    Console.WriteLine($"visit {visits}: {current.Value}");
}

public class TraversalNode<T>
{
    public T Value { get; }
    public TraversalNode<T>? Next { get; set; }
    public TraversalNode(T value) => Value = value;
}

## Worked Example: A Small Dynamic Array



This class stores integers in an internal array. `Add` appends to the next free slot. The indexer reads an existing value by index.


var values = new DynamicIntArray();
for (int value = 10; value <= 50; value += 10)
{
    values.Add(value);
    Console.WriteLine($"added={value}, count={values.Count}, capacity={values.Capacity}");
}

Console.WriteLine($"values[3]={values[3]}");

public class DynamicIntArray
{
    private int[] items = new int[2];
    public int Count { get; private set; }
    public int Capacity => items.Length;

    public void Add(int value)
    {
        if (Count == items.Length)
        {
            int[] larger = new int[items.Length * 2];
            Array.Copy(items, larger, items.Length);
            items = larger;
        }

        items[Count] = value;
        Count++;
    }

    public int this[int index]
    {
        get
        {
            if (index < 0 || index >= Count)
                throw new IndexOutOfRangeException();
            return items[index];
        }
    }
}

```{index} Insertion After a Node

## Insertion After a Node



If you already have a reference to a node, inserting after it is local. Create a new node, point it to the old next node, then point the current node to the new node.

```text
before: [A] -> [C]
after:  [A] -> [B] -> [C]
```


static void InsertAfter<T>(InsertNode<T> node, T value)
{
    InsertNode<T> inserted = new InsertNode<T>(value);
    inserted.Next = node.Next;
    node.Next = inserted;
}

InsertNode<string> head = new InsertNode<string>("A");
head.Next = new InsertNode<string>("C");
InsertAfter(head, "B");

for (InsertNode<string>? current = head; current is not null; current = current.Next)
{
    Console.WriteLine(current.Value);
}

public class InsertNode<T>
{
    public T Value { get; }
    public InsertNode<T>? Next { get; set; }
    public InsertNode(T value) => Value = v

## Trace Growth Before Writing Code



Start with capacity two. Appending `WO-10` and `WO-30` uses both slots. Before a third append, allocate four slots, copy the two live references, and replace the private storage reference. The logical sequence has not changed yet. Only then write the new value and increase `Count`.

```text
Before growth: items -> [WO-10][WO-30]                 Count = 2
New storage:   larger -> [WO-10][WO-30][unused][unused]
After growth:  items -> [WO-10][WO-30][unused][unused]   Count = 2
After append:  items -> [WO-10][WO-30][WO-40][unused]    Count = 3
```

For reference-type elements, copying the array copies references, not the referenced objects. The work order objects would retain their identity. Our string labels let you concentrate on the sequence rather than object mutation.

| Append number | Count after append | Capacity | Existing entries copied |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| 3 | 3 | 4 | 2 |
| 4 | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| 5 | 5 | 8 | 4 |
| 6 | 6 | 8 | 0 |
| 7 | 7 | 8 | 0 |
| 8 | 8 | 8 | 0 |
| 9 | 9 | 16 | 8 |

## Resizing by Copying



When the array fills up, the dynamic array cannot stretch the existing array. It allocates a larger array, copies the existing values, then continues adding into the new storage.

A common strategy is to double the capacity each time resizing is needed. This makes individual resize steps expensive, but keeps most `Add` operations cheap.


static int[] Grow(int[] oldStorage)
{
    int[] larger = new int[oldStorage.Length * 2];
    for (int i = 0; i < oldStorage.Length; i++)
    {
        larger[i] = oldStorage[i];
    }
    return larger;
}

Console.WriteLine($"Length of storage: {storage.Length}");

Console.WriteLine();

newStorage[2] = 30;

Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", newStorage));
Console.WriteLine($"Length of new storage: {newStorage.Length}");

1401_dynamic_arrays.ipynb · cells 32–36
```{index} Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost
```

## Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost



For nine appends, the trace copies `2 + 4 + 8 = 14` existing entries and writes nine new entries. Counting these array writes gives 23 writes across nine operations. Some individual appends are costly, but the total grows in proportion to the number of appends.

For a longer sequence, copy sizes form `2 + 4 + 8 + ...`. Each term is twice the previous one, so the sum stays below twice the final number of inserted items. Adding one write per appended item still gives a total proportional to `n`. Dividing total work by `n` gives a constant amortized cost. This is a bound over an operation sequence, not an assumption about random inputs.

Growing by one slot each time would copy `2 + 3 + 4 + ... + (n - 1)` entries. That total grows quadratically. Avoiding spare capacity would therefore make repeated appends progressively expensive.

The tradeoff is spare storage. Doubling leaves unused slots after growth, and a resize temporarily keeps both old and new arrays alive. Amortized O(1) also does not guarantee a short pause for every append. A system with a strict response deadline may reserve capacity ahead of time.

// 1. Count storage writes during growth.
// Complete the loop: count copied entries only when capacity doubles,
// and count one new-entry write per append. Predict totals for nine appends.
using System;
int capacity = 2;
int count = 0;
int copied = 0;
int writes = 0;
for (int item = 1; item <= 9; item++)
{
    if (count == capacity) { copied += count; writes += count; capacity *= 2; }
    count++;
    writes++;
}

## A Sequence Contract and Its Invariants



A service desk keeps work orders in processing order. The values might be strings such as `WO-10` and `WO-30`, but the representation should work for other types too. Chapter 13 separated an ADT's behavior from its implementation. Here the behavior is an ordered sequence: append a work order, read its position, insert an urgent order, and remove a completed order.

For an array-backed implementation, three facts must remain true after every public operation:

1. `0 <= Count <= Capacity`.
2. The live sequence occupies indexes `0` through `Count - 1` without gaps.
3. Values outside that range are storage, not members of the sequence.

A zero in an integer array is not a reliable empty marker: zero might be a real value. `Count` determines membership. With `Count = 3` and `Capacity = 5`, reading index `4` must fail even though the underlying array physically has that slot. An insertion at index `3` is valid because it appends; a read at index `3` is invalid.

```{index} References Are Paths, Not Copies
```

## References Are Paths, Not Copies



Work orders may also be represented by separate node objects. A node's `Next` is a reference to another node, not an embedded copy of the remaining list. Assigning `current = head` copies a reference: both variables initially identify the same object. Changing `current` to `current.Next` moves a cursor without moving `head`.

```text
head ----> [WO-10 | next] ---> [WO-30 | null]
current --^
```

If you traverse by repeatedly assigning to `head`, you lose your entry point to the sequence. A separate cursor preserves the list. Also distinguish changing a reference from changing an object: setting `current = current.Next` moves the cursor; setting `current.Next = ...` changes a link in the sequence.

## Insertion Order and Lost Links



You know the node for `WO-10` and want to insert `WO-20` before `WO-30`. Preserve the old successor before overwriting its only incoming list link.

| Step | References | What remains reachable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create B | `A.Next = C`, `B.Next = null` | A still reaches C. |
| Save successor | `B.Next = A.Next` | B now reaches C too. |
| Connect B | `A.Next = B` | A reaches B, then C. |

The correct two assignments are `inserted.Next = node.Next; node.Next = inserted;`. Reversing them makes `inserted.Next` refer to `inserted` itself. The result is a cycle, and the original successor is disconnected from this chain. A traversal waiting for `null` would never finish.

For an empty list there is no predecessor. Inserting at the front sets `newNode.Next = head` before replacing `head`. The same steps work when the old head is null. A list wrapper is useful because it owns the head reference and can update it safely.

## Linked Traversal



A linked representation visits nodes by following references. There is no direct index jump.


Node<int> head = new Node<int>(12);
head.Next = new Node<int>(7);
head.Next.Next = new Node<int>(19);

int target = 15;
for (Node<int>? current = head; current is not null; current = current.Next)
{
    visits++;
    if (current.Value == target)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Found {target} after {visits} node visits.");
        break;
    }
}

## Count a Concrete Workload



Use eight initial orders and spare array capacity. Compare a front insertion, a last-position read, and a front removal.

| Operation | Array work | Linked work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert at front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |
| Read last position after insertion | One indexed read | Eight link advances from head |
| Remove front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |

If readers request the last position 100 times between these updates, the array uses 100 indexed reads while the linked sequence uses 800 link advances. If the workload instead performs many front updates and few index reads, the preference may reverse. Include the whole operation mix.

Counts of different primitives are not interchangeable seconds. Copying a reference, following a link, allocating a node, and checking a bound have different costs. Counts explain how work grows; benchmarks answer a narrower question about a specific implementation and machine.

## Separate Location Cost from Update Cost



A service desk stores `n` work orders. Two requests that sound similar can require different work: “insert at position 400” supplies an index; “insert after this node” supplies a location handle. Compare the same request and the same assumptions before claiming a speed advantage.

| Request | Dynamic array | Singly linked list with head and tail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read index i | O(1) | O(i + 1), O(n) worst case |
| Append | O(1) amortized, O(n) on resize | O(1) with stored tail |
| Insert at front | O(n) shifts | O(1) |
| Insert by index in middle | O(n) shifts, possibly growth | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove by index in middle | O(n) shifts | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove last | O(1), without shrinking | O(n) find predecessor |
| Search unsorted values | O(n) | O(n) |
| Visit every item once | O(n) | O(n) with cursor |

The linked wrapper in this chapter exposes indices rather than public node handles. Its middle insertion therefore includes traversal. A different API could expose validated handles, but it must specify ownership and what happens when a handle refers to a removed node.

## Test the Contract Before Comparing Speed



Both implementations should produce the same logical result for the same legal operation sequence. Test correctness first. A fast implementation that loses an order is not an alternative representation of the same ADT.

| Test | Operations | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty start | Construct | Count zero; read index zero throws. |
| Single element | Add A; remove index zero | Returns A; count zero. |
| Reuse after emptying | Previous test; add B | Read index zero returns B. |
| Middle insertion | Add A, C; insert B at one | A, B, C in that order. |
| Middle removal | Previous test; remove one | Returns B; leaves A, C. |
| Duplicate values | Add A twice; remove zero | One A remains. |
| Invalid insertion | Insert at count plus one | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |
| Invalid removal | Remove at count | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |

Do not test only printed output from the happy path. Check count after each operation, and verify remaining values after removal. A useful additional check compares a generated operation sequence against C# `List<T>` as a reference implementation. It does not make timing comparisons fair; it checks observable behavior.

**Design (applied):** Write the smallest operation sequence that reveals a stale-tail bug. State the expected result before running it.

```{index} Stack Behavior

## Stack Behavior



A **stack** is an abstract data type where the most recently added item is the next item removed. This access rule is called **last in, first out**, or **LIFO**.

The core operations are small:

- `Push(value)` adds a value to the top.
- `Pop()` removes and returns the top value.
- `Peek()` returns the top value without removing it.
- `Count` reports how many values are currently stored.

The point of a stack is not that it stores data in a new magical way. The point is that it restricts access so the program can only work with the top item.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var undoHistory = new Stack<string>();
undoHistory.Push("Open report");
undoHistory.Push("Add chart");
undoHistory.Push("Save report");

Console.WriteLine($"Undo now: {undoHistory.Pop()}");
Console.WriteLine($"Next undo: {undoHistory.Peek()}");
Console.WriteLine($"Actions left: {undoHistory.Count}");


The last action pushed was `Save report`, so it is the first action popped. The stack keeps the order of pending undo actions aligned with how users expect undo to work.


```{index} stack; underflow
```



```{index} Empty Stacks and Safe Access
```

## Empty Stacks and Safe Access



Calling `Pop` or `Peek` on an empty stack is an **underflow** error. In C#, `Stack<T>` throws an exception if the stack is empty. Production code should usually check `Count` before removing an item, or use `TryPop` and `TryPeek` when available.

using System.Collections.Generic;

var pages = new Stack<string>();
pages.Push("home");
pages.Pu
1502_queue_deque.ipynb · cells 6–24
```{index} Queue Behavior
```

## Queue Behavior



A **queue** is an abstract data type where the earliest added item is the next item removed. This access rule is called **first in, first out**, or **FIFO**.

The core operations are:

- `Enqueue(value)` adds a value to the back.
- `Dequeue()` removes and returns the front value.
- `Peek()` returns the front value without removing it.
- `Count` reports how many values are waiting.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var serviceLine = new Queue<string>();
serviceLine.Enqueue("Amina");
serviceLine.Enqueue("Diego");
serviceLine.Enqueue("Mina");

Console.WriteLine($"Serving: {serviceLine.Dequeue()}");
Console.WriteLine($"Next: {serviceLine.Peek()}");
Console.WriteLine($"Still waiting: {serviceLine.Count}");


The first customer enqueued is the first customer served. Unlike a list, a queue communicates that callers should not pick arbitrary positions from the middle.

```

```

## Worklists and Scheduling



Queues often represent work that should be processed in arrival order: help-desk tickets, print jobs, messages, or search states. This pattern is called a **worklist** because the collection stores work that remains to be done.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var work = new Queue<string>();
work.Enqueue("Validate order");
work.Enqueue("Charge card");
work.Enqueue("Send receipt");

int step = 1;
while (work.Count > 0)
{
    string task = work.Dequeue();
    Console.WriteLine($"Step {step}: {task}");
    step++;
}

## Empty Stacks and Safe Access



Calling `Pop` or `Peek` on an empty stack is an **underflow** error. In C#, `Stack<T>` throws an exception if the stack is empty. Production code should usually check `Count` before removing an item, or use `TryPop` and `TryPeek` when available.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var pages = new Stack<string>();
pages.Push("home");
pages.Push("products");

while (pages.Count > 0)
{
    string previousPage = pages.Pop();
    Console.WriteLine($"Back to {previousPage}");
}

Console.WriteLine("No more page history.");


The loop checks `Count` before each `Pop`, so it never tries to remove a value after the stack has become empty.

## Worklists and Scheduling



Queues often represent work that should be processed in arrival order: help-desk tickets, print jobs, messages, or search states. This pattern is called a **worklist** because the collection stores work that remains to be done.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var work = new Queue<string>();
work.Enqueue("Validate order");
work.Enqueue("Charge card");
work.Enqueue("Send receipt");

int step = 1;
while (work.Count > 0)
{
    string task = work.Dequeue();
    Console.WriteLine($"Step {step}: {task}");
    step++;
}


A queue makes the scheduling policy explicit: new work joins the back, and existing work leaves from the front.

## Ring Buffers



An array-backed queue cannot simply remove index `0` by shifting every element left. That would make each dequeue expensive. A **ring buffer** solves this by letting the front and back indexes wrap around the array.

For a bounded queue, the important state is:

- `front`: the index of the next item to remove
- `back`: the index where the next item will be added
- `count`: the number of stored items

```{index} Trace the Stack Invariant

## Trace the Stack Invariant



A report editor saves versions in order. With count three, the live array slots are `0..2`, and the top is index two. `Peek` must preserve count; `Pop` removes only that top value.

| Operation | Bottom to top | Count | Returned value |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Push Draft | Draft | 1 | None |
| Push Reviewed | Draft, Reviewed | 2 | None |
| Peek | Draft, Reviewed | 2 | Reviewed |
| Pop | Draft | 1 | Reviewed |
| Pop | Empty | 0 | Draft |

An invariant is a rule preserved after every completed operation. Here `0 <= Count <= Capacity`, the live values occupy consecutive slots, and `items[Count - 1]` is the top when count is positive. An empty pop must reject the request before decrementing count. Zero or null can be valid data; count determines emptiness.

**Predict:** Push A, push B, pop, push C, then peek. Give the returned values and final count. Which slots are live?

```

## A Complete Generic Array Stack



Chapter 14's dynamic array becomes a stack by exposing only the final live slot. This implementation doubles capacity when full and clears popped slots so unused storage does not retain object references. `default!` suppresses a nullable warning for unused storage; it is not a runtime check.

`TryPop` returns false on empty input and places a default value in its output parameter. Always check the Boolean: a default value could also have been successfully popped. Expect Approved, Reviewed, Draft, fol
1502_queue_deque.ipynb · cells 26–35
```{index} Trace Wraparound and Distinguish Full from Empty
```

## Trace Wraparound and Distinguish Full from Empty



A ring buffer stores logical order across the end of physical storage. Start with capacity four, `front = back = count = 0`. Back is the next insertion slot, not the last occupied slot.

| Operation | Slots 0, 1, 2, 3 | Front | Back | Count | Logical order |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Enqueue A, B, C | A, B, C, unused | 0 | 3 | 3 | A, B, C |
| Dequeue | unused, B, C, unused | 1 | 3 | 2 | B, C |
| Enqueue D | unused, B, C, D | 1 | 0 | 3 | B, C, D |
| Enqueue E | E, B, C, D | 1 | 1 | 4 | B, C, D, E |
| Dequeue B | E, unused, C, D | 2 | 1 | 3 | C, D, E |

`front == back` occurs when the buffer is empty and when it is full. Count distinguishes those states. For logical position i, the physical slot is `(front + i) % Capacity`. The invariants are positive capacity, a front index inside the array, and `0 <= Count <= Capacity`. The next insertion slot is `(front + Count) % Capacity`.

**Trace:** Continue until empty, then enqueue F. Give every front, back, and count. Explain why physical slot zero does not always hold the oldest item.

```



```{index} A Complete Bounded Generic Queue
```

## A Complete Bounded Generic Queue



This implementation derives back from front and count, so it does not maintain a redundant third state variable. Enqueue checks for full storage before writing; dequeue checks emptiness before advancing front. Both clear or fill one slot and update count once.

Capacity is fixed

| Enqueue E | E, B, C, D | 1 | 1 | 4 | B, C, D, E |

`front == back` occurs when the buffer is empty and when it is full. Count distinguishes those states. For logical position i, the physical slot is `(front + i) % Capacity`. The invariants are positive capacity, a front index inside the array, and `0 <= Count <= Capacity`. The next insertion slot is `(front + Count) % Capacity`.

## A Complete Bounded Generic Queue

C15-O4 · supported

Distinguish worst-case and amortized operation costs and compare representation tradeoffs.

Complexity reasoning is attached to actual implementations.

Explanation

1501_stack.ipynb · cells 30–31
```{index} Correctness and Cost of Stack Operations
```

## Correctness and Cost of Stack Operations



`Push` preserves the invariant by growing without changing count, writing to the first unused slot, and increasing count once. `Pop` first obtains the current top, then reduces count and clears precisely the slot that left the live range. It never shifts other values.

Pop and peek take O(1) time. Push takes O(1) on most calls, O(n) when growth copies n live values, and O(1) amortized across repeated pushes using the chapter 15 doubling argument. A linked stack can push and pop at the head in O(1) link operations, but allocates a node per push. Array locality and spare capacity are different memory tradeoffs.

**Check:** For five pushes starting at capacity two, count the existing entries copied. Explain why removing every item from this array stack needs only n pops, while repeatedly removing index zero from an array sequence moves `n(n - 1)/2` entries.
1503_applications_lab.ipynb · cells 18–20
```{index} Comparing Costs
```

## Comparing Costs



For the restricted operations, these structures are usually designed to make the main access rule fast:

| Structure | Operation | Typical cost |
|---|---|---:|
| Growable array stack | Push / pop | O(1) amortized push; O(n) growth; O(1) pop |
| Bounded ring queue | Enqueue / dequeue | O(1); full enqueue rejects |
| Growable array queue | Enqueue / dequeue | O(1) amortized enqueue; O(n) growth; O(1) dequeue |
| Deque | Add/remove either end | O(1) with the right representation |
| List used as queue | Remove index 0 | O(n) |

The tempting implementation is not always the right one. Removing from the front of a plain array or list usually shifts many values.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var slowQueue = new List<string> { "A", "B", "C" };
string first = slowQueue[0];
slowQueue.RemoveAt(0);

Console.WriteLine(first);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", slowQueue));
