```{index} Matching Delimiters
```

## Matching Delimiters



Stacks are useful for nested structures because the most recent opening item must be closed first. Parentheses, brackets, braces, HTML tags, and method calls all have this nested shape.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
foreach (string text in new[] { "{ items[0] + (total - 1) }", "([)]", ")(", "((", "" })
    Console.WriteLine($"{text}: {IsBalanced(text)}");

static bool IsBalanced(string text)
{
    var openings = new Stack<char>();
    foreach (char ch in text)
    {
        if (ch == '(' || ch == '[' || ch == '{') openings.Push(ch);
        else if (ch == ')' || ch == ']' || ch == '}')
        {
            if (!openings.TryPop(out char open)) return false;
            bool matches = (open == '(' && ch == ')')
                        || (open == '[' && ch == ']')
                        || (open == '{' && ch == '}');
            if (!matches) return false;
        }
    }
    return openings.Count == 0;
}

The stack stores exactly the unmatched opening delimiters, with the most recent one on top. A mismatched type or a closing delimiter with no opening returns false immediately. Success also requires an empty stack at the end. This checks delimiter characters only; it does not parse C# strings or comments.

**Trace:** For `([)]`, show the stack after each character until rejection. Why would merely counting openings and closings accept some invalid expressions? Each character is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(d) auxiliary space for maximum nesting depth d.
1503_applications_lab.ipynb · cells 3–31
```{index} Choosing the Access Rule
```

## Choosing the Access Rule



Stacks, queues, and deques are easiest to choose when you name the rule for the next item:

| Situation | Next item should be | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| Undo the most recent edit | Most recently saved | Stack |
| Serve customers fairly | Earliest waiting | Queue |
| Process both urgent and normal work | Either front or back | Deque |

The access rule is more important than the English noun. A "list of tasks" might be a stack, a queue, or a deque depending on how tasks should be removed.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var urgent = new Stack<string>();
urgent.Push("Restart failed service");
urgent.Push("Rollback broken update");

var normal = new Queue<string>();
normal.Enqueue("Update documentation");
normal.Enqueue("Clean old logs");

if (urgent.Count > 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Handle now: {urgent.Pop()}");
}
else if (normal.Count > 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Handle next: {normal.Dequeue()}");
}


This example uses two structures because there are two policies: urgent tasks use most-recent-first, and normal tasks use first-come-first-served.

Backtracking means trying a path, then returning to an earlier choice if that path does not work. A stack records the path because the most recent choice is the first one to undo.

path.Push("Start");

```{index} Undo and Redo Require Two Histories
```

## Undo and Redo Require Two Histories



A realistic undo operation restores a prior state, rather than just printing an action name. Save the previous report state on undo before an edit. Undo saves the current state on redo and restores the latest undo state. Redo reverses that transfer.

| Request | Current state | Undo, bottom to top | Redo, bottom to top |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Draft | Empty | Empty |
| Edit Reviewed | Reviewed | Draft | Empty |
| Edit Approved | Approved | Draft, Reviewed | Empty |
| Undo | Reviewed | Draft | Approved |
| Redo | Approved | Draft, Reviewed | Empty |
| Undo; edit Revised | Revised | Draft, Reviewed | Empty |

A new edit after undo clears redo because it creates a new branch of history. This small editor stores complete immutable string snapshots. Large editors may store inverse commands or smaller changes to limit memory use.

**Predict:** Undo twice after the final edit. What states return? What should an extra undo do when its history is empty?


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
string current = "Draft";
var undo = new Stack<string>();
var redo = new Stack<string>();
void Edit(string next)
{
    undo.Push(current); current = next; redo.Clear();
}
bool Undo()
{
    if (!undo.TryPop(out string? previous)) return false;
    redo.Push(current); current = previous; return true;
}
bool Redo()
{
    if (!redo.TryPop(out string? next)) return false;
    undo.Push(current); current = next; return true;
}
Edit("Reviewed"); Edit("Approved");
Undo(); Console.WriteLi

C16-O1 · supported

Specify first-match search and missing-result behavior, including the meaning of a library search result.

Search contracts and library sign results are practiced.

Explanation

1601_searching.ipynb · cells 5–14
A roster contains codes A, C, C, F. Searching for C could mean finding any occurrence, the first position, every matching position, or simply whether it exists. Those are different result contracts. A faster implementation of a weaker task is not automatically a better solution to the original task.

A first-match linear search examines positions in arrival order. Before examining position i, the invariant is that no earlier position matches. On C, it visits A and then the first C, returning position one. On a missing Z, it reaches the end, and the empty unexamined suffix establishes that no position matched. Empty input reaches that conclusion without reading any element.

| Target | Positions visited by first-match scan | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 0 |
| C | 0, 1 | 1 |
| Z | 0, 1, 2, 3 | Missing |

Binary search answers a question using an ordered region. Each comparison rules out part of the search interval only because the ordering policy is consistent with the ordering used to prepare the data. A visually sorted report using one policy cannot safely be searched using another. Also do not return the position in a sorted snapshot as though it were the original arrival position.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

## Library Results Have Their Own Contract




```{index} Library Results Have Their Own Contract
```


Array.IndexOf uses -1 for a missing value. Array.BinarySearch returns a negative encoded insertion position instead; test result >= 0 before using it as an index. The bitwise complement ~result decodes the position where a missing value could be inserted while preserving order.

Do not mix a teaching method's sentinel with a library method's contract. Read the API promise and check boundaries before using a returned index. The required learning is the sign test; insertion-position encoding is an applied extension.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

int[] ids = {8, 17, 42};
int found = Array.BinarySearch(ids, 20);
Console.WriteLine(found >= 0 ? "Found" : "Missing");
if (found < 0) Console.WriteLine($"Insertion position: {~found}");

Worked example/case/trace

1601_searching.ipynb · cells 14–14
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

int[] ids = {42, 17, 42, 8};
Console.WriteLine(BasicSearch.LinearFirst(ids, 42, EqualityComparer<int>.Default));
Console.WriteLine(BasicSearch.LinearFirst(ids, 99, EqualityComparer<int>.Default));
Console.WriteLine(BasicSearch.LinearFirst(Array.Empty<int>(), 42, EqualityComparer<int>.Default));

public static class BasicSearch
{
    public static int LinearFirst<T>(T[] values, T target, IEqualityComparer<T> equality)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < values.Length; i++)
            if (equality.Equals(values[i], target)) return i;
        return -1;
    }
    public static int BinaryAny<T>(T[] sorted, T target, IComparer<T> comparer)
    {
        int low = 0, high = sorted.Length;
        while (low < high)
        {
            int middle = low + (high - low) / 2;
            int comparison = comparer.Compare(sorted[middle], target);
            if (comparison == 0) return middle;
            if (comparison < 0) low = middle + 1;
            else high = middle;
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

## Trace a Shrinking Candidate Region



For a half-open interval [lo, hi), every candidate is at least lo and strictly before hi. Empty means lo equals hi. A midpoint comparison removes a region that cannot contain the desired result under the contract. The important progress argument is that every continuing iteration strictly shrinks the candidate region. Merely changing lo or hi is not enough if an update can leave the same interval.

A common off-by-one mistake mixes an inclusive upper bound with a loop intended for half-open intervals. Trace an empty array, one element, and a missing target outside each end before celebrating a successful middle match. For duplicates, an ordinary any-match binary search need not return the first occurrence; Chapter 23 develops lower and upper bounds for that stronger query.

Guided workload decision: a report is prepared once and searched one thousand times. List the preparation work as well as the query work. Now suppose a new record arrives after every query. Explain which assumption changed and why the original recommendation may need revision. The following preserved workload material develops that comparison without equating one quick benchmark with a universal threshold.

C16-O3 · partial

Implement insertion sorting and verify order, occurrence preservation, and behavior at boundaries.

Homework restores the saved item or increments a counter inside a complete sort; it does not independently implement or verify the whole insertion algorithm.

Explanation

1602_basic_sorting.ipynb · cells 5–24
Sorting has at least two obligations: output order must satisfy the chosen comparison policy, and output must contain exactly the input occurrences. Producing 1, 2, 3 from input 3, 1, 2 looks right, but so would returning a fixed 1, 2, 3 regardless of input. Tests need to challenge preservation as well as ordering.

Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix. The next item is saved outside the moving region. Larger prefix items shift one position right until the saved item fits. Assigning the saved item back closes the hole. This explains why writing over the next item before saving it can lose data even though the remaining positions appear ordered.

| Input prefix and next item | Work | Resulting prefix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [4], next 2 | Save 2, shift 4, insert 2 | [2, 4] |
| [2, 4], next 3 | Save 3, shift 4, insert 3 | [2, 3, 4] |

Before each outer iteration, the processed prefix is sorted and is a permutation of the corresponding original prefix. The inner shifts preserve all saved occurrences while opening the correct position. When the prefix includes the full array, both obligations hold. This is a reasoning structure, not simply a description of what a successful example happened to print.

Equal keys reveal another contract. If the inner loop moves only items strictly greater than the saved key, equal-key items retain their previous relative order. This is stability. Moving equal items as well can change that order. Use labeled records, such as two invoices with the same total but different IDs, to see the distinction; identical integer values cannot show which o

Worked example/case/trace

1602_basic_sorting.ipynb · cells 14–22
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

int[] amounts = {30, 10, 20, 10};
long comparisons = BasicSort.InsertionSort(amounts, Comparer<int>.Default);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", amounts));
Console.WriteLine($"Comparisons: {comparisons}");

public static class BasicSort
{
    public static long InsertionSort<T>(T[] values, IComparer<T> comparer)
    {
        long comparisons = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < values.Length; i++)
        {
            T current = values[i];
            int position = i;
            while (position > 0)
            {
                comparisons++;
                if (comparer.Compare(values[position - 1], current) <= 0) break;
                values[position] = values[position - 1];
                position--;
            }
            values[position] = current;
        }
        return comparisons;
    }
}

## Sorting Objects Uses an Ordering Policy




```{index} Sorting Objects Uses an Ordering Policy
```


The comparer returns a negative value, zero, or a positive value. These mean before, tied, or after; callers should test the sign rather than assume the magnitude is exactly one. Define ordering separately from object identity and business equality.

The invoice comparer orders by amount only. Two invoices with the same amount are tied even though they have different identifiers. Stable sorting retains their arrival order. If the business requires amount then ID, include that second key in the comparer rather than relying on an accidental order.

public static class BasicSearch
{
    public static int LinearFirst<T>(T[] values, T target, IEqualityComparer<T> equality)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < values.Length; i++)
            if (equality.Equals(values[i], target)) return i;
        return -1;
    }
    public static int BinaryAny<T>(T[] sorted, T target, IComparer<T> comparer)
    {
        int low = 0, high = sorted.Length;
        while (low < high)
        {
            int middle = low + (high - low) / 2;
            int comparison = comparer.Compare(sorted[middle], target);
            if (comparison == 0) return middle;
            if (comparison < 0) low = middle + 1;
            else high = middle;
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

1701_tree_structure.ipynb · cells 11–24

## Base Case and Recursive Case




```{index} Base Case and Recursive Case
```

A **base case** returns an answer directly. A **recursive case** calls the same method on a smaller input and uses that result to build the current answer.

using System;
using System.Linq;

foreach(int n in new[]{0,4})Console.WriteLine($"sum({n})={SumDown(n)}");
try{SumDown(-1);}catch(ArgumentOutOfRangeException){Console.WriteLine("negative input rejected");}
long SumDown(int n)
{
 if(n<0 || n>100)throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(n),"Teaching demo accepts 0 through 100.");
 return n==0?0:n+SumDown(n-1);
}

The contract accepts integers 0 through 100; zero returns zero and negative input is rejected. The cap keeps this linear-depth teaching demo small, rather than promising an unlimited safe recursion depth. For n>0, the nonnegative integer measure n decreases strictly. Assume the smaller call returns the correct sum of 1 through n−1; adding n gives the required sum through n. This is an induction argument: direct base case, smaller correct result, correct combination.

```{index} Tracing the Call Stack
```

```{index} Tracing the Call Stack
```

The call stack stores each active method call until that call returns. A trace can make the order of calls and returns visible.

Console.WriteLine($"Result: {Factorial(4)}");
Console.WriteLine($"0!={Factorial(0)}");
try{Factorial(-1);}catch(ArgumentOutOfRangeException){Console.WriteLine("negative factorial rejected");}

```{index} Complete a Recursive Summary Before Designing a New Query
```

## Complete a Recursive Summary Before Designing a New Query


A tree call returns a summary of its subtree. Counting nodes and counting leaves have different meanings even though both visit the same structure. Before inventing another query, decide what null contributes, what a leaf contributes, and how an internal node combines its children.

Use root 8 with left child 3 and right child 10; node 3 has only a left child 1. For a leaf count, null contributes zero and a real leaf contributes one. An internal node contributes the sum of its child leaf counts, without adding one for itself.

## Tree Vocabulary




```{index} tree; root; leaf; subtree
```


A **tree** is a collection of nodes connected by parent-child relationships. The **root** is the starting node. A **leaf** has no children. A **subtree** is a node together with everything below it.

Many real systems have this shape: folders contain folders, supervisors manage teams, expressions contain subexpressions, and web pages link to lower-level navigation sections.


using System;

var root = new TreeNode("Courses");
root.Left = new TreeNode("Programming");
root.Right = new TreeNode("Databases");
root.Left.Left = new TreeNode("C#");
root.Left.Right = new TreeNode("Python");

Console.WriteLine(root.Value);
Console.WriteLine(root.Left.Value);
Console.WriteLine(root.Left.Left.Value);

class TreeNode
{
    public string Value { get; }
    public TreeNode? Left { get; set; }
    public TreeNode? Right { get; set; }

    public TreeNode(string value)
    {
        Value = value;
    }
}


This first representation uses `Left` and `Right` references, so it is a **binary tree**. The values could represent labels, numbers, records, or any other data.


A tree models a hierarchy with one route from the root to each node. In a nonempty tree, every node except the root has exactly one parent. There are no cycles, and all nodes belong to the same connected structure. A structure with shared children or a link back to an ancestor needs graph algorithms instead of these tree algorithms.

A company's departments form a general tree: a manager can have more than two direct reports. `Le
1702_binary_search_trees.ipynb · cells 3–6
```{index} The BST Invariant
```

## The BST Invariant




```{index} binary search tree; BST invariant
```


A **binary search tree** is a binary tree with an ordering rule, often called an **invariant**:

- every value in a node's left subtree is less than the node's value;
- every value in a node's right subtree is greater than the node's value.

This rule must be true at every node, not only at the root.


using System;

var root = new Node(8);
root.Left = new Node(3);
root.Right = new Node(10);
root.Left.Left = new Node(1);
root.Left.Right = new Node(6);
root.Right.Right = new Node(14);

Console.WriteLine($"valid tree: {IsValidBst(root, long.MinValue, long.MaxValue)}");
root.Left!.Right = new Node(9);
Console.WriteLine($"ancestor violation: {IsValidBst(root, long.MinValue, long.MaxValue)}");
Console.WriteLine($"minimum int: {IsValidBst(new Node(int.MinValue), long.MinValue, long.MaxValue)}");
Console.WriteLine($"maximum int: {IsValidBst(new Node(int.MaxValue), long.MinValue, long.MaxValue)}");

bool IsValidBst(Node? node, long min, long max)
{
    if (node is null)
    {
        return true;
    }

    if (node.Value <= min || node.Value >= max)
    {
        return false;
    }

    return IsValidBst(node.Left, min, node.Value)
        && IsValidBst(node.Right, node.Value, max);
}

class Node
{
    public int Value { get; }
    public Node? Left { get; set; }
    public Node? Right { get; set; }

    public Node(int value) => Value = value;
}

## A Visit and a Returned Result Are Different Events



A traversal chooses when to visit a node relative to its children. A recursive aggregation also returns results from children to their caller. These events can happen at different times. Printing a node before recursing gives preorder; computing its subtree size cannot finish until the child sizes are known.

Use a small tree with root B, left child A and right child C. Preorder visits B, A, C; inorder visits A, B, C; postorder visits A, C, B. These names describe timing, not three different storage layouts. The same nodes and edges support all three orders.

| Moment during Count(B) | Known information | What must wait? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enter B | B exists | Its subtree count |
| Left call returns | Left count is 1 | Right count |
| Right call returns | Right count is 1 | Nothing needed for the sum |
| Return from B | 1 + 1 + 1 is 3 | Caller may now use 3 |

An empty subtree returns zero directly. That is not an arbitrary special case appended to the algorithm; it makes the recurrence Count(node) = 1 + Count(left) + Count(right) valid for a leaf. A missing return, or adding one for an empty subtree, changes the contract across every ancestor that uses the result.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Count Active Calls Separately from Visited Nodes
```



```{index} Count Active Calls Separately from Visited Nodes
```

1703_tree_lab.ipynb · cells 12–15

## Level Order with a Queue




```{index} tree; level order traversal; queue
```

Depth-first traversals finish descendants before moving to another branch. **Level order** visits nodes by depth: root first, then its children, then their children. Use the Chapter 15 queue as a worklist of nodes discovered but not yet processed.

When you remove a node from the queue, append its existing children from left to right. The queue keeps earlier levels ahead of later ones. In a proper tree, each non-root node has exactly one parent, so it is enqueued once. Graphs with shared descendants or cycles need an additional visited set, a topic for Chapter 20.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var root = new Node(40)
{
    Left = new Node(20) { Left = new Node(10), Right = new Node(30) },
    Right = new Node(60) { Left = new Node(50), Right = new Node(70) }
};
var pending = new Queue<Node>();
pending.Enqueue(root);
while (pending.Count > 0)
{
    Node node = pending.Dequeue();
    Console.WriteLine($"visit={node.Id}; pending before children={pending.Count}");
    if (node.Left is not null) pending.Enqueue(node.Left);
    if (node.Right is not null) pending.Enqueue(node.Right);
}

class Node
{
    public int Id { get; }
    public Node? Left { get; set; }
    public Node? Right { get; set; }
    public Node(int id) => Id = id;
}

void Preorder(TreeNode? node)

    Preorder(node.Left);
    Preorder(node.Right);
}

void Inorder(TreeNode? node)
{
    if (node is null) return;
    Inorder(node.Left);
    Console.Write(node.Value + " ");
    Inorder(node.Right);
}

void Postorder(TreeNode? node)
{
    if (node is null) return;
    Postorder(node.Left);
    Postorder(node.Right);
    Console.Write(node.Value + " ");
}

{
    public int Value { get; }
    public TreeNode? Left { get; set; }
    public TreeNode? Right { get; set; }

    public TreeNode(int value) => Value = value;
}

## Height and Shape




```{index} tree height; tree depth
```


A node's **depth** is its distance from the root. A tree's **height** is the longest downward path from the root to a leaf. Height matters because many tree operations follow one path from the root toward a leaf.


using System;

var root = new TreeNode(8);
root.Left = new TreeNode(3);
root.Right = new TreeNode(10);
root.Left.Left = new TreeNode(1);
root.Left.Right = new TreeNode(6);
root.Left.Right.Left = new TreeNode(4);

Console.WriteLine($"Height: {Height(root)}");

int Height(TreeNode? node)
{
    if (node is null)
    {
        return -1;
    }

    return 1 + Math.Max(Height(node.Left), Height(node.Right));
}

class TreeNode
{
    public int Value { get; }
    public TreeNode? Left { get; set; }
    public TreeNode? Right { get; set; }

    public TreeNode(int value) => Value = value;
}
1701_tree_structure.ipynb · cells 21–29
```{index} Recursive Structure
```

## Recursive Structure




```{index} tree; recursive structure
```


Trees are recursive because each child is the root of a smaller tree. That means many tree algorithms follow the same pattern:

1. Stop if the current node is `null`.
2. Do some work at the current node.
3. Recur into one or more child subtrees.

This is not recursion for its own sake. It mirrors the structure of the data.


using System;

var root = new TreeNode(8);
root.Left = new TreeNode(3);
root.Right = new TreeNode(10);
root.Left.Left = new TreeNode(1);
root.Left.Right = new TreeNode(6);

Console.WriteLine($"Node count: {Count(root)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Leaf count: {CountLeaves(root)}");

int Count(TreeNode? node)
{
    if (node is null)
    {
        return 0;
    }

    return 1 + Count(node.Left) + Count(node.Right);
}

int CountLeaves(TreeNode? node)
{
    if (node is null)
    {
        return 0;
    }

    if (node.Left is null && node.Right is null)
    {
        return 1;
    }

    return CountLeaves(node.Left) + CountLeaves(node.Right);
}

class TreeNode
{
    public int Value { get; }
    public TreeNode? Left { get; set; }
    public TreeNode? Right { get; set; }

    public TreeNode(int value) => Value = value;
}


`Count` treats the current node as one item plus the size of each child subtree. `CountLeaves` changes the base case: a node with no children contributes one leaf.


The recursion needs two guarantees. First, a null reference represents an empty subtree and contributes zero. Second, each recursive call receives a smaller subtree. In a fi

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var tickets = new TicketTree();
foreach (int id in new[] { 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70 }) tickets.Add(id);
Console.WriteLine($"duplicate added={tickets.Add(30)}");

public class TicketTree
{
    private Node? root;
    public int Count { get; private set; }
    public int Height => NodeHeight(root);

    public bool Add(int id)
    {
        bool added = false;
        root = Insert(root, id, ref added);
        if (added) Count++;
        return added;
    }

## Search




```{index} binary search tree; search
```


BST search uses comparison to discard one subtree at each step. If the target is smaller than the current node, search left. If it is larger, search right. If it is equal, the value has been found.


using System;

var tree = new BinarySearchTree();
foreach (int value in new[] { 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13 })
{
    tree.Insert(value);
}

Console.WriteLine(tree.Contains(7));
Console.WriteLine(tree.Contains(2));

class BinarySearchTree
{
    private Node? root;

    public void Insert(int value)
    {
        root = Insert(root, value);
    }

    public bool Contains(int value)
    {
        Node? current = root;
        while (current is not null)
        {
            if (value == current.Value) return true;
            current = value < current.Value ? current.Left : current.Right;
        }

        return false;
    }

    private static Node Insert(Node? node, int value)
    {
        if (node is null) return new Node(value);
        if (value < node.Value) node.Left = Insert(node.Left, value);
        else if (value > node.Value) node.Right = Insert(node.Right, value);
        return node;
    }

    private sealed class Node
    {
        public int Value { get; }
        public Node? Left { get; set; }
        public Node? Right { get; set; }

        public Node(int value) => Value = value;
    }
}


This `Contains` method is iterative: it walks one path from the root down. A recursive version would follow the same comparisons.

## Verify Updates Against a Model




```{index} binary search tree; testing; SortedSet
```

A test should check the operation's result and the structure left behind. Use `SortedSet<int>` as an independent reference for membership and sorted output. It implements the same unique-key contract through a different library implementation. Comparing only printed output from one hand-built tree would miss many reference-update errors.

After each update, compare the returned Boolean, Count, inorder keys, and ordering validator. Also check the minimum and membership. The example deliberately removes a root with two children while its successor has a right child, drains the tree, and reuses it.

using System;
using System.Linq;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var tree = new TicketTree();
var model = new SortedSet<int>();
void Check()
{
    if (!tree.IsValid() || tree.Count != model.Count
        || !tree.InOrder().SequenceEqual(model)) throw new Exception("Tree/model mismatch.");
    bool found = tree.TryMinimum(out int minimum);
    if (found != (model.Count > 0) || (found && minimum != model.Min))
        throw new Exception("Minimum mismatch.");
}

}
foreach (int id in new[] { 8, 99, 3, 12, 1, 6, 10, 14, 11, int.MinValue, int.MaxValue })
{
    if (tree.Remove(id) != model.Remove(id)) throw new Exception("Remove result mismatch.");
    Check();
}

## Shape and Performance




```{index} binary search tree; height; balanced tree
```


A BST is efficient when its height stays small. If inserted values arrive in sorted order, the tree can become a chain. Then search behaves like scanning a linked list.


using System;

var balancedLike = new BinarySearchTree();
foreach (int value in new[] { 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13 })
{
    balancedLike.Insert(value);
}

var chain = new BinarySearchTree();
foreach (int value in new[] { 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14 })
{
    chain.Insert(value);
}

Console.WriteLine($"Mixed insertion height: {balancedLike.Height()}");
Console.WriteLine($"Sorted insertion height: {chain.Height()}");

class BinarySearchTree
{
    private Node? root;

    public void Insert(int value) => root = Insert(root, value);
    public int Height() => Height(root);

    private static Node Insert(Node? node, int value)
    {
        if (node is null) return new Node(value);
        if (value < node.Value) node.Left = Insert(node.Left, value);
        else if (value > node.Value) node.Right = Insert(node.Right, value);
        return node;
    }

    private static int Height(Node? node)
    {
        if (node is null) return -1;
        return 1 + Math.Max(Height(node.Left), Height(node.Right));
    }

    private sealed class Node
    {
        public int Value { get; }
        public Node? Left { get; set; }
        public Node? Right { get; set; }
        public Node(int value) => Value = value;
    }
}

## Range Queries and Pruning




```{index} binary search tree; range query; pruning
```

Suppose staff want all active IDs from 25 through 60, inclusive. One method gets every ID and filters the resulting list. A BST can also skip subtrees that cannot contain a match. **Pruning** means using a proved constraint to avoid visiting part of a structure.

At key 20, the entire left subtree is below the lower bound 25. At key 60, the entire right subtree is above the upper bound 60. For keys within the interval, process left, node, and right to keep the result ordered. Bounds are inclusive for the query even though the BST's ordering invariant is strict.

The standalone example exposes nodes only to make the recursion visible. The same method could be private inside `TicketTree`, with a public `Range(lower, upper)` wrapper.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var root = new Node(40)
{
    Left = new Node(20) { Left = new Node(10), Right = new Node(30) },
    Right = new Node(60) { Left = new Node(50), Right = new Node(70) }
};
var matches = new List<int>();
int visited = 0;
Range(root, 25, 60, matches);
Console.WriteLine("matches=" + string.Join(", ", matches));
Console.WriteLine($"nodes visited={visited}");

void Range(Node? node, int lower, int upper, List<int> result)
{

    visited++;
    if (lower < node.Id) Range(node.Left, lower, upper, result);
    if (lower <= node.Id && node.Id <= upper) result.Add(node.Id);
    if (node.Id < upper) Range(node.Right, lower, upper, resu

**Question 2: Height computation**

Computing uncached height takes O(log n) time whenever the tree has logarithmic height.

- True
- False

```{dropdown} Answer
False. The recursive height method visits every node, so it takes Θ(n) time. Height limits path length, not the work of a full traversal.
```

**Question 3: Successor removal**

A two-child deletion may discard the successor's entire subtree because the successor has no left child.

- True
- False

```{dropdown} Answer
False. The successor may have a right child. Return that child to preserve its keys.
```

**Question 4: Sorted output**

Sorted inorder output alone proves that insertion preserved every intended key.

- True
- False

```{dropdown} Answer
False. A lost subtree can leave sorted output. Compare membership and Count with the expected set as well.
```

**Question 5: Traversal storage**

A level-order traversal can use more auxiliary storage than recursive depth-first traversal on a wide, shallow tree.

- True
- False

```{dropdown} Answer
True. The queue can hold many nodes at a level, while the recursive stack follows height.
```

C18-O1 · supported

Specify priority order, tie behavior, and empty-removal behavior for a priority queue.

Priority direction and ties are assessed through API behavior.

Explanation

1801_priority_queues.ipynb · cells 5–12
A service desk chooses the lowest numbered priority next. That is a removal contract. It does not require that every stored element be maintained in complete sorted order, nor does it say that equal priorities must leave in arrival order. State the priority direction and tie policy before interpreting a printed storage array.

A min-heap requires each parent's priority to be no greater than its children's. The root is therefore a minimum, but siblings need not be ordered. In the array [1, 4, 2, 7, 6, 3], the values 4 and 2 can appear in that order without violating the heap. Reading the array from left to right is not the same as repeatedly removing the minimum.

| Operation needed | Heap property helps with it? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inspect the minimum | Yes | It is at the root |
| Remove the minimum and restore the property | Yes | Only a repair path is needed |
| Print everything in sorted order without changing storage | Not directly | Heap order is weaker than total order |
| Find an arbitrary ID | Not directly | Priority ancestry does not locate arbitrary keys |

The complete-tree shape lets an array encode parent/child positions without one node object per edge. With zero-based positions, a non-root index i has parent (i-1)/2 using integer division; its potential children are 2i+1 and 2i+2. A child position must still be checked against Count. Capacity is not the number of live heap entries.

Guided drawing: place the six array values above into the implicit tree. Check each parent-child relation. Then compare positions one and two: their values are out of

Worked example/case/trace

1801_priority_queues.ipynb · cells 9–12
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var tasks = new PriorityQueue<string, int>();
tasks.Enqueue("Process invoice", 2);
tasks.Enqueue("Respond to outage", 0);
tasks.Enqueue("Send summary", 3);
tasks.Enqueue("Reset password", 1);

while (tasks.Count > 0)
{
    string task = tasks.Dequeue();
    Console.WriteLine(task);
}


The outage has priority `0`, so it is processed before lower-urgency work. Priority queues are useful for schedulers, event simulations, pathfinding, triage, and any workflow where "next" means most important rather than oldest.


A priority queue defines how you select the next element. It does not promise that enumeration is sorted or that arbitrary keys are easy to locate. The numerical priority has an application meaning: here zero is most urgent. Dequeue from an empty queue is an error; `TryDequeue` reports false instead.

Equal priorities need a policy. The .NET library does not guarantee arrival order for ties. If the service desk requires first-arrived service among equally urgent tickets, use the pair `(urgency, arrivalNumber)` as the priority. Tuple comparison considers urgency first and arrival second. Each arrival number is unique within the queue, so the resulting order is deterministic.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

var queue = new PriorityQueue<string, (int Urgency, long Arrival)>();
long arrival = 0;
queue.Enqueue("T-100", (2, arrival++));
queue.Enqueue("T-101", (0, arrival++));
queue.Enqueue("T-102", (2, arrival++));
while (queue.TryDequeue(out string? ticket, out var priority))

## Heap Representation




```{index} heap; min-heap; complete tree
```


A **heap** is a common priority-queue representation. A binary heap has two key rules:

- **Shape rule**: the tree is complete, filled level by level from left to right.
- **Order rule**: in a min-heap, each parent priority is less than or equal to its child priorities.

Because the shape is complete, a heap can be stored compactly in an array. For an item at index `i`, the children are at `2 * i + 1` and `2 * i + 2`.


using System;

int[] heap = { 1, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6, 4 };

for (int parent = 0; parent < heap.Length; parent++)
{
    int left = 2 * parent + 1;
    int right = 2 * parent + 2;

    if (left < heap.Length)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{heap[parent]} -> left child {heap[left]}");
    }

    if (right < heap.Length)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{heap[parent]} -> right child {heap[right]}");
    }
}


The array is not fully sorted. It only guarantees that each parent is no larger than its children. That weaker rule is enough to keep the minimum at the root.


For a non-root index i, its parent is `(i - 1) / 2`, using integer division. Valid child indexes must be less than Count. Count describes occupied positions; the backing array may have extra capacity that is not part of the heap.

```text
          1 (0)
        /       \
     3 (1)     2 (2)
    /    \     /    \
 7 (3) 5 (4) 6 (5) 4 (6)
```

The values obey parent-child order, but siblings and separate subtrees can be out of numerical order. For example, 3 precedes 2 in the array. Repeatedly

public class BinaryMinHeap<T>
{
    private readonly List<T> items = new List<T>();
    private readonly IComparer<T> comparer;
    public int Count => items.Count;
    public int Capacity => items.Capacity;
    public BinaryMinHeap(IComparer<T>? comparer = null)
        => this.comparer = comparer ?? Comparer<T>.Default;

    public void Enqueue(T item)
    {
        items.Add(item);
        int child = items.Count - 1;
        while (child > 0)
        {
            int parent = (child - 1) / 2;
            if (comparer.Compare(items[parent], items[child]) <= 0) break;
            (items[parent], items[child]) = (items[child], items[parent]);
            child = parent;
        }
    }

    public T Peek()
    {
        if (items.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Heap is empty.");
        return items[0];
    }

    public T Dequeue()
    {
        T minimum = Peek();
        T last = items[^1];
        items.RemoveAt(items.Count - 1);
        if (items.Count == 0) return minimum;
        items[0] = last;
        int parent = 0;
        while (parent < items.Count / 2)
        {
            int left = 2 * parent + 1;
            int right

The array is not fully sorted. It only guarantees that each parent is no larger than its children. That weaker rule is enough to keep the minimum at the root.


For a non-root index i, its parent is `(i - 1) / 2`, using integer division. Valid child indexes must be less than Count. Count describes occupied positions; the backing array may have extra capacity that is not part of the heap.

```text
          1 (0)
        /       \
     3 (1)     2 (2)
    /    \     /    \
 7 (3) 5 (4) 6 (5) 4 (6)
```

The values obey parent-child order, but siblings and separate subtrees can be out of numerical order. For example, 3 precedes 2 in the array. Repeatedly removing the root produces a sorted sequence; reading the raw array does not. The complete shape guarantees height Θ(log n) for a nonempty binary heap.

C18-O3 · gap

Trace and implement sift-up and sift-down repairs for insertion and removal.

The explicit implement-repairs outcome has no independent repair-body task: the complete heap is supplied and students insert values or change a draining condition.

Explanation

1802_heap_implementation.ipynb · cells 5–19
Enqueue adds a new entry at the next open leaf position so the complete shape is preserved. All old parent-child relations are unchanged. Only the new entry's path toward the root can violate min-heap order. Bubble-up compares with the parent and swaps while the child is smaller. Moving upward strictly decreases its index, so repair terminates.

Start with [2, 5, 4] and enqueue 1. Appending produces [2, 5, 4, 1]. Comparing 1 with parent 5 gives [2, 1, 4, 5]. Comparing that 1 with root 2 gives [1, 2, 4, 5]. Do not sort the whole array; that would enforce a stronger and more expensive condition than the operation needs.

Dequeue first saves the root result. Move the last live entry to the root and reduce Count. The only possible ordering defects now lie downward from that replacement. Choose the smaller existing child before swapping; exchanging with an arbitrary child can leave a smaller sibling above a larger parent relation.

| Heap after removing 1 | Inspection | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [5, 2, 4] | Children 2 and 4 | Choose 2 |
| [2, 5, 4] | 5 has no child | Stop |

A singleton removal needs no child access after Count becomes zero. An empty removal must follow the stated failure policy without first reading position zero. Also clear unused reference slots when the implementation owns a backing array and should release references to removed objects. Reducing Count hides a slot from the abstract sequence, but it does not itself erase a stored reference.

The height of a complete heap is logarithmic in its live size, which bounds the number of repair levels. Array

1802_heap_implementation.ipynb · cells 9–19
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var heap = new List<int> { 1, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6, 4 };
heap.Add(0);

int child = heap.Count - 1;
while (child > 0)
{
    int parent = (child - 1) / 2;
    if (heap[parent] <= heap[child])
    {
        break;
    }

    (heap[parent], heap[child]) = (heap[child], heap[parent]);
    child = parent;
}

Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", heap));


The new value `0` starts at the end. It swaps with larger parents until the min-heap property is restored.


Trace the appended zero from index seven to the root:

| Stage | Index path | Array |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Append | 7 | 1, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6, 4, 0 |
| Swap with 7 | 7 → 3 | 1, 3, 2, 0, 5, 6, 4, 7 |
| Swap with 3 | 3 → 1 | 1, 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 4, 7 |
| Swap with 1 | 1 → 0 | 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 4, 7 |

Before insertion, every old parent-child relation satisfies the order rule. Appending adds only one possible violation between the new item and its parent. Each swap repairs that relation and moves the possible violation upward. Stop at the root or when the parent is no larger. This explains why repairing one path is sufficient.

C18-O4 · partial

Explain heap operation costs and distinguish a valid heap from a fully sorted array.

No independent operation-count derivation or worst/amortized distinction task matches the cost outcome.

Explanation

1802_heap_implementation.ipynb · cells 17–19
In the removal example, replacing root 1 with the last value 4 gives `4, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6`. Compare both children before choosing the swap: 2 is smaller than 3, so swap indexes zero and two. The result is `2, 3, 4, 7, 5, 6`. The next child is 6; 4 is already no larger, so stop.

Choosing a larger child can leave the root larger than the other child. Sink-down must choose the smaller existing child and handle a last parent with only a left child. Removing the last array position preserves the complete shape. For a singleton, removal leaves no root to repair.

The complete generic heap below hides the backing list and accepts an optional comparer. The element type must support the default ordering, or you must supply a comparer. `Peek` and `Dequeue` throw on empty; `TryDequeue` distinguishes empty from a stored default value. Equal values are legal, but this heap does not impose stable arrival order on equal comparisons.

while (priorities.TryDequeue(out int urgency)) Console.WriteLine(urgency);
priorities.Enqueue(0);
Console.WriteLine($"reused zero={priorities.Dequeue()}, empty={priorities.Count == 0}");

Explanation

1803_priority_applications.ipynb · cells 5–18
A sales report needs the largest three amounts from a stream. Sorting every amount is one possible solution, but the requested result is smaller than the full sorted input. A min-heap of the currently retained best three exposes the weakest retained amount at its root. That is exactly the boundary a new candidate must beat.

For amounts 7, 2, 9, 4, 10, retain 7, 2 and 9 first. Their minimum is 2. Candidate 4 replaces 2; candidate 10 replaces the new minimum 4. The retained values are 7, 9 and 10. Their heap storage need not be printed in sorted report order; sorting only the final retained values is a separate reporting step.

| Candidate | Decision | Retained values as a set of amounts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7, 2, 9 | Fill three places | 2, 7, 9 |
| 4 | Replace the smallest retained amount | 4, 7, 9 |
| 10 | Replace the smallest retained amount | 7, 9, 10 |

After each processed prefix, the heap contains the best min(k, processed count) entries under the chosen comparison policy. If a new candidate is no better than the root and the heap is full, at least k retained entries are already as good, so discarding it preserves the invariant. If it is better, replacing the weakest retained entry restores the best-k claim. This argument explains the algorithm rather than just observing a successful result.

Decide whether k zero is a valid request, what to do when fewer than k entries exist, and how tied amounts affect which record IDs are retained. Keeping amounts alone loses record identity. A report requiring deterministic tie order needs a secondary policy, not an assumption

Worked example/case/trace

1803_priority_applications.ipynb · cells 10–11
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

int[] amounts = { 72, 91, 84, 99, 67, 88, 95, 95 };
int k = 3;
Console.WriteLine("top=" + string.Join(", ", TopK(amounts, k)));
Console.WriteLine($"zero-k count={TopK(amounts, 0).Count}");

List<int> TopK(IEnumerable<int> values, int k)
{
    if (k < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(k));
    if (k == 0) return new List<int>();
    var retained = new PriorityQueue<int, int>();
    foreach (int value in values)
    {
        if (retained.Count < k) retained.Enqueue(value, value);
        else if (value > retained.Peek())
        {
            retained.Dequeue();
            retained.Enqueue(value, value);
        }
    }
    var result = new List<int>();
    while (retained.TryDequeue(out int value, out _)) result.Add(value);
    result.Reverse();
    return result;
}

For k = 3, retained values after the first three inputs are 72, 84, 91. Processing 99 drops 72; 67 changes nothing; 88 drops 84; 95 drops 88; the second 95 drops 91. The final result is `99, 95, 95`. Repeated equal amounts remain separate observations.

For n inputs and positive k, maintenance has an O(n log(k + 1)) upper bound and O(k) storage, or fewer entries when n < k. Producing the final ordered result costs O(k log(k + 1)) in the worst case. k = 0 returns immediately; negative k is rejected. If record identity or tie order matters, include an explicit secondary priority and define which tied records to retain.

C19-O1 · supported

Choose a key equality policy and explain why equal keys must have compatible hash codes.

Equality/hash consistency and case-policy selection have assessment.

Explanation

1901_hashing.ipynb · cells 5–14
A hash function maps keys to a finite bucket range, so different keys can map to the same bucket. The hash narrows the search; equality identifies the actual key. In a table of five buckets using a simple remainder demonstration, integer keys 2, 7 and 12 all map to bucket two. Keeping only one value at that position would lose entries unless the ADT intentionally replaces an equal key.

A chained bucket can examine the entries for actual equality. An open-addressed representation follows a probe sequence instead. Removing an entry in open addressing must preserve the ability to find later entries whose probe passed through its slot. Turning a deleted slot directly into never-used can stop a search too soon; the distinction between deleted and never occupied matters.

Guided trace: insert the three colliding keys, remove seven, then find twelve. Explain why a search must still reach twelve. Now grow the bucket range and recompute placement; copying each entry to its old numeric slot is not sufficient because the mapping depends on the table size. Hash distribution, equality consistency, load and deletion policy work together.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]


```{index} Dictionary Contracts and Key Equality
```

## Dictionary Contracts and Key Equality




```{index} dictionary; key equality; hashing
```

A dictionary associates one value with each distinct key. Looking up a customer ID asks for that ID's record; it does not ask for the first record in order. C# `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` uses hashing for key-based access. `Add`
1902_dictionaries_sets.ipynb · cells 8–8
If product IDs are case-insensitive under the business contract, B and b must use compatible equality in both collections. Normalizing only one side can produce false missing-ID reports. For hashed keys, equal keys must have equal hash codes under the selected policy. A good hash distribution improves performance but cannot repair inconsistent equality.

Do not mutate fields that determine a key's hash/equality while that key is stored. The entry may remain physically present in a bucket chosen by its old meaning while a new lookup examines another location. Immutable key data or remove/change/reinsert workflows make that boundary explicit.

Set-operation APIs also have mutation contracts. Some operations modify the receiving set; query-based forms may produce a sequence instead. If the original warehouse membership must remain available, work on a copy or choose a nonmutating approach deliberately. Assigning another variable to the same set object does not create independent storage.

Guided exercise: add B twice and lowercase a once to the sales input. Produce two answers: a unique-ID reconciliation under a stated case policy and a repeated-ID report. Explain which information a set has discarded and why the frequency report cannot be reconstructed from that set alone.

Worked example/case/trace

1901_hashing.ipynb · cells 9–14
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

var owners = new Dictionary<string, string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
owners.Add("T-100", "Amina");
owners["t-100"] = "Diego";
Console.WriteLine($"count={owners.Count}, owner={owners["T-100"]}");
Console.WriteLine($"missing={owners.TryGetValue("T-999", out _)}");
Console.WriteLine($"removed={owners.Remove("T-100")}, count={owners.Count}");

This dictionary treats `T-100` and `t-100` as equal, so assignment changes the owner rather than adding another key. Choose the equality policy when creating the collection and apply it consistently. For symbolic ticket IDs, ordinal comparison avoids culture-dependent language rules. This example deliberately ignores case; other applications may need case-sensitive identifiers.

Hashing and equality must agree: equal keys must have equal hash codes. Different keys may have the same hash code, so a lookup must still compare actual keys. A custom comparer supplies both operations. Do not modify fields that determine a stored key's equality or hash code; its new bucket may no longer match the location used during insertion. Strings are immutable, which avoids that particular mutation hazard. [Microsoft's GetHashCode contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode) explains this agreement.

## Separate Chaining and Complete Operations




```{index} separate chaining; collision; hash-table update
```

A collision occurs when different keys choose the same bucket. **Separate chaining** stores a collection of entries at each bucket. A lookup computes the bucket and compares keys within that chain. An update must search the chain before appending; otherwise it can create duplicate keys. Removal must preserve the other colliding entries.

With four buckets, IDs 101, 105, and 109 all choose bucket one. To find 109, inspect 101, then 105, then 109. To report that 113 is absent, inspect the entire chain. A successful lookup may stop early; an unsuccessful one must establish that no matching key exists.

The complete `TicketMap` stores integer ticket IDs and string owners. `Put` returns true for a new key and false for replacement. `Remove` reports whether membership changed. `TryGetValue` returns false on absence; ignore its output value in that case.

1901_hashing.ipynb · cells 23–28
Define load factor α = n / m, where n is the number of entries and m is the number of buckets. Before adding 113, the map has three entries in four buckets, so α = 0.75. A fourth new key would exceed the teaching threshold, so the map doubles to eight buckets before inserting it.

Changing the bucket count changes placement. Copying old bucket lists to the same array indexes is insufficient. Recompute every entry's bucket under the new capacity, a process called **rehashing**.

| ID | Bucket with m = 4 | Bucket with m = 8 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 101 | 1 | 5 |
| 105 | 1 | 1 |
| 109 | 1 | 5 |
| 113 | 1 | 1 |

Growth splits this collision group into two chains. It does not guarantee that all collisions disappear. A poor hash function can keep many keys in one chain even at low load factor.

Under well-distributed hashes and constant-time hashing/equality, chaining operations have expected O(1 + α) work. A pathological chain can require O(n) work. This resize visits all entries and initializes a larger bucket array, giving O(n + m) work for that operation. Geometric growth contributes amortized constant work per new key when load is kept bounded; one growth-triggering insertion can still be linear.

The threshold 0.75 belongs to this teaching map, not to a universal hash-table rule. Separate chaining permits α greater than one. Open addressing needs unused slots and becomes much more expensive as occupancy approaches one. Key hashing itself is an additional cost, such as scanning characters in a long string.

C19-O3 · partial

Use dictionaries, sets, and frequency counts to distinguish lookup, membership, and multiplicity.

Membership/lookup are assessed; a new frequency-count solution is not required in these assignments, though Chapter 8 has one.

Explanation

1902_dictionaries_sets.ipynb · cells 5–22
Two departments submit product IDs for reconciliation. A set represents which IDs occur, regardless of how many times they were entered. A dictionary of counts represents how often each ID occurs. Choosing between them changes the information retained, not merely the syntax of the container.

Let the warehouse IDs be {A, B, C} and the sales IDs be {B, C, D}. Intersection gives IDs recognized by both: {B, C}. Warehouse minus sales gives {A}; sales minus warehouse gives {D}. The direction of difference matters. A union gives all recognized IDs {A, B, C, D}; it does not establish that either department's quantities agree.

| Question | Operation | Result for this example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which IDs are shared? | Intersection | B, C |
| Which warehouse IDs are absent from sales? | Warehouse minus sales | A |
| Which sales IDs are absent from warehouse? | Sales minus warehouse | D |
| Which IDs appear anywhere? | Union | A, B, C, D |

Now suppose sales submits B twice. A set still contains one B. That is correct for unique membership and wrong for a task that must detect repeated submissions. A frequency dictionary can increment B's count to two. State whether duplicates are errors, repeated events, or information to discard before building either representation.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

The set has two distinct statuses, and the counts are open three and closed two. The example prints keys in an explicit order; a hash collection's enumeration order is not a sorting contract. Sort keys separately when a report requires an order. Neither a set nor a dictionary supplies the priority-selection operation of a heap.

Explanation

1902_dictionaries_sets.ipynb · cells 8–18
If product IDs are case-insensitive under the business contract, B and b must use compatible equality in both collections. Normalizing only one side can produce false missing-ID reports. For hashed keys, equal keys must have equal hash codes under the selected policy. A good hash distribution improves performance but cannot repair inconsistent equality.

Do not mutate fields that determine a key's hash/equality while that key is stored. The entry may remain physically present in a bucket chosen by its old meaning while a new lookup examines another location. Immutable key data or remove/change/reinsert workflows make that boundary explicit.

Set-operation APIs also have mutation contracts. Some operations modify the receiving set; query-based forms may produce a sequence instead. If the original warehouse membership must remain available, work on a copy or choose a nonmutating approach deliberately. Assigning another variable to the same set object does not create independent storage.

Guided exercise: add B twice and lowercase a once to the sales input. Produce two answers: a unique-ID reconciliation under a stated case policy and a repeated-ID report. Explain which information a set has discarded and why the frequency report cannot be reconstructed from that set alone.


Keyed access and membership answer different questions. A dictionary maps an ID to a record. A set records whether an ID belongs to a group. Business reconciliation often needs set operations as well as individual lookups.

Use the same equality rule for all collections that participate in one calculation

C19-O5 · gap

Choose and coordinate collection indexes for a workload, test cancelled or updated entries, and explain consistency and operation costs.

The coordinated dictionary/queue cancellation and workload choice taught in 19.3 have no matching independent assessment; assignments stay with isolated map/set calls.

Explanation

1903_collection_selection.ipynb · cells 5–22
A dispatch system wants quick lookup by ticket ID and repeated service by priority. One collection may not efficiently supply both operations under the required policies. A dictionary can locate the current ticket by ID while a priority queue selects service candidates. Using two indexes introduces an obligation: their views must not cause cancelled or superseded work to be served.

One design permits stale queue entries and checks them when removed. The dictionary holds authoritative current state. A queue candidate is served only if its ID still exists and its version matches the current ticket. Cancellation removes or marks the authoritative record; old queue entries can be skipped later. Versioning matters when the same ID can be updated: mere presence is not proof that the old priority entry still describes the current work.

| Event | Authoritative lookup | Old queue entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Register ticket | Present with current version | Eligible when selected |
| Cancel ticket | Absent or explicitly cancelled | Skip |
| Change priority/version | Updated current version | Skip if its version is stale |

The alternative is to remove/update queue entries eagerly, which needs suitable index support and its own maintenance rules. Compare complete workflows rather than declaring either approach universally faster. Lazy cleanup simplifies some updates but can retain stale storage and make later removals perform extra work.

Guided trace: register ticket A, cancel A, register a new version of A, then remove an old queue candidate. Explain why matching only the ID can

Worked example/case/trace

1903_collection_selection.ipynb · cells 19–20
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

var active = new Dictionary<string, string>();
var registered = new HashSet<string>();
var pending = new PriorityQueue<string, (int Urgency, long Arrival)>();
long arrival = 0;
bool Register(string id, string owner, int urgency)
{
    if (!registered.Add(id)) return false;
    active.Add(id, owner);
    pending.Enqueue(id, (urgency, arrival++));
    return true;
}
Register("T-100", "Amina", 2);
Register("T-101", "Diego", 0);
Register("T-102", "Mina", 2);
Console.WriteLine($"duplicate accepted={Register("T-100", "Other", 0)}");
active.Remove("T-101");
while (pending.TryDequeue(out string? id, out _))
{
    if (!active.TryGetValue(id, out string? owner)) { Console.WriteLine($"skip cancelled {id}"); continue; }
    active.Remove(id);
    Console.WriteLine($"serve {id}: {owner}");
}
Console.WriteLine($"active={active.Count}, pending={pending.Count}");

The cancelled urgent ticket is skipped, then T-100 and T-102 are served in their arrival order. Immediately after cancellation, the dictionary has two entries but the queue still has three. Equal Counts are not the invariant. Every active record has one live pending entry, while pending may also contain inactive IDs.

Skipping one stale entry costs one heap removal. Across a batch, each enqueued entry is removed at most once, but a single request for the next active ticket may skip many cancelled entries. Cancellation also leaves queue storage occupied until cleanup. Analyze both the whole workload and an individual call; do not promise that lazy deletion makes e

2001_graph_vocabulary.ipynb · cells 4–25
```{index} graph; vertex; edge; isolated vertex
```

A graph consists of a set of **vertices** and a set of **edges** connecting them. A vertex models an item; an edge models a relationship. A facilities team might model rooms as vertices and direct passageways as edges. A dependency model might instead use tasks as vertices and prerequisite relationships as edges.

Keep the vertex set separate from the edge set. A room with no modeled passageways is still a vertex. Such an **isolated vertex** has degree zero. If you create vertices only while reading edges, you can silently lose isolated rooms, devices, or customers.

The following office-route model has six vertices and four undirected edges. Labels are symbolic identifiers, not measured physical locations. The diagram expresses the relationships, while the arrays store them.

```text
Lobby -- Hall -- Lab       Remote
          |
        Office -- Storage
```

The drawing is not a floor plan: line lengths do not represent distance, and a crossing in a drawing would not create a new vertex unless the model explicitly added one.

using System;
string[] rooms = { "Lobby", "Hall", "Lab", "Office", "Storage", "Remote" };
(string A, string B)[] edges =
{
    ("Lobby", "Hall"), ("Hall", "Lab"),
    ("Hall", "Office"), ("Office", "Storage")
};
Console.WriteLine($"vertices={rooms.Length}, edges={edges.Length}");
foreach (var (a, b) in edges) Console.WriteLine($"{a} <-> {b}");
Console.WriteLine("Remote is present even though no edge touches it.");

## Directed and Undirected Relationships




```{index} directed graph; undirected graph; arc; indegree; outdegree
```

An **undirected edge** represents a two-way relationship. One logical edge between Hall and Lab connects them in both directions. A **directed edge**, also called an arc, has a source and destination; Hall → Lab does not imply Lab → Hall.

Direction depends on the question. A prerequisite arrow from Programming I to Programming II means the first must precede the second. An import arrow might instead mean that the source file depends on the destination file. State the convention before interpreting incoming and outgoing edges.

For directed graphs, **outdegree** counts outgoing edges and **indegree** counts incoming edges. A workflow approval step can have several incoming prerequisites and one outgoing next step.

Compare adjacency matrices and adjacency collections in terms of storage, density, and required operations.

Worked matrix/density analysis exists, but no standard lab/homework asks students to compare storage and operation counts or construct another representation.

Explanation

2002_adjacency_representations.ipynb · cells 4–27
```{index} adjacency matrix; vertex index; symmetry
```

An adjacency matrix reserves one cell for each ordered pair of vertices. A row describes outgoing connections from its vertex; a column describes incoming connections to its vertex. Map symbolic labels to dense integer indexes before accessing the array.

For the six-room undirected graph, a Boolean matrix has 36 cells, although only eight are true. Four logical edges appear twice, once in each direction. Its diagonal is false because the model rejects self-loops. An isolated vertex still has a row and column, both empty.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

string[] rooms = { "Lobby", "Hall", "Lab", "Office", "Storage", "Remote" };
var index = rooms.Select((room, i) => (room, i)).ToDictionary(x => x.room, x => x.i);
bool[,] connected = new bool[rooms.Length, rooms.Length];
foreach (var (a, b) in new[] { ("Lobby", "Hall"), ("Hall", "Lab"), ("Hall", "Office"), ("Office", "Storage") })
{
    connected[index[a], index[b]] = true;
    connected[index[b], index[a]] = true;
}
foreach (string room in rooms)
{
    int row = index[room];
    Console.WriteLine($"{room}: {string.Join(" ", Enumerable.Range(0, rooms.Length).Select(col => connected[row, col] ? 1 : 0))}");
}

The Hall row is `1 0 1 1 0 0`; the Remote row is all zeros. In an undirected matrix, `[i, j]` equals `[j, i]`. A directed matrix need not be symmetric. Do not infer a reverse arc merely because an undirected example wrote both cells.

Once indexes are known, direct edge lookup reads one cell in O(1) time. Enumerating a vertex's

foreach (var (a, b) in new[] { ("Lobby", "Hall"), ("Hall", "Lab"), ("Hall", "Office"), ("Office", "Storage") })

    connected[index[b], index[a]] = true;
}
foreach (string room in rooms)

    int row = index[room];
    Console.WriteLine($"{room}: {string.Join(" ", Enumerable.Range(0, rooms.Length).Select(col => connected[row, col] ? 1 : 0))}");
}

The Hall row is `1 0 1 1 0 0`; the Remote row is all zeros. In an undirected matrix, `[i, j]` equals `[j, i]`. A directed matrix need not be symmetric. Do not infer a reverse arc merely because an undirected example wrote both cells.

Once indexes are known, direct edge lookup reads one cell in O(1) time. Enumerating a vertex's neighbors scans its entire row, Θ(V) time. Adding or removing vertices in a tightly sized matrix can require a new array and remapping many indexes. Keeping spare capacity or inactive indexes changes that tradeoff and needs its own policy.

2003_graph_traversal.ipynb · cells 5–24
A facilities graph answers which rooms can be reached and how many doorways a shortest route uses. Every edge in this lesson contributes one hop. The queue is not a list of completed rooms; it holds discovered rooms whose neighbors still need examination. This is the queue policy from Chapter 15 applied to the graph model from the preceding sections.

Use directed edges A→B, A→C, B→D and C→D, plus an isolated E. Neighbor order is written explicitly. Begin with A discovered, distance zero and no predecessor. The small program exposes the traversal core; the full graph class and validation examples remain below.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
var next = new Dictionary<string, string[]>
{
    ["A"] = new[] { "B", "C" }, ["B"] = new[] { "D" },
    ["C"] = new[] { "D" }, ["D"] = Array.Empty<string>(), ["E"] = Array.Empty<string>()
};
var distance = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["A"] = 0 };
var previous = new Dictionary<string, string>();
var waiting = new Queue<string>();
waiting.Enqueue("A");
while (waiting.Count > 0)
{
    string current = waiting.Dequeue();
    foreach (string neighbor in next[current])
    {
        if (distance.ContainsKey(neighbor)) continue;
        distance[neighbor] = distance[current] + 1;
        previous[neighbor] = current;
        waiting.Enqueue(neighbor);
        Console.WriteLine($"Discover {neighbor}: distance {distance[neighbor]}, from {current}");
    }
}
Console.WriteLine($"D hops: {distance["D"]}; E reached: {distance.ContainsKey("E")}");

## Guide the Route and Tie-Policy Checks


Fill this reverse chain before writing code:

| Current room | Recorded predecessor | Reverse route so far |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D | B | D |
| B | A | D,B |
| A | None; this is the source | D,B,A |

Guided task: change A's neighbors to C,B. Predict the new predecessor of D and the hop count. Then add D→A and check how many times A and D are discovered. Finally, ask for E and specify the result without indexing a missing map entry.

```{dropdown} Check the graph reasoning
D's predecessor becomes C, giving A→C→D, but its distance stays two. The cycle cannot rediscover A because A is already in the distance map. A and D are each discovered once. E is a known but unreachable vertex and has no route from A. Tie-dependent routes can differ while their minimum hop counts agree.
```

Trace DFS with explicit suspended frames and identify components only under the appropriate direction assumptions.

The assignments call supplied DFS/Components; they do not independently trace or implement suspended frames or component discovery.

Explanation

2004_depth_first_components.ipynb · cells 5–27
Depth-first search is ordinary recursive control flow applied to a graph. A call must remember which neighbor it is considering while a child explores its branch. This connects the suspended calls in Chapter 17 to Chapter 20's cycles and shared destinations. A discovered set avoids repeated discovery; it does not erase the caller's unfinished neighbor loop.

Use the undirected diamond A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, and isolated E. In each array below, the listed neighbor order determines the trace. Watch enter and exit events separately. A vertex is entered once; returning from a child resumes an already active parent rather than entering that parent again.


using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
var neighbors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>
{
    ["A"] = new[] { "B", "C" }, ["B"] = new[] { "A", "D" },
    ["C"] = new[] { "A", "D" }, ["D"] = new[] { "B", "C" }, ["E"] = Array.Empty<string>()
};
var seen = new HashSet<string>();
void Visit(string room, int depth)
{
    seen.Add(room);
    Console.WriteLine($"Enter {room} depth {depth}");
    foreach (string next in neighbors[room])
        if (!seen.Contains(next)) Visit(next, depth + 1);
    Console.WriteLine($"Exit {room}");
}
Visit("A", 0);
Console.WriteLine($"E reached: {seen.Contains("E")}");


C is first entered from D, not from A. A's neighbor loop has not finished, but C is already discovered by the time A resumes and considers it. C's DFS depth is three although A has a direct edge to C. A first DFS route therefore need not minimize hops.

| Event | Active frames from oldest to newest | What waits in the caller? |

Console.WriteLine($"E reached: {seen.Contains("E")}");


C is first entered from D, not from A. A's neighbor loop has not finished, but C is already discovered by the time A resumes and considers it. C's DFS depth is three although A has a direct edge to C. A first DFS route therefore need not minimize hops.

| Event | Active frames from oldest to newest | What waits in the caller? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enter A | A | A will consider C after B returns |
| Enter B | A,B | B will finish after D returns |
| Enter D | A,B,D | D will finish after C returns |
| Enter C | A,B,D,C | C finds no undiscovered neighbor |
| Exit C | A,B,D | D resumes its neighbor loop |
| Exit D | A,B | B resumes |
| Exit B | A | A sees that C is already discovered |
| Exit A | Empty | Source traversal is complete |

Do not use the number of discovered vertices as the current stack depth. Four vertices have been discovered after C exits, but only three calls remain active at that point. Likewise, a visited neighbor alone is not enough to classify a directed

## Costs and Contracts




```{index} Costs and Contracts
```


With adjacency lists and expected constant-time dictionary and set operations, a complete traversal takes O(V+E) time: each vertex is discovered once and each stored adjacency is examined once. An undirected edge is stored twice, which changes a constant factor. Visited state, predecessor state, and the queue or recursion stack require O(V) auxiliary space. Matrix traversal instead scans V potential neighbors per visited vertex and can take O(V²). Graph snapshots returned by Vertices and Neighbors protect the stored lists; the strings themselves are immutable. Unknown sources are rejected. The examples do not modify the graph during a search.

## Traversal Verification Contracts




```{index} graph traversal; verification
```


Verify a BFS result by checking that the source has distance zero, each reachable non-source has a predecessor one layer earlier, and every examined edge satisfies the layer bound. Check unreachable vertices separately. A shortest path in edge count need not minimize weighted cost; Chapter 24 supplies Dijkstra’s algorithm for nonnegative weights.

For DFS, check that each reached vertex enters and exits exactly once, every child interval is nested in its parent interval, and cycles do not cause repeated discovery. An explicit stack of suspended neighbor positions reproduces recursive order; a stack that pushes all neighbors at once may produce another order.

C01-P1 · Core conceptual review

Explain number representation and address-space assumptions

Existing conceptual coverage; no new curriculum gap inferred.

Explanation

0101_cs_ideas.ipynb · cells 23–23
A **binary**, or base-2, number uses the digits `0` and `1`. Each position has a value that is a power of two, just as decimal positions represent powers of ten. A byte contains eight bits, so it has `2^8 = 256` possible patterns, from `0000 0000` through `1111 1111`.

The ASCII code for uppercase `A` is decimal 65. Its eight-bit representation is `0100 0001`. Work from right to left to convert the pattern:

| Bit position | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Place value | 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1 |
| Bit in `0100 0001` | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

Only the 64 and 1 positions are set, so the value is `64 + 1 = 65`. The pattern is a number until an encoding gives it an interpretation. Under ASCII it denotes `A`; under another interpretation the same byte can represent the number 65. C# uses Unicode for text; the ASCII characters share the corresponding Unicode values. Chapter 2 connects `char` values with their numeric codes.

The number of bits also limits the number of distinct addresses. A hypothetical byte-addressed machine with 32 address bits has `2^32` distinct addresses, covering 4 GiB of byte locations. A 64-bit address has many more possible patterns. A real computer's usable memory also depends on its processor, operating system, and hardware configuration; a label such as “64-bit” does not promise that every theoretically possible address is available.

**Check Your Understanding:** Convert `0000 1101` to decimal, and explain why `0000 1101` and `0100 0001` can both fit in one byte.

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
`8 + 4 + 1 = 13`. Both patterns use eight bit positions. The number of available positions determines the byte's capacity; leading zeros still occupy positions.
```

Use Random and a repeatable simulation

Explanation

additional_practice.ipynb · cells 9–9
A simulation uses generated values to model possible outcomes. Create one `Random` object and reuse it throughout the experiment. For `low < high`, `r.Next(low, high)` includes `low` and excludes `high`, so `r.Next(0, 2)` can return only zero or one. Map zero to Heads and one to Tails.

First print one flip, then 10 flips. Count the two outcomes; the counts must add to the number of flips. Randomness does not guarantee equal counts in a short run. A seed makes a run repeatable in the same runtime environment; it does not make the outcomes alternate.

For Group Flips, print `total` outcomes, `groupSize` per line. The last line may be shorter. End the final nonempty line with exactly one newline. Require `total >= 0` and `groupSize > 0`. Test totals zero, one, an exact multiple, and a remainder. In Chapter 5, turn this into `GroupFlips(int total, int groupSize)` and give `Flip` a return value that the caller can count and print.

Worked example/case

additional_practice.ipynb · cells 13–13
using System;
Random r = new Random(17);
int total = 10, groupSize = 4, heads = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < total; i++)
{
    bool isHead = r.Next(0, 2) == 0;
    if (isHead) heads++;
    Console.Write(isHead ? "Heads" : "Tails");
    if ((i + 1) % groupSize == 0 || i + 1 == total) Console.WriteLine();
    else Console.Write(" ");
}
Console.WriteLine($"Heads: {heads}; Tails: {total - heads}; Total: {total}");

C09-P1 · Supporting reading

Use regex matching, extraction, and validation

Developed supporting lesson; no separate standard assessment. This does not make regex a missing core requirement.

Explanation

0906_regex.ipynb · cells 5–38
A product label consists of two uppercase ASCII letters, a hyphen and four digits. Before choosing regular-expression symbols, write accepted and rejected examples. AB-0042 fits; A-0042 has too few letters; AB-42 has too few digits; and a larger sentence containing AB-0042 is not itself one complete label. This last distinction separates finding a matching substring from validating an entire field.

For this deliberately narrow label, the pattern `\A[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}\z` uses beginning/end-of-input anchors, a range of letters repeated twice, a literal hyphen and four ASCII digits. It states shape, not whether AB is a known department. In a C# verbatim string literal the pattern can be written `@"\A[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}\z"`; ordinary C# string escaping and regex escaping are different layers. The @ belongs to the string literal form, not to the regex language.

| Pattern part | Meaning under this contract |
| --- | --- |
| \A | Beginning of the input |
| [A-Z]{2} | Exactly two letters from the stated ASCII range |
| - | The separator |
| [0-9]{4} | Exactly four ASCII digits |
| \z | End of the input |

A group such as `(?<number>[0-9]{4})` names a captured part. Extracting number as text retains leading zeros; converting it to an integer would answer a different question. Check whether a match succeeded before treating group contents as a valid field. A match object exists even when the match is unsuccessful, so object existence alone is not the success test.

Regex replacement also has a policy. Removing every nondigit character may produce a digit-only result while silently discarding an unexpected department or separator. Decide whether malformed input should be repaired, rejected or retained with a warning. A cleaning rule is not equivalent to a validation rule.

## Common Pattern Elements




| Pattern | Meaning | Example match |
|---------|---------|---------------|
| `\d` | any digit | `7`, `0` |
| `\w` | word character (letter, digit, `_`) | `a`, `Z`, `3` |
| `\s` | whitespace | space, tab |
| `.` | any character except newline | `x`, `!` |
| `^` | start of string | `^Hello` matches `Hello world` |
| `$` | end of string | `\.txt$` matches `file.txt` |
| `[abc]` | one of a, b, c | `[aeiou]` matches any vowel |
| `[A-Z]` | range | any uppercase letter |
| `+` | one or more | `\d+` matches `42` |
| `*` | zero or more | `\d*` matches `` or `99` |
| `?` | zero or one | `colou?r` matches `color` or `colour` |

Mask data and validate privacy-safe logging
