Explanation

0905_privacy_security.ipynb · cells 7–25
Privacy laws differ by place, but they share common ideas. Three examples:

- **GDPR** (EU Regulation 2016/679, applies from May 25, 2018) sets principles for processing personal data, including *purpose limitation* (use data only for the stated purpose), *data minimisation* (collect only what is needed), and *storage limitation* (do not keep it longer than needed).[^0905_privacy_security-gdpr]
- **CCPA** (California Consumer Privacy Act, in effect since January 1, 2020, and expanded by the CPRA from January 1, 2023) gives California residents rights to know about, delete, and opt out of the sale of their personal information.[^0905_privacy_security-ccpa]
- **FERPA** (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974) protects the privacy of student education records in the United States, including your grades in this course.[^0905_privacy_security-ferpa]

You do not need to be a lawyer to follow the habits these laws have in common: **collect less, show less, and keep less.**

## Show Less: Masking



Many screens and documents need only enough of a value to recognize it. A support agent confirming an account needs to see `a***@example.com`, not the full address. Masking uses the string methods from {ref}`string-methods`:

using System;

// Show enough to recognize the address, hide the rest.
static string MaskEmail(string email)
{
    int at = email.IndexOf('@');
    if (at < 1)
    {
        return "(invalid email)";
    }
    return email.Substring(0, 1) + "***" + email.Substring(at);
}

Console.WriteLine(MaskEmail("ana.diaz@example.com"));   // a***@example.com
Console.WriteLine(MaskEmail("@example.com"));           // (invalid email)

Receipts and order confirmations conventionally show only the last four digits of a card:

using System;

// Receipts and support screens need only the last four digits of a card.
static string MaskCard(string cardNumber)
{
    string digits = cardNumber.Replace(" ", "").Replace("-", "");
    if (digits.Length < 4)
    {
        return "(invalid card number)";
    }
    return "**** **** **** " + digits.Substring(digits.Length - 4);
}

Console.WriteLine(MaskCard("4111 1111 1111 1234"));   // **** **** **** 1234
Console.WriteLine(MaskCard("12"));                    // (invalid card number)

Masking is for display. A program that does not need a value at all should not collect or store it in the first place.

## Tuples: When a Class Is Too Much



A class bundles data with the behavior that belongs to it. Sometimes a program only needs to keep two or three values together for a moment, such as a product code and its price, or the lowest and highest sales day of a week. A **tuple** groups a few values into one value without declaring a class.[^1001_class_syntax-tuple-types]

```csharp
(Type1 Name1, Type2 Name2) variableName = (value1, value2);
```

```{index} tuple; creating
```



```{index} Creating Tuples
```

### Creating Tuples



Tuple fields can be unnamed or named. Unnamed fields are read as `Item1`, `Item2`, and so on. Named fields make the code say what each value means, so prefer them.

using System;

// Unnamed fields: read them as Item1 and Item2
var item = ("SKU-1042", 19.99m);
Console.WriteLine($"{item.Item1} costs ${item.Item2:F2}");

// Named fields: much clearer
var product = (Sku: "SKU-1042", Price: 19.99m);
Console.WriteLine($"{product.Sku} costs ${product.Price:F2}");

{

    foreach (decimal sales in dailySales)
    {
        if (sales < low) low = sales;
        if (sales > high) high = sales;
    }
    return (low, high);
}

### Returning Multiple Values



A method returns one value. Before tuples, returning two results required `out` parameters or a small class written just for that purpose. A tuple return type lets one method report both the lowest and the highest sales day:

using System;

static (decimal Low, decimal High) SalesRange(decimal[] dailySales)
{

```{index} tuple; destructuring, discard
```




### Destructuring



**Destructuring** unpacks a tuple into separate variables in one statement. Use the discard `_` for a value you do not need.

using System;

static (decimal Low, decimal High) SalesRange(decimal[] dailySales)
{
    decimal low = dailySales[0], high = dailySales[0];
    foreach (decimal sales in dailySales)
    {
        if (sales < low) low = sales;
        if (sales > high) high = sales;
    }
    return (low, high);
}

// Unpack both values into separate variables in one statement
var (low, high) = SalesRange(new[] { 1250.00m, 980.50m, 1610.25m });

This array form is sufficient for the exercise; modern C# supports additional params collection forms.[^params]

using System;
SumOverloads math = new SumOverloads();
Console.WriteLine(math.Sum(2, 3)); Console.WriteLine(math.Sum(2, 3, 4));
SumManyArgs many = new SumManyArgs();
Console.WriteLine(many.Sum()); Console.WriteLine(many.Sum(7));
Console.WriteLine(many.Sum(2, 3, 4)); Console.WriteLine(many.Sum(new int[] {5, -2, 1}));
class SumOverloads {
    public int Sum(int a, int b) { return checked(a + b); }
    public int Sum(int a, int b, int c) { return checked(a + b + c); }
}
class SumManyArgs {
    public int Sum(params int[] values) {
        int total = 0; foreach (int value in values) total = checked(total + value); return total;
    }
}

C11-P1 · Supporting reading

Distinguish nullable data and runtime guards; use null operators

Required-value guards are assessed in the core model. Deeper nullable-flow and operator tasks remain section practice, not a separately assessed core outcome.

Explanation

1104_nullability.ipynb · cells 6–30
An unrecorded score, a recorded zero and an empty label are different states. Replacing every missing value with zero may make a screen easy to print while making its calculation wrong. Connect nullability to Chapter 11's object contracts: choose what may be absent, what absence means, and where a required value is enforced.

For a value type, the schematic declaration `ValueType? name = null;` creates a nullable value that can hold either an ordinary value or no value. `int?` is shorthand for Nullable<int>. Read `HasValue` before an explicit `.Value` access; accessing Value when HasValue is false throws. `GetValueOrDefault()` supplies the type's default, which may erase the distinction your business rule needs.

For a reference type, `string?` annotates a reference that may be null. Under nullable analysis, `string` expresses an intended non-null contract to the compiler. These annotations guide warnings; they do not install runtime validation. Required constructor input still needs a guard, and the null-forgiving `!` operator only suppresses a warning.


using System;
#nullable enable
static string Describe(int? score)
{
    if (!score.HasValue) return "Not recorded";
    return $"Recorded {score.Value}";
}
Console.WriteLine(Describe(null));
Console.WriteLine(Describe(0));
string? absent = null;
string empty = "";
Console.WriteLine($"Absent: {absent is null}; empty length: {empty.Length}");
Console.WriteLine($"Absent length: {absent?.Length ?? -1}");


The output preserves absence separately from zero. Empty is a real string object with Length zero; absent has no object whose Length can be read. `absent?.Length` produces a nullable length, and `?? -1` supplies a display fallback only when that result is missing.

| Expression or policy | Missing reference | Empty stri

Worked example/case

1104_nullability.ipynb · cells 7–27
using System;
#nullable enable
static string Describe(int? score)
{
    if (!score.HasValue) return "Not recorded";
    return $"Recorded {score.Value}";
}
Console.WriteLine(Describe(null));
Console.WriteLine(Describe(0));
string? absent = null;
string empty = "";
Console.WriteLine($"Absent: {absent is null}; empty length: {empty.Length}");
Console.WriteLine($"Absent length: {absent?.Length ?? -1}");


The output preserves absence separately from zero. Empty is a real string object with Length zero; absent has no object whose Length can be read. `absent?.Length` produces a nullable length, and `?? -1` supplies a display fallback only when that result is missing.

| Expression or policy | Missing reference | Empty string | Nonempty string |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `text?.Length` | null | 0 | Actual length |
| `text?.Length ?? -1` | -1 | 0 | Actual length |
| `text ?? "Unknown"` | Unknown | Empty string retained | Original text |

Read `?.` as conditional access, not a request to manufacture a default object. In `order?.ShippingAddress?.City ?? "Unknown"`, a missing order or address stops that access chain, then the final fallback provides a display value. An empty City is retained because empty is not null. If blank cities are also unacceptable, validate that separately.

## Reading Short Expressions and Queries




```{index} Reading Short Expressions and Queries
```


Later collection examples sometimes use compact C# forms. The expression x => x > 0 is a lambda: a function receiving x and returning the comparison result. A library method can call that function for each value. Where filters values, Select transforms them, OrderBy orders them, and ToArray materializes a separate array. These LINQ extension methods require using System.Linq. Prefer an explicit loop when it makes the algorithm or mutation clearer. Query pipelines can defer work until enumeration; ToArray executes the pipeline now.


using System.Collections.Generic;
using System;
using System.Linq;
int[] arrivals = { 30, -1, 10, 20 };
int[] report = arrivals.Where(value => value >= 0).OrderBy(value => value).Select(value => value * 2).ToArray();
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", report));
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", arrivals));


An expression-bodied member such as public int Count => items.Count; is shorthand for a getter returning that expression. A target-typed new() uses the declared variable type, so List<int> values = new(); constructs a List<int>. Neither abbreviation changes the data-structure contract. Named classes and explicit constructors remain useful while learning a new model.
